The Sūtra says: "Transcending all meditative absorptions, maintaining mindfulness before one, he opens the gate of wisdom and skillfully cultivates expedient means."
The commentary states:
These Bodhisattvas, from the eighth stage upward, double their progress in every thought-moment and surpass the Two Vehicles; thus it is called "transcending.
Because they are constantly in meditative concentration, it is called "binding mindfulness to the present."
To propagate and exalt the teachings of the Dharma is called "opening and revealing the gate of wisdom.

Thus, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "The gate of its wisdom is named the profound Āgama; its definitive discernment and harmonious integration is named the skillful cultivation of expedient means (*upāya*)."
Furthermore, one skillfully cultivates the power of expedient means, vows, and so forth, or else fully cultivates the twelve types of skillful means.
The meaning of this scriptural passage is that by purely upholding [the teachings] for immeasurable kalpas, one simultaneously masters all the perfections (pāramitās).
The brief chapter on the six perfections is as found in the original *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*.
Regarding the sūtra’s passage, “He sports with mastery in subtle supernatural powers,” the commentary says:

The fourth virtue: According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the sons of the Buddha possess ten kinds of playful supernatural powers (*vikrīḍita-abhijñā*), namely: first, manifesting the relinquishment of celestial lifespan; second, manifesting birth; third, manifesting as a youth; fourth, manifesting renunciation of the world; fifth, delighting in ascetic practices; sixth, proceeding toward the Bodhi tree; seventh, manifesting the subduing of Māra; eighth, manifesting delight in tranquility and attaining unsurpassed enlightenment; ninth, turning the wheel of Dharma; and tenth, entering parinirvāṇa.
The intention behind manifesting these various signs is to benefit sentient beings, as explained at length in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "Assembly of the Most Victorious Heavenly King.
The sūtra states: "He attains dhāraṇī and possesses inexhaustible eloquence."
The commentary says:
This is the fifth virtue.
"Dai" (逮) means to reach or arrive at.
They attain the four dhāraṇīs and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), all of which are inexhaustible.
It is not merely that these seven are uninterrupted; because they are supreme, because they are inexhaustible, and because their benefit for others never ceases, they are all inexhaustible.
Sūtra: All afflictions and defilements are severed and utterly extinguished. Commentary:
This is the sixth virtue.
The three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are, in their respective order, afflictions, accumulations, and defilements;

alternatively, "affliction" and "accumulation" refer to the seeds and manifest states, while "defilement" refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) along with the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as these are spoken of under the same name because they coexist with the afflictions.
Since they are already on the verge of being severed, it can be said that "all" [afflictions] are attained [as such].
Sūtra: "Before long, they shall realize all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Commentary:
Seventh is the virtue of continuing the Buddha’s lineage without interruption.
These bodhisattvas, having transcended the previous two kalpas or dwelling in the Cloud of Dharma stage, are all but one birth away from buddhahood and are thus called "not long."
Since bodhi is yet to be attained, it is said that "one shall achieve it.
Attaining *samyak-saṃprajñā* is called "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Aspect" (*ākāra*) refers to categories; whether they be emptiness or existence, principle or phenomena, these are termed "all aspects."
To have attained mastery in all these is called "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. "All aspects" refers here to the term for the objects [of cognition].
Sūtra: Having subdued the hosts of Māra’s army, he strikes the Dharma drum.
The commentary states:
Eighth, the virtue of subduing the enmity of Māra.
The "Māra" refers to the four Māras, and the "army" refers to the ten armies, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Destroying Māra" in the *Fayuan*.
When the army of Māra was converted, he who had triumphed over the enemy gave the first signal.
Revealing the ultimate truth and opening the provisional means, it serves as the beating of the Dharma drum.
The Sūtra restrains all heterodox paths, causing them to give rise to a pure mind.
The Commentary says:
Ninth, he crushes the doctrines of all non-Buddhists.
Possessing the four fearlessnesses, he subdues the various non-Buddhists so that they may give rise to right faith and arouse pure minds.
Through the sutras, he turns the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of devas and humans.
The commentary states:
Tenth, the virtue of continuing the Buddha’s proclamation.
Within the five stages, such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), one transforms four of those stages.
Second is the wheel of non-retrogression, as explained in the original *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
The sutra says: "The Buddha-lands of the ten directions are all already adorned.
The commentary states:
Eleventh is the virtue of purifying the Buddha-field.
It closes the gates to all evil realms.
The meaning of "purifying the field" is as explained in the original *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*.
Sūtra: No sentient beings within the six realms of existence fail to receive benefit.
Commentary: Twelfth, the virtue of non-futile altruism.
In Sanskrit it is called *tiryag-yoni*, which is translated here as "animals" (*pāngshēng*).
In Sanskrit it is called *preta*, translated as "hungry ghosts" (*èguǐ*), also known as *vighna*.
In Sanskrit it is called *manuṣya*, which is translated as "human.
Regarding the names of the three destinies—devas, asuras, and *naraka*—as well as the meaning of the six destinies, they are as explained in the original *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).

He thoroughly understands the dispositions of sentient beings and manifests his body within the five realms of existence; through the power of skillful means, he manifests various forms and preaches the Dharma, so that all who see or hear him receive benefit.

Because one is able to accomplish four kinds of dharmas, one can transform sentient beings so that they all receive benefit. Thus, the first chapter of the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra* states: "First, constantly seeking to bring benefit and peace to sentient beings; second, personally relinquishing one's own pleasure; third, harmony of mind and patience; and fourth, the elimination of arrogance."
Sūtra: Having accomplished great wisdom, he is endowed with patience.
Commentary: Thirteenth, self-benefit through the perfection of the virtue of patience.
The perfection of wisdom brings about self-benefit; the great patience possesses three aspects.
Because they are associated with those seven "great" qualities, they are all termed "great.
Alternatively, great wisdom is itself the nature of the greatness of wisdom, as it fully understands the two types of emptiness.

However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the "Section on the Compendium of Synonyms" (*Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī*), states: "One of great wisdom is called 'of great wisdom' because they have practiced for immeasurable kalpas.
This refers to the "greatness of time" among the seven types of greatness; thus, we know that patience is called "great" for the same reason it is called "wisdom."
Another explanation states:

as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle six, says, "One who has accomplished great patience is so named because of the increase of these two: equanimity-patience (*samaropa-kṣānti*) and dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*)."
"Endowed with" means "accomplished.
There are many further instances [of this usage].
Alternatively, it may mean that this is an accomplishment, namely, that attaining a superior grade is designated as "Great Patience" (mahākṣānti).
Therefore, that treatise’s commentary states:
"The increase of these two types of patience is called 'great patience' (mahākṣānti).
Furthermore, it is explained:

What is now called "being fully endowed" refers to being endowed with the three types of patience (*kṣānti*): namely, the patience of enduring enmity and harm (*āghāta-kṣānti*), the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkha-adhivāsana-kṣānti*), and the patience of discerning the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, according to the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra*, it is precisely by being fully endowed with great patience that one is able to accomplish great wisdom.

That sutra states: "Cultivating the four kinds of patience and being fully endowed with wisdom: first, enduring the abuse of others when seeking the Dharma; second, not avoiding cold, heat, wind, rain, and so forth; third, following the conduct of one's preceptor and ācārya; and fourth, enduring emptiness and signlessness when seeking the Dharma."
According to this principle, one should explain the reason for the aforementioned "Great Wisdom" based on what follows.
The Sūtra says: "Abiding in a mind of great compassion, he possesses great and firm power.
The Commentary states:
It constantly gathers in the virtues of sentient beings.
Thus, the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra* states: "The skillful means for gathering in sentient beings is, as the sūtra says, cultivating the body with loving-kindness."

Since loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness upon those who lack it, and compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering from those who possess it, one is thus able to gather in and sustain sentient beings.

Both are termed "Great" because they differ from the vehicles of the two [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha]; for among the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*), this is not merely "great compassion," as that term is applied exclusively to the Buddha to signify its uniqueness.

Regarding "possessing great, firm, and steadfast power": to constantly practice without abandoning [the path] is called "steadfastness. Thus, the first chapter of the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which they make their mind steadfast and do not grow weary:

first, giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings; second, being diligent and untiring; third, having faith and understanding that birth and death are like a dream; and fourth, correctly contemplating the wisdom of the Buddha."

This intention arises from diligent and tireless effort out of compassion for sentient beings; seeing the suffering of birth and death as unreal, like a dream, and seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, they practice loving-kindness and compassion with a firm mind.
Sūtra: Having served various Buddhas, one does not enter parinirvāṇa.
Commentary: This praises the virtue of attending the Buddhas without passing into extinction.
One constantly cultivates correct practice toward all Buddhas; this is called serving successive Buddhas because one never ceases the effort to deliver sentient beings and does not seek parinirvāṇa.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states: "Because of not ceasing to benefit others. The Sūtra says:
"One gives rise to the mind of great vows to reach the end of the future.
The Commentary says:
With boundless virtue through great vows,
he has made the Four Great Vows, capable of extending to the end of the future.
In this sutra, he has extensively planted pure causes at the Buddha’s place.
The commentary states:
"Deeply planting the roots of virtue" refers to what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and other texts say: "Planting the foundations of all virtues in the presence of the Buddhas."
To cultivate the ten offerings before the Buddha is called the "pure cause.
Both that which is sought—bodhi—and that which is cultivated—the ten offerings—are causes; they are either the cause of purity, or the cause itself is purity.
Sūtra: Having awakened to the non-arising of phenomena throughout the three periods of time, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Commentary: This refers to the virtue of realizing that all phenomena are without arising.

One awakens to the three kinds of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). By relying on the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), one contemplates the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and awakens to the patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature;

by relying on the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), one contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and awakens to the patience regarding the non-arising of spontaneity.

By relying on the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), one contemplates the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions and suffering (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Question:

Since the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent in essence and the perfected nature is eternally abiding, how can this scriptural passage—which speaks of "dharmas of the three periods of time"—be said to mean that by contemplating the three natures one attains the three types of patience?

Answer: When one observes the non-existence of the two selves within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is also present within that very dependent nature, for they are neither identical nor separate.
Thus, the verse in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "The false imagination exists; herein both [selves] are entirely absent; herein there is only emptiness."

This mind possesses false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); upon this [mind], both types of self are entirely absent, and within this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is only true emptiness.
Therefore, the "three times" are mentioned merely to illustrate the dependent nature and thereby reveal the other two natures.
Sūtra: It transcends the sphere of activity of the two vehicles.
Commentary: This is the virtue of the uncommon objective condition.
The cognitive objects and modes of activity of the two vehicles can be apprehended;

it is not so for the Bodhisattva. Therefore, the eighth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Non-conceptual wisdom operates in a manner that accords with the object of True Suchness."
This mind is suchness, devoid of all characteristics; wisdom that accords with suchness likewise lacks any active mental image (*ākāra*).
Furthermore, while [the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] realize both types of emptiness, he realizes only one; therefore, he surpasses the two vehicles.
Sūtra: By means of great skillful means, he transforms the world.
Commentary: This praises his virtue of skillfully transforming sentient beings.

Relying upon the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the twelve kinds of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), he transforms the world through the six external perfections; alternatively, relying upon the Mahāyāna, he transforms the world by teaching the various skillful dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*).
Because it simplifies the Hīnayāna, it is called "great skillfulness.
Sūtra: "One is able to expound upon the teachings of the Great Master. Commentary:
Regarding the virtue of propagating the holy teachings:

because he is able to rely upon the method of explanation found in the eighty-first chapter, the "Section on Compendium of Exegesis" (*Vyākhyāsaṃgraha*), of that *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is said that he is "able to expound the Master’s teachings."
Having attained the dhāraṇīs and the four supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), they are thus able to expound them; for they dwell on the stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
They have fully realized the secret Dharma and the profound emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and no longer harbor any doubt.
The commentary states:
"To realize the Dharma without doubt is the virtue.
"Secret" refers to the four secrets.
That is to say, the three kinds of emptiness are termed "profound.
This is as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*.
There are five kinds of profundity in the wisdom of all Buddhas; because the nature of wisdom is itself also called "wisdom," it is profound.

First, the meaning is profound; second, its essence; third, internal realization; fourth, its basis; and fifth, its unsurpassed nature. It is called "profound" because it is not the domain of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) can comprehend it, and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) knows it; as doubts regarding phenomena and principles are exhausted, there is no further delusion.

The sūtra lists their names as follows: the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Constantly Arousing the Mind to Turn the Wheel of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence, and the Bodhisattva Non-Cessation.
The commentary states:
Third, the enumeration of names.
There are fifty-three.
Their virtue is vast and their renown high; those who see or hear them obtain benefit that cannot be fully enumerated, though I have briefly cited this much.
Their names were established therein, either derived from their original vows or from their virtuous conduct, being named according to the benefits for themselves and others.
The first two [aspects] refer to preaching the Dharma, and the latter two to diligent application.

These pairs—preaching the Dharma and diligent cultivation—are both capable of subduing the four types of Māras. Therefore, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is without obstruction; because one attains the state of non-retrogression in preaching, it is called the "non-retrogressive wheel," and thus there is no hindrance.
The propagation of the Dharma is ceaseless because of compassionate concern for sentient beings.
He constantly arouses the mind to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of others, having attained the non-retrogressive eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).

Because he has attained uninterrupted eloquence and analytical skill, he constantly arouses the mind to turn the Dharma; his self-benefit is ever-diligent, and thus he is called "Ever-Diligent" (*sadā-vīrya*).
Because one constantly exerts oneself for the benefit of others, it is called "unresting.
Alternatively, this refers to the contrast between the benefit of others and self-benefit.
[The Sūtra mentions] the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The commentary states:
Maitreya; in the Sanskrit language, *Maitreya*, which here is translated as "Compassionate One" (*Cishi*), or alternatively as "Na.
This refers to one born into the clan of Maitra, or one whose innate nature practices compassion.
Some call her Eṇī; this is a feminine term used because a mother harbors compassion.
Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Auspiciousness. Avalokiteśvara means "Observing Sovereignty."

Of these three, the first pair consists of bestowing bliss and extracting suffering: Śrī (Auspiciousness) bestows bliss, and Avalokiteśvara extracts suffering; thus they correspond to bestowing bliss and extracting suffering.
[The sūtra mentions] the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāvyūharāja.
The commentary states:
In the ninth stage, one is able to abandon two delusions and become fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges; therefore, one attains mastery over dhāraṇīs.
Being fully endowed with the seven types of eloquence and constantly acting for the sake of the Mahāyāna, this is called the "Adornment of Great Eloquence."
The Sūtra on the Pair of Bodhisattvas Upholding and Expounding the Dharma:
Bodhisattva King of Mount Sumeru and Bodhisattva King of the Deep Great Ocean.
The eulogy says:
His wisdom is difficult to look up to, like the King of Mountains, Sumeru; his meditative concentration is unfathomable, like the great ocean.
Wisdom and concentration are both sovereign, comparable to a king; wisdom is lofty while concentration is profound.
Sūtra: [The assembly includes] Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, Mahāratnaketu Bodhisattva, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, and Gaganagañja Bodhisattva.
The eulogy states:

"To realize the excellence of existence is like a jewel banner (Ratnaketu); to realize the excellence of emptiness is named the Great Jewel Banner (Mahāratnaketu). These two constitute the pair of realizing existence and realizing emptiness."
Great Compassion bears the burden of the entire world as its treasury; it is able to take empty space itself as a precious storehouse. This is the Sūtra of Great Compassion and Great Wisdom.
[It was addressed by] the Bodhisattva Jewel-Hand Sovereignty, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Joyful Power, and the Bodhisattva Great Dharma Power.
The commentary states:
This consists of two pairs.
His hands produce precious jewels, which are able to destroy poverty.
The hand of wisdom can destroy the two obscurations of both self and others; thus he is named Vajrapāṇi.
He relieves poverty and shatters obstacles;
his joyful intention is ever-acting and difficult to bend, hence he is called Pramuditabala.

The Dharma-gift of the Mahāyāna can subdue the obscurations of others, such as ignorance, or eliminate various obscurations by relying on the Dharma oneself; therefore, it is called "great Dharma-power.
It is difficult for opponents to overcome or defeat.
Sūtra: The Bodhisattva Great Adornment Light and the Bodhisattva Great Golden Light Adornment.
The commentary states:
Because he adorns himself with the light of great wisdom and meditative concentration, he is named Great Adornment Light.
Because it benefits all beings through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, it is called the "Great Golden Light Adornment.
It is termed "Great" because it distinguishes itself by encompassing both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
The *Svayambhū-purāṇa* (The Scripture on Adorning Oneself and Others).
Translated by the Bodhisattvas Viśuddha-śīla, Nitya-samādhi, and Suviśuddhamati.
The eulogy states:
These three causes for the three trainings are each fully perfected.
In reality, they are cultivated simultaneously; this is explained according to their original vows.
They correspond to great merit and great wisdom.
Virtue, merit, wisdom, and knowledge consist of two types: meditative concentration and supernormal powers.
Alternatively, they proceed from knowledge, because they are able to give rise to knowledge.
Sūtra: The Bodhisattva Firm and Resolute Diligence, the Bodhisattva Mind Like Space, and the Bodhisattva Uninterrupted Great Vow.
The commentary states:
To exert diligence through the three types of refinement without retreat is called "firm and steadfast vigor.
Its mind is unimpeded like space.
Not abandoning the four great vows is called the uninterrupted great vow.
Non-retrogression is the constant cultivation of the antidotes.
Like space, it pervades both.
Sūtra: [The Bodhisattvas] Bestower of Medicine, Healer of All Afflictions, and King of Physicians.
The Commentary says:
The Bestower of Medicine cures physical illnesses; the Healer of Afflictions removes mental maladies; the King of Physicians possesses the means to eliminate both.
The Sūtra on Healing the Body and Healing the Mind through Contemplation.
Praised by the Bodhisattva Joyful High King and the Bodhisattva Who Has Attained the Prediction of Supreme Bestowal. It says:
If one sees sentient beings smiling, one first speaks to them so as to inspire joy; thus attaining mastery, one is named "High King.
Abiding in the position of consecration, one receives the supreme prediction of enlightenment.
He entered into self-entry and correspondence.

The sūtra states: the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Pure Light, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Upholder of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Renowned Joy, and the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Manifesting Boundless Fame.
The commentary states:
The Great Dharma is a cloud of wisdom that contains the rain of manifold virtues; thus it is named "Great Cloud. The others are all to be understood accordingly.

Wisdom can remove the darkness of defilement, hence it is named "Pure Light. Its grasping of various merits is named "Upholding the Dharma. Thus, the removal of darkness and the upholding of the Dharma form a pair.
His excellent reputation spreads far and wide, and all who hear it rejoice.
"Rejoice" (lè) is pronounced with the fifth tone (xiào).
His name pervades the ten directions, which is called manifesting boundless renown.
The Sūtra on the Joyful Hearing of the Distant Sound,
translated by Da-yun Shi-zi-hou Pusa, Da-yun Niu-wang-hou Pusa, Da-yun Ji-xiang Pusa, and Da-yun Bao-de Pusa.
The commentary states:

That which is decisive in its action is called the "Great Lion’s Roar," and that which can crush enemies is called the "Roar of the Great Cloud-Bull King. These two superior [roars] are capable of acting upon and subduing their adversaries.
Capable of producing great benefit and merit, he is named Śrī; naturally adorned with wholesome dharmas, he is named Ratnaguṇa. He is the counterpart who brings benefit to both others and himself.
[The Sūtra mentions] the Bodhisattvas Mahāmeghasūryagarbha, Mahāmeghacandragarbha, Mahāmeghajyotiṣprabha, and Mahāmeghāgniprabha.
The commentary states:
It destroys the darkness of unwholesomeness like the sun; it can bring about peace and happiness like the moon—these are the pairs of "destruction" and "realization.
Its various illuminations are like the stars; its fulfillment according to circumstances is like the light of a fire—these are the pairs of "illumination" and "fulfillment."
Sūtra: The Bodhisattvas Great Cloud Lightning-Radiance and Great Cloud Thunder-Sound.
The eulogy says:

"In the night of birth and death, they are able to provide illumination; showing the correct path is named 'Lightning-Radiance. Their preaching of the Dharma is startling and beneficial like the sound of thunder; showing the path and startling awakening is the 'Thunder-Sound' counterpart."
Sūtra: The Bodhisattva Great Cloud Wisdom-Rain Pervasive and the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Pure Rain King.
The commentary states:
The Dharma that can generate wisdom is called "wisdom-rain"; the Dharma that can eliminate hindrances is called "pure rain."
Because they possess majestic power, they are like rain; because there is nothing that is not beneficial, they are all-pervasive.
This is the section on the arising of the wholesome and the cessation of the unwholesome.
From the *Sūtra*: the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Flower-Tree King, the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Blue Lotus Fragrance, and the Bodhisattva Great Cloud Jewel Sandalwood Fragrance Cool Body.
The commentary states:
Because his causal practices are already perfected and he is about to attain the fruit of enlightenment, he is named King of the Flowering Tree.
Because he can unfold sublime principles to open the eyes of sentient beings and his merit is renowned afar, he is named Fragrance of the Blue Lotus.
One attains the pure Dharma-body, endowed with the fivefold fragrance known as precious sandalwood incense.
With this cool and refreshing body, one abides on the stage of the Dharma-cloud (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), wherein all merits are attained to fill the Dharma-body.
This is a correspondence between causes and present fruits.
The first two are the causes, because one obtains the fruit by means of the flower;
the latter one is the fruit, as it is called the "cool body."
Sūtra: [The Bodhisattvas] Great Cloud Dispelling Darkness and Great Cloud Breaking Obscuration. Commentary:

One who can destroy the darkness of ignorance is named "Dispelling Darkness"; one who can destroy the two types of grasping is named "Breaking Obscuration. These names correspond to the destruction of darkness and the removal of grasping, respectively.
The Sūtra.
Thus, this immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas praised [the Buddha], saying:
In summary:

At the time of late afternoon, they each arose from their meditative absorption, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The commentary states:
There are four sections in the text concerning the approach to the Buddha, as previously distinguished.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there were five hundred and eighty million Licchavi youths."
The commentary states:
The third section is divided into four parts; this [initial part] identifies the category and enumerates the number.
Formerly called Licchavi or Licchubhi, it is now called Licchavī. Some say they are of royal lineage, while others say they are of Brahmin descent.
According to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Vimalakīrti refers to "five hundred sons of elders" (*gṛhapati-putra*) and does not mention them as being of royal lineage.
Alternatively, those of royal lineage may also be called elders, as in the case of the elder Jīvaka.
The Sūtra lists their names as follows: the youth Siṃhaprabha, the youth Siṃhamati, and the youth Dharmadatta.
The commentary states:
Second, the enumeration of names has two parts.
There is an initial enumeration and a final conclusion.
There is the light of definitive knowledge and there is definitive wisdom, which can bestow the True Dharma upon all sentient beings; these correspond respectively to the three [categories].
Sūtra: Bestowed by the youths Indradata, Mahāprabha, Mahācaṇḍa, Buddhārakṣita, Dharmārakṣita, and Saṃghārakṣita.
The commentary states:
He requested [the teachings] from the Heavenly Emperor, and what was bestowed by the Emperor is called "Indra-bestowed" (*Indra-datta*).

Because he is able to shatter the darkness of himself and others with the fire of wisdom, he is named "Fire-Light" (*Jyotiṣprabha*). Because he cultivates the path with courageous decisiveness, he is named "Greatly Fierce" (*Mahātejas*).
The mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is called "Buddha-protection" and so forth.
From the *Sūtra*: the youth Vajrapāla, the youth Gaganapāla, the youth Gaganagarjita, the youth Ratnagarbha, and the youth Śrīgarbhakusuma.
The commentary says:
As the names suggest, these individuals are the leaders as described in the sutra. Thus it is said: "With such persons as their leaders."
The commentary says:
This concludes the sutra. All have come to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi, possessing deep faith and joy within the Mahāyāna.
The commentary says:
This is a praise of his virtues.
From the stage of non-retrogression up to the point where he is said to "abide securely in Bodhi."
Furthermore, being able to act as guardians of the city of the Dharma and to uphold the True Dharma, they are said to be "dwelling securely in bodhi.
Having realized indestructible faith, they gave rise to profound joy.
At the time of late afternoon, they each went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The commentary says:
[They] approached the Buddha.
Furthermore, there were forty-two thousand devaputras, whose names were as follows:

The Devaputra Priyadarśana, the Devaputra Pramoda, the Devaputra Sūryaprabha, the Devaputra Candracūḍa, the Devaputra Prajñāloka, the Devaputra Gaganaviśuddhaprajña, the Devaputra Kleśaprahāṇa, and the Devaputra Śrī.

With these and other devaputras as their leaders, all of whom had made vast vows to protect and uphold the Mahāyāna and to ensure that the True Dharma flourishes and is never interrupted, each went at the hour of *pradoṣa* to the place where the Buddha was.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The commentary states:
Next, the various devas are listed; this passage also consists of four parts, as before.
These are mostly the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, which are listed first because they are situated nearest [to the human realm].
The worldly designations of names cannot be explained in full detail.
Within the praise of his virtues, there are two parts:
first, the formulation of the Four Great Vows; second, the protection of the Mahāyāna.

To protect the Mahāyāna is to embrace the true Dharma; embracing the true Dharma enables one to shoulder the four great responsibilities, as stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and thus one is able to perpetuate and glorify the true Dharma.
The True Dharma is threefold: namely, right realization, right practice, and right teaching.
Because it enables oneself and others to rely upon the right teaching, initiate right practice, and realize the right fruit, it ensures that the lineage remains unbroken.
The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra* states that there are five factors for upholding the sublime Dharma:

first, to repay the Buddha's kindness; second, to cause the sublime Dharma to endure for a long time within oneself; third, to make offerings to all Buddhas; fourth, out of a desire to benefit sentient beings; and fifth, because the sublime Dharma is difficult to encounter.
In accordance with the tenth chapter of the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, there are ten dharmas that enable one to uphold the True Dharma:
first, when during the final age there is no one capable of upholding it, to reverently make offerings to those who are able to receive the great sūtras;
second, to preach the Dharma for others.
Third, they are able to cultivate and study with deep joy;
fourth, they listen to the true Dharma without expectation;
fifth, they conceive the thought of the Dharma Master as a guide.
Sixth, they are able to conceive the thought that the True Dharma is nectar;
seventh, they are able to conceive the thought that the sages of the True Dharma are medicine;
eighth, they are able to conceive the thought that the True Dharma is excellent medicine.
Ninth, they are able to seek the True Dharma exclusively, regardless of body or life;
tenth, they aspire to the True Dharma and give rise to the thought of practicing it.

Furthermore, there were twenty-eight thousand nāga kings, headed by Nāga King Padma, Nāga King Śarapatraka, Nāga King Mahābala, Nāga King Mahārava, Nāga King Laghutaranga, Nāga King Vegadhārin, Nāga King Suvarṇamukha, and Nāga King Manasvin. These and other nāga kings constantly delighted in receiving and upholding the Mahāyāna Dharma; they gave rise to deep faith, praising and protecting it.
Each went to the place where the Buddha was at the hour of late afternoon, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The praise says:
"The text also has four parts, as before."
Padma (lotus): this refers to that which dwells in a lotus pond.
Kilima (eyira): this is translated as "tree.
Bhanna (panna): this is translated as "leaf."
Depending on these tree leaves for their dwelling, or eating these leaves, they are the dragon kings known as "Well-Dwelling" (*Susthitā*).
Up to this point, they are named according to their wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*).
There are three ways of praising their virtues:
First, upholding the True Dharma; second, giving rise to deep faith; third, praising, explaining, and protecting it.
Furthermore, there were thirty-six thousand yakṣas, with the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa as their leader. Their names were:

Āmra Yakṣa, Āmradhara Yakṣa, Padmaprabhagarbha Yakṣa, Padmavaktra Yakṣa, Bhṛkuṭi Yakṣa, Mahābhayadarśin Yakṣa, Kṣobhaṇabhūmi Yakṣa, and Grāsaka Yakṣa. All these yakṣas delighted in the Tathāgata’s True Dharma, and with profound resolve they protected and upheld it without weariness.
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa*, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The commentary states:
"The array of the yakṣa hosts is also divided into four sections."
Yakṣa is translated here as "valiant and strong," or "swift and agile"; it also includes the terrestrial rākṣasas.
Rākṣasa is translated here as "violent and evil."
There are three aspects to praising their virtues:
first, their love for the True Dharma; second, their ability to protect and uphold it; and third, their lack of weariness.
The sutra continues: "Furthermore, there were forty-nine thousand *garuḍa* kings, with the King of Fragrant Elephant Power as their leader."
The commentary states:
Regarding the "Assembly of Bird Kings":
this is translated here as *Miaochi* (Wonderful Wing); following the older translations, it is also called *Jinshi* (Golden Wing).
His power and majesty were like those of a fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*); some possessed the strength to terrify even such fragrant elephants.
Perhaps the birds and elephants belong to different categories, yet he was indeed a king of fragrant elephants.

Thereupon, the *sūtra* states that other *gandharvas*, *asuras*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, and all the seers (*ṛṣi*) of the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas, along with the assemblies of kings from all great nations, the ladies of the inner palace and their consorts, men and women of pure faith, and the great multitudes of gods and humans, all gathered there like clouds.
The commentary states:
This collectively enumerates the remaining assemblies.
The Sūtra says: "May they all vow to protect and uphold the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, reciting, receiving, upholding, copying, and disseminating it."

The commentary states: There are four ways of extolling his virtues: first, by vowing to protect him; second, by reciting and upholding [the sūtra] oneself; third, by transcribing it; and fourth, by disseminating it. The sūtra says:
Each at the hour of *pradoṣa* (late afternoon) went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Commentary says: Regarding the passage "Approaching the Buddha.

After this great assembly of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans, devas, and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits had gathered like clouds, each with a sincere heart joined their palms in reverence and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance, never once averting their eyes.
The commentary states:
There are two concluding sections:
first, the summary; second, the ritual procedure.
Because one seeks the Dharma with single-minded sincerity, one is "sincere" (zhìxīn); because one expresses what is taught in the profound darkness [of ignorance], one "joins the palms" (hézhǎng).
To revere and look up to is called "respect" (gōng); when such respect is profound, it is called "veneration" (jìng).
Beholding the majestic form of the marks, one aspires to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, one gazes up at the Honored Countenance.
Without casting another glance, it is said that they do not abandon [the teaching] for even a moment.
The Sūtra says: "They wish and desire to hear the sublime and wondrous Dharma.
The commentary states:
The accomplishment of the causes is explained:
the Buddha may only speak when the assembly desires to hear.
Sūtra: At that time, the Bhagavat arose from meditative absorption in the late afternoon and surveyed the great assembly.
The commentary states:
Regarding the introductory section on the occasion of the teaching, there are two parts:

first, the accomplishment of the time and the accomplishment of the majestic deportment that serves as the basis for preaching the Dharma; this refers precisely to the careful examination of the suitability of the audience.
Alternatively, it is called the "Perfection of the Ritual of Exposition," because it fully encompasses the meaning.
The sutra then speaks in verse:
"The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra, the wondrous Dharma, The most supreme king among all sūtras, Profound and difficult to hear, The realm of all Buddhas."
"I shall, for the sake of the great assembly, proclaim such a sutra.
The commentary states:
This indicates the accomplishment of the proclamation.
There are twenty-four verses, which are broadly divided into three parts:
first, one and a half lines that generally indicate the profound and subtle nature [of the teaching], granting permission to proclaim it to the assembly;
second, twenty and a half lines that specifically indicate what is being taught, praising its excellence to encourage practice.
The final two lines provide a summary of the superior benefits, praising the person [who practices] and exhorting them to study.
This is the first [of those two lines].
As for "verse" (*gāthā*), it was formerly called *jie*; in Sanskrit it is *gāthā*, which was erroneously transcribed as *jie*.
"Geya" (Verse) has the meaning of "singing praises," which refers to this very act of chanting.
This is because, prior to the prose (*gadya*), it was composed as a recitation.
Question:
Regarding the distinction between *geya* (recitation) and *gāthā* (verse):
the answer is that the verses of *geya* are the teaching (*śāsana*), whereas the recitations of *geya* are the words (*vāk*).
Question:
What is meant by "reciting these words" and "teaching through verses"?
Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states: "That which is to be chanted (geya) refers to verses (gāthā) proclaimed after the prose exposition.
This means that these verses directly expound the various meanings [of the preceding prose].
Regarding "reciting," the *Śāstra* states: "It means explaining by means of phrases.
This implies that one explains what has been taught by means of phrases.

Within these one and a half lines, the first two phrases indicate the teaching (*deśanā*) which is the signifier; the next two phrases indicate the meaning (*artha*) which is the signified; and the final two phrases grant permission to explain it accordingly.
Because it can express the profound causes and wondrous fruits of that bodhi and nirvāṇa, it is the most supreme and the king of all sūtras.
Regarding what is expressed [by this title], according to the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, it says: "There are four causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma:
first, for the sake of form; second, for the sake of the non-form; third, for the sake of supernormal powers; and fourth, for the sake of the True Dharma."
It serves as the cause for physical form (*rūpa*) because it is the cause for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
It serves as the cause for that which is non-physical (*arūpa*) because it is the cause for the extinction of the disease of afflictions (*kleśa*).
It serves as the cause for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because it is the cause for mastery (*vaśitā*).
"One who upholds the True Dharma does so because it is an inexhaustible cause.
As stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "A bodhisattva seeking the Dharma possesses four perceptions:
first, the perception of it as a sublime jewel, because its meaning is difficult to obtain."
Second, the perception of it as excellent medicine, because it has the sense of removing illness;
third, the perception of it as wealth, because it has the sense of not being dissipated;
fourth, the perception of it as nirvāṇa, because it has the sense of the cessation of suffering.
Because the Dharma is the cause for the adornment of the marks and signs [of a Buddha], it is regarded as being like a wondrous jewel.
Because the Dharma is the cause for extinguishing the disease of afflictions, it is regarded as being like an excellent medicine.
Because this Dharma is the cause for mastery over supernormal powers, it is regarded as being like wealth;
because this Dharma is the cause for the inexhaustibility of the True Dharma, it is regarded as being like nirvāṇa.
In this sutra, what is profoundly deep and difficult to hear is indicated by the first three causes, as all three are equally rare to encounter.

The realm of the Buddhas is indicated by the fourth cause; because the Great Nirvana can only be fully realized by Buddha after Buddha, it is that which the Buddhas have attained, and is thus called the realm of the Buddhas.
This indicates that all the mundane and supramundane causes and effects explained below are fully encompassed; thus, this refers collectively to this sutra. The Sutra states:

“Together with the four Buddhas of the four directions, their majestic spiritual power shall provide joint protection: the Honored One Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnaśrī Buddha in the south, Amitāyus in the west, and Devadundubhisvara in the north.”
The commentary states:
The following twenty and a half lines constitute a separate heading.
This section is divided into four parts:
The first three and a half lines constitute the introduction.
From the "Life Span" chapter down to the end of the "Fulfillment of Vows" chapter constitutes the main body of the sutra.
The doctrine correctly elucidated therein refers to the two causes and two fruits.
2. Following "The Incomplete Bodies of Sentient Beings," there are six lines of verse that, within the Main Teaching (śāstramūla), set forth the exhortation to study.

3. Following "The Assembly of the Four World-Protecting Kings," there are five lines of verse that, from the "Chapter on Contemplation" (*parīkṣā*) onwards through the section on Entrustment and Circulation (*pariṇāmanā*), set forth the actual practice to be cultivated.
IV. The six verses beginning with "If there are those who hear this sutra" mark the praise and exhortation for the recitation and retention found within the various chapters.
Within the first three and a half lines, they are further divided into seven parts;
the first is one and a half lines marking the "Chapter on the Lifespan."
2. The single phrase, "I further expound the wondrous Dharma," indicates the "Chapter on the Three Bodies";
3. The two phrases, "Supreme among auspicious repentances," etc., indicate the "Chapter on Repentance";
4. The two phrases, "Purifying all evil karma," etc., indicate the "Chapter on Eliminating Karmic Obstructions."
5. "Constantly Bestowing Immeasurable Bliss" indicates the "Chapter on the Pure Ground," the "Chapter on the Lotus Simile Praise," and the "Chapter on the Golden Victorious Dhāraṇī";
6. "The Root of All-Knowledge" indicates the "Chapter on the Repeated Manifestation of Emptiness";
7. "Adorned with All Virtues" indicates the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows Based on Emptiness."
This refers to the first [Buddha].
Śākyamuni and the four Buddhas together preached this sutra; therefore, it says "along with the four Buddhas of the four directions.
The causes and conditions regarding these four Buddhas are as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*.
The four Buddhas, beginning with Akṣobhya, said:
"We remember that in the past, at the place of the Buddha Śūnyarāja, we left the household life to study the Way; at that time, there were four bhikṣus who were our fellow students."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he entered a stupa to contemplate the image and saw that the mark between the eyebrows was no different from that of the Buddha himself. He prayed, "May my sins be eradicated," and like a great mountain collapsing, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to repent for all his transgressions.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, for eighty billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas thereafter, he shall not fall into the evil realms; he shall constantly behold all Buddhas and, in the presence of those Buddhas, uphold the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
Having attained samādhi, all the Buddhas appeared before me and bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In the east there is a land named Abhirati; the Buddha there is named Akṣobhya, who is none other than this foremost bhikṣu."
In the south there is a land named Abhirati; the Buddha there is named Ratnaketu, who is none other than the second bhikṣu.
In the west there is a land named Sukhāvatī; the Buddha there is named Amitāyus, who is none other than the third bhikṣu.
"In the north there is a land named Lotus Adornment; the Buddha there is named Subtle Sound—it is this fourth bhikṣu.
Question: "For what reason do these four Buddhas together preach this sūtra?"
Answer:

This is to manifest the four virtues along with Śākyamuni, thereby revealing all five factors of the Buddha-fruit; that is to say, the four wisdoms and suchness encompass and exhaustively include both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Sūtra: “I shall further expound the sublime Dharma, the most excellent among auspicious confessions, which can extinguish all transgressions and completely purify all evil karma.
Commentary: This refers to the second, third, and fourth [sections].
Furthermore, he expounds the wondrous Dharma, designating the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Three Bodies; thus it is called the "Wondrous Dharma.
It is superior among auspicious repentances, for one performs repentance based on the vow to realize the Three Bodies; thus it is superior among all forms of repentance.

Regarding "able to extinguish all sins": this refers to the three karmas of the three periods of time, the fruits of suffering within the three realms, and the three afflictions; it is that which can subdue, eliminate, and extinguish them. Thus, the subsequent scripture says: "The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* drum produces wondrous sounds that pervade the trichiliocosm, able to extinguish the most grievous sins of the three miserable paths, as well as the various sufferings and calamities of humans and devas."
The phrase "purifying all evil karma" introduces the chapter titled "Extinguishing Karmic Obstructions.
Since both the action and its causes are termed "evil karma," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The attendants of karma are also designated by the name 'karma.'"
Alternatively, karma produced by evil causes and karma that brings about evil results are also called "evil karma.
Because they are loathsome, this applies to all three realms.
Alternatively, for those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*), it refers only to the exclusion of karma leading to the three miserable destinies and the eight difficult conditions.
Sūtra: “Furthermore, it eliminates all suffering and affliction, constantly bestows immeasurable bliss, is the root of all-knowledge, and is adorned with every merit.
Commentary: The first phrase belongs to the heading of the "Chapter on the Extinguishing of Karmic Obstructions."
The preceding verse states that all evil karmas are the cause, and the resulting evil fruits encompass the fruits of all three realms.

If categorized by their lack of inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they consist merely of the three miserable destinies, the eight difficult conditions, and a small portion of the eight types of suffering; these do not depart from birth, old age, death, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

It constantly bestows immeasurable bliss; as indicated by the three chapters below—“Pure Ground,” “Lotus Praise,” and “Golden Victory”—by practicing the six perfections, one attains the fruit of the ten kings as well as the rank of Buddhahood. Therefore, for those without the Buddha-nature, it grants the bliss of humans and devas; for those with the Buddha-nature, it grants the rank of Buddhahood and so forth.
The root of all-knowledge is indicated by the "Chapter on the Repeated Manifestation of Emptiness.
Because the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is the nature of true emptiness, it is named the Tathāgatagarbha, as it serves as the basis and support for all meritorious qualities.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* explains the "beginningless realm" (*anādikāliko dhātuḥ*); "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to the cause of phenomena.
That is to say, true suchness (*tathatā*) is the cause of all phenomena.
Since the cause is termed the "root," it is the root of wisdom.
Because one realizes *tathatā* (suchness) by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is specifically termed the basis of all-knowledge.
In reality, however, the understanding of the conventional arises from the realization of the ultimate.

It is also the basis of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); when explained according to the realized wisdom, the "knowledge of all aspects" is omitted, or perhaps this "all-knowledge" is not the "all-knowledge" among the two [i.e., the knowledge of all aspects].
This is a general statement regarding all forms of knowledge; that is, the ten knowledges, the four knowledges, and so forth, are termed "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*).
Since these are all the source, it is called the "root of all-knowledge."
The "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Emptiness" (*Āśraya-śūnyatā-praṇidhāna-paripūraṇa-paṭala*) marks the adornment of all virtues.
Because one initiates cultivation by relying on ultimate truth, once the root of merit is realized, one is able to perfect the true adornment of all virtues.
As in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, where the adornment of the land and the adornment of the body both require the contemplation of principle before they can be perfected, this sūtra is likewise.
The sūtra says: "When the bodies of sentient beings are incomplete and their lifespans are about to diminish, various evil signs appear before them, and the celestial deities all abandon them."
The commentary states:
Below, within the section designating the orthodox teaching, the capacity to encourage study is presented.
This is divided into two parts:
The first three and a half lines cite various sufferings and hardships to inspire weariness with and detachment from them;
the final two and a half lines reveal that this sutra can eliminate these [sufferings], inspiring joy in its cultivation and study.
The first section is further divided into two parts:
the first two lines clarify the results of evil, and the subsequent one and a half lines clarify the causes of suffering.
Within the first of these, there are again two sub-sections.
The first line concerns internal bodily suffering, while the latter line concerns external conditional suffering.
This refers to the internal body;
when the body is incomplete or lacks its various faculties, it is subsumed under the arising of suffering, or categorized as the suffering of illness.
When one’s lifespan is about to end, karma is exhausted, and conditions terminate—whether by a natural death or by an untimely, violent loss of life—this is the suffering of death.

As for the manifestation of various evil signs: the crying of birds, a hundred strange portents, flowers falling from the head, the discordance of the four great elements, and the decay of physical appearance—these are the sufferings of illness and old age.
These correspond, in order, to the sufferings of birth-and-death, old age, and illness.
As long as one's lifespan is not yet exhausted, one is protected and sustained by a hundred deities through the cultivation of meritorious deeds;
once those karmic forces are exhausted, if one is unable to cultivate goodness in the present life, the benevolent deities will abandon one.
Sūtra: "One's close friends harbor resentment, one's kinsmen all part ways, each side becomes estranged, and all precious wealth is lost.
Commentary: This refers to suffering caused by external conditions.
When close friends harbor resentment, this is the suffering of encountering what one hates.
When one's kinsmen and associates are all separated, this is the suffering of being parted from what one loves.
The final two lines, concerning mutual discord, refer to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Sūtra: “When malevolent stars cause portents and anomalies, or when one is afflicted by evil sorcery, or further experiences abundant sorrow and grief, one is oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Commentary: This clarifies the causes of suffering.
The first line [of the verse] concerns external causes of suffering, while the latter half concerns internal causes of suffering.
The Sūtra says: “Sleeping and seeing bad dreams, because of these, afflictions arise.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the internal causes of suffering, the Sūtra states: "This person should bathe and put on fresh, clean clothes; then, with a focused mind free from distraction, they should read, recite, listen to, and uphold this wondrous King of Sūtras, which is profound and praised by the Buddha."
Commentary: The following clarifies that the power of the sūtra can eliminate [afflictions], thereby inspiring one to joyfully practice and study.
This section has three parts:
The first half of the verse concerns the ritual of practice; the next line concerns the actual practice itself; and the final line concludes with the power and efficacy of the sutra.
Within the section on actual practice, the first two phrases clarify the Dharma to be studied, while the latter two phrases clarify the actual practice.

Whether reading, reciting, listening, or upholding [the teachings], one must focus the mind with undistracted attention; thus, reading and reciting give rise to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), upholding gives rise to the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and these together manifest the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Alternatively, focusing the mind so that no distraction arises constitutes reflection (*cintā*); the remainder consists of hearing (*śruta*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), whereby the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are fully perfected.

Furthermore, bathing and wearing clean clothes constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*); focused concentration constitutes the training in meditative absorption (*samādhi-śikṣā*); and recitation and the like constitute the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
It causes one to rely on this sutra to cultivate the three trainings.

The sutra states: "By the power of this sutra, one is able to leave behind all calamities and misfortunes, as well as other manifold sufferings and difficulties; there are none that are not entirely extinguished."
The commentary states:
This concludes the power of merit.
The Sūtra says: "The Four World-Protecting Kings, along with their ministers and retinues, and immeasurable yakṣas, shall all protect [the practitioner] with a single mind."
The commentary states:
The following marks the section on the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*).
It consists of five lines, which mark the actual practice to be performed.
This indicates the "Chapter on Examining Humans and Devas," the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings Protecting the Nation," the "Chapter on Non-Attachment," and the "Chapter on Sovereign Power."
Sūtra: “The Great Goddess of Eloquence, the River Goddess of the Nairañjanā, the Mother Goddess Hārītī, and the assembly of the Earth Goddess Dhṛtarāṣṭrī. Commentary:
This single line indicates the chapters on the Great Goddess of Eloquence, the Auspicious Goddess, the Increase of Wealth, and the Earth Goddess Dhṛtarāṣṭrī.
Hārītī—here translated as "Azure"—is the mother of the rākṣasa demons. She has five hundred sons and is a supreme protector of the Triple Gem, as well as of children and young men.

As the Sūtra says: "The Brahma King and Śakra, the Lord of Devas; the Dragon Kings and Kiṃnaras; the Garuḍa Kings and the hosts of Asuras and gods—all such celestial beings, together with their retinues, shall come to protect this person, never departing by day or night."
The commentary states:

It designates the "Chapter on the Great Yakṣa General Saṃjñeya," the "Chapter on the Correct Treatise on Royal Law," the "Chapter on King Śūrabhūti," and the "Chapter on the Protection by Devas and Yakṣas."
Another interpretation is as follows: "Correctly understanding" (*samyag-ājñā*) is indicated within the section on the goddess Hārītī.
As for the *Rājanīti-śāstra* and the "Chapter on King Sujāta," both are indicated within the verses of this sutra; because they were spoken by the Buddha, they are indicated in a single location.
Sūtra: "I shall now proclaim this sūtra, the profound sphere of activity of the Buddhas, the secret teaching of all Buddhas, which is difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas.
Commentary: This marks the section beginning with the "Chapter on Bestowal of Prophecy" (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta).

The profound sphere of the Buddha’s activity is indicated by the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies," the "Chapter on Healing Illness," the "Chapter on the Householder’s Son Flowing Water," and the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body."
Unsurpassed Bodhi can only be realized by a Buddha; this is called the sphere of a Buddha’s activity.
The chapters such as "Treating Illness" describe the causal practices of the Buddhas.
The two phrases beginning with "The secret teachings of all Buddhas" serve as headings for the subsequent chapters.

Protected by all Buddhas, this is designated as "secret" because it is bestowed only upon those whose roots for the Mahāyāna have matured; it is designated as "esoteric" because it is profound, subtle, and difficult to understand.
Since it has been difficult to hear throughout ten million kalpas, one should now rejoice in having heard and read it, and it is hereby entrusted to you.
Sūtra: "If there are those who hear this sūtra, are able to expound it for others, give rise to sympathetic joy in their hearts, or provide offerings.
Commentary: The following six lines constitute the fourth section, which marks the *parīndanā* (transmission) portion and encourages the upholding and recitation of the various chapters.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, one line indicating the exhortation to uphold and recite; second, three lines clarifying the benefits gained; and third, two lines teaching the method of upholding.
This is the first part.

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* contains ten verses on the practices of the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*): "Namely: making offerings, copying, giving to others, listening, reading aloud, receiving and upholding, as well as expounding, reciting, reflecting, and cultivating."

The ten are: first, making offerings; second, copying; third, giving to others; fourth, hearing; fifth, reading aloud; sixth, receiving and upholding; seventh, expounding; eighth, reciting; ninth, reflecting; and tenth, practicing.
In the beginning, there is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Herein, "hearing" refers to listening to this sutra; "expounding" means to explain it in detail; and "making offerings" refers to the initial practice.
To provide a brief summary, three practices are mentioned: hearing and making offerings for one's own benefit, and expounding the teachings for the benefit of others;
thus, while only three are cited here, there are actually ten types in total.
Regarding rejoicing (*anumodanā*), there are four types for each of the ten dharma-practices:
first, performing the ten dharma-practices oneself; second, instructing others; third, offering congratulations and comfort; and fourth, rejoicing.
This has been briefly illustrated by means of what is easy to understand, with its implications extending to other cases.
The Sūtra says: "Such persons as these shall, for immeasurable kalpas, always be revered by devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits."
The commentary states:
Second, the clarification of the benefits received has three parts;
first, the attainment of protection.
This is the first [section].
Sūtra: "This mass of merit is immeasurable, exceeding the sands of the Ganges; those who read and recite this sūtra shall obtain such merit."
The commentary states:
Second, establishing the superior causes.

The Sūtra says: “They shall also act as protectors for the Honored Ones of the ten directions and for all Bodhisattvas who practice the profound path, shielding those who uphold this sūtra and causing them to be free from all suffering and hardship.”
Commentary: Third, protection by the Noble Ones.

Sūtra: “Those who make offerings to this sūtra shall, as previously described, bathe their bodies, provide food and drink, and offer incense and flowers, while constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.”
"If one wishes to listen to this sutra, it will cause the mind to be pure and free from defilement; by constantly giving rise to thoughts of joy, one can increase all merits.
The commentary states:
The instructions for upholding the ritual of the sutra are divided into two parts:
The first line brings benefit to others; the last, benefit to oneself.
Sūtra: "If one listens to this sūtra with a heart of reverence, should one be reborn in the human realm, one will be far removed from all suffering and hardship."
"Only those whose roots of goodness have matured and who are praised by all Buddhas shall be able to hear this sutra as well as the method of repentance.
Commentary: This concludes the exhortation.
There are two parts:
first, one verse concluding with an exhortation to attain the supreme fruit; second, one verse concluding with an exhortation to accomplish the supreme cause.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit, there are two [aspects]:
Those newly born into the human realm obtain the fruit of outflow (sāsrava);
they are far removed from all sufferings and difficulties. It is not merely that they are freed from these difficulties, but they also attain the fruit of nirvana.
Alternatively, as the fundamental tenet was first established, the profound fruit had not yet been explained; it simply stated that those in the human realm may escape the eight difficulties.
If one were to speak of the supreme fruit, I fear that beginners would be unable to believe it.
*Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle One;
*Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree;
compiled by the Sramana Huizhao.
Chapter 21: King Sujāta (Part 6). Chapter Twenty-one: King Sujāta is analyzed according to three sections.

Regarding the intent of this discourse: within the sixteen chapters, there are five sections concerning the transmission of study and practice; the fourth section specifically clarifies the upholding and learning [of the precepts].
This upholding and learning consists of two parts:
the first two chapters cite past instances of upholding and learning, while the final chapter exhorts present-day upholding and learning.
To begin with, there are two intentions:
first, that for worldly results, which is the path of higher rebirth;
second, that for supramundane results, which is the path of definitive excellence.
Because of the distinction between initial cultivation and long-term cultivation, and because both the practices of great compassion and great wisdom increase,
the preceding chapter clarified practicing according to the teachings based on others for the sake of attaining worldly fruits;
this chapter clarifies personally upholding and studying this sutra to seek supramundane fruits.

Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: the preceding chapter established that, for the sake of protecting the land, this sutra should be circulated and practiced; this present chapter establishes that, for the sake of attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and so forth, the circulation and practice of the sutra must be carried out. Therefore, this chapter begins.
Regarding the explanation of the title: in Sanskrit it is called *Kuśala*, which here means "skillful" (*shan*); *Pāpa* means "birth" (*sheng*).
The old translation, "Skillful Accumulation," is a semantic rendering that is not literal.
This chapter clarifies the conduct of Kuśala seeking the Dharma and upholding the sutra in the past; therefore, it is named accordingly.
Regarding the resolution of obstacles:
Question—The original intent was to exhort the upholding of this sutra;
thus, past events were cited to provide clarification.
Since this has already clarified that *Sujāta* went to seek the Dharma,
why is it not titled "The Chapter on Sujāta Seeking the Dharma"? Answer:
One should say "seeking the Dharma," but it is not mentioned here due to brevity.
Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of seeking; one also attains hearing the Dharma and the practice of making offerings.
If one were to speak only of "seeking the Dharma," other dharmic practices would be omitted; therefore, it simply says "well-born" (Sujāta).
Question:

During the first stage of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he first encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin. Why, then, does this chapter state that the Buddha Ratnaśikhin has entered parinirvāṇa and King Sujāta has appeared? Answer: [The text continues...]
There were many Buddhas named Ratnaśikhin.
Furthermore, it was not necessarily King Sujāta who appeared at the beginning of the second kalpa, as this occurred at another time.
The Sūtra states: At that time, after the World-Honored One had expounded the *Rājadharma-samyak-śāstra* for the great assembly, he further addressed the assembly:
"You all should listen, for I shall now explain to you the causes and conditions of his past service to the Dharma.
The commentary states:

The text of this chapter is divided into three parts: first, this section which concludes the preceding and introduces what follows; second, the actual account of his practice; and third, the aspiration of the great assembly to learn from him.
This is the first [chapter].
The Sūtra then speaks a verse at that time, saying:
"In the past, I was once a Cakravartin King; I gave away this great earth together with its oceans, filled with the treasures of the four continents, to offer as a gift to all the Tathāgatas."
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, in order to seek the pure and true Dharmakāya, I relinquished all things I held dear, even my own body and life, without a single thought of stinginess.
The following section formally describes the practice in thirty-two verses.
It is divided into four parts:

first, two verses that generally indicate the past worship of Buddhas and the seeking of the Dharma; second, twenty-three verses that specifically clarify the past cultivation and study of this sutra; third, two verses that resolve the doubts of the assembly by synthesizing the ancient and the present; and fourth, five verses that clarify the benefits of cultivation and study, exhorting the multitude.
The first part has two sections:
the first verse concerns drawing near to the Buddhas, and the second verse concerns seeking the supreme Dharma. The Sūtra says:

"Furthermore, in the past, during inconceivable kalpas, there was a Tathāgata named Ratnaśikhin, known throughout the five directions. After that Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, a king named Sujāta appeared in the world. He was a Cakravartin who ruled over the four continents; extending to the very limits of the great oceans, all submitted to his authority."
There was a city named *Svararuta* (Wondrous Sound), where that Wheel-Turning King resided at that time.
This concludes the second section, which specifically clarifies the past cultivation and study of this sutra.
Within this, there are four parts:

The first two verses concern those who seek the Dharma; the next sixteen verses concern the actual seeking of the Dharma; the following single verse concerns hearing it upon attainment; and the final four verses concern practicing and studying based upon it.

Regarding the first section on those who seek [the Dharma], there are four parts: first, clarifying the time of seeking the Dharma; second, from "There was a king who appeared" onwards, clarifying the person who seeks the Dharma; third, from "He was a wheel-turning monarch" onwards, clarifying the king’s transformation of the world; and fourth, from "There was a city" onwards, clarifying the place of residence.

Sūtra: "In a dream at night, I heard the discourse on the Buddha’s merit and wisdom; I saw a Dharma Master named Ratnakūṭa, seated with a dignified majesty like the orb of the sun, expounding the subtle and wondrous scripture of the Golden Light."

At that time, the king awoke from his dream; great joy arose within him, pervading his entire body. When dawn had broken, he departed from the royal palace and proceeded to where the community of bhikṣus was staying.
Having paid respectful homage and made offerings to the noble assembly, he immediately questioned that great multitude:
"Is there a Dharma Master named Ratnakūṭa who has accomplished meritorious virtues and transforms sentient beings?"

At that time, the great Dharma Master Ratnākara was dwelling in a single room; with right mindfulness, he recited this subtle and wondrous scripture, remaining upright and unmoving, his body and mind in bliss.
At that time, a bhikṣu led the king to the dwelling of Ratnakūṭa; there he saw him sitting upright within the room, his body suffused with a sublime radiance and wondrous marks.
He addressed the King, saying: "This is indeed Ratnakūṭa.
He is able to uphold the profound sphere of the Buddha's practice, namely the subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king among all sūtras and the most supreme."
At that time, the king immediately prostrated before Ratnakūṭa and, with palms joined in reverence, made this request:
"I pray only that you, whose full moon face is so dignified and beautiful, will preach for me the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Golden Light."
The Dharma Master Ratnakūṭa accepted the King’s invitation and consented to preach this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Throughout the trichiliocosm, the great assemblies of devas were filled with joy.

In a vast, pure, and spacious place, the king adorned it with wondrous and precious jewels; he sprinkled superior fragrant water to settle the dust and scattered various kinds of mixed flowers everywhere.

He then prepared high seats in the excellent locations, adorning them with suspended silk banners and canopies; various powdered incenses and unguents were applied, their fragrant scents pervading everywhere.
Devas, nāgas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and yakṣas—all the devas rained down māndārava flowers, coming together to make offerings to that high seat.

Furthermore, there were thousands of millions of devas who, desiring to hear the true Dharma, gathered together; as soon as the Dharma Master rose from his original seat, they all made offerings to him with celestial flowers.

At that time, the great Dharma Master Ratnakara, having bathed himself clean and put on fresh garments, went to the place where the assembly’s Dharma seat was located; with palms joined and a reverent heart, he paid his respects.

The Lord of Devas, the hosts of devas, and the celestial maidens all together scattered mandārava flowers; hundreds of thousands of inconceivable celestial instruments, suspended in the air, produced wondrous sounds.

At that time, the Great Dharma Master Ratnākara ascended the high seat and sat cross-legged. He brought to mind the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Great Compassionate Honored Ones throughout the lands of the ten directions, who universally reach all suffering sentient beings and give rise to thoughts of impartial compassion. For the sake of his host, the noble Saṃjīva, he expounded the subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Second, the correct seeking of the Dharma has eleven parts:
the first verse concerns what was seen and heard in a dream.
In Sanskrit it is called *ratna*, which here is translated as "Jewel."
*Kuṭa* means "accumulation" (*cita*) in this [language].
The former translations "Precious Radiance" (*Baoming*) and "Precious Obscurity" (*Boming*) are both erroneous.
The second pair of verses concerns seeking after having awakened.
The dwelling place of the Dharma Master is described in three verses.

"Even if there were a great mass of fire filling a hundred *yojanas*, for the sake of hearing this King of Sutras, one would pass straight through it without complaining of suffering.
