"Within this Jambudvīpa, the deities of the forests, fruits, and crops, through the majestic power of this sutra, shall always have their hearts filled with joy. Their sprouts and grains will all reach fulfillment; wondrous flowers will appear everywhere, and fruits and seeds will grow in profusion, filling the entire earth."
All fruit-bearing trees and various groves and gardens are entirely covered with exquisite flowers, their fragrances perpetually sweet and pervasive.
All the grasses and various trees likewise produce subtle and wondrous blossoms and bear sweet fruits, filling every place to overflowing.
In this Jambudvīpa, immeasurable nāga maidens, their hearts filled with great joy, all entered the pond together.
They planted padmas and puṇḍarikas—the two lotuses, blue and white—until they completely filled the pool.

By the power of this sutra, the void becomes pure and free from obscuration; clouds and mist are all dispelled, and the deep darkness is entirely filled with light. The sun rises, emitting a thousand rays; its stainless flames are utterly pure.
By the power of this King of Sūtras, its radiance flows and encircles the four continents.
By the majestic power of this sūtra, it assists the celestial sons, all of whom construct their palaces out of Jambūnada gold.
When the Sun Deity first rises, he beholds this continent with joy and constantly illuminates it everywhere with his great radiance.
Within this great earth, all the lotus ponds, as soon as they are reached by the sunlight, do not fail to blossom fully.
In this Jambudvīpa, may all fields, fruits, and medicinal herbs ripen well and fill the great earth.
By the power of this sutra, wherever the sun and moon shine, the stars shall not lose their courses, and wind and rain shall follow their proper seasons.
Throughout this Jambudvīpa, all lands shall be abundant and joyful; wherever this sutra resides, it will be far more excellent than other regions.
The following fourteen verses praise the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of the sutra, which consists of eight parts:

first, four verses on how the hundred grains become abundant and exquisite through the sutra’s power; next, two verses on the many flowers in ponds and pools; next, one verse on the sky being pure and ever-bright; next, three verses on the sun’s palace increasing its radiance; next, one verse on lotuses opening in accordance with the sun; next, one verse on fruits and medicinal herbs being perpetually full; next, one verse on wind and rain falling according to the seasons and the seven luminaries following their proper courses; and finally, one verse summarizing the power of the sutra.
Sūtra: "Wherever this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* scripture circulates, those who are able to lecture upon or recite it shall all obtain the aforementioned merit.
This final verse summarizes the merit obtained by both the teacher and the listener.

Sūtra: At that time, the Great Goddess Śrī and all the devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were filled with great joy; they single-mindedly protected this King of Sūtras and those who uphold it, ensuring they were free from sorrow and affliction and always attained peace and happiness.
The third major section below concerns the Great Assembly’s Vow of Protection.
Chapter Twenty-three: The Bestowal of Prophecy (6). Chapter Twenty-three: The Bestowal of Prophecy is analyzed according to three sections.

Regarding the purpose of this coming, there are five aspects concerning the study and practice of the circulation [of the teaching]; this is the fifth, which serves to establish the intent for study and practice as presented in the preceding chapters.
It consists of three parts:
first, bestowing predictions; second, removing doubts; and third, further exhortation.
This is the first [section].

Regarding the "Bestowal of Prophecy" (vyākaraṇa): it clarifies that practice will necessarily result in fruit, and that the fruit is certain because the cause has been established; therefore, following the "Sustaining" (parigraha) chapter, there is the "Prophecy" (vyākaraṇa) chapter.
Regarding the explanation of the names: "bestowing" (*śāsana*) means to entrust or to give; "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) means to distinguish and to verify.
Because one distinguishes [the potential], verifies the appropriate fruit, and then bestows it, it is called "bestowing a prediction."
Regarding the "explanation of the obstacles," the question is asked:
Since the Wondrous Banner (Miaochuang) had not yet received a prediction upon hearing this sutra, how can it now be said that this chapter arises to fulfill his previous conduct?
The answer is:
This was not granted as a formal prediction of enlightenment for her own sake, nor for that of the Wondrous Banner or her two sons.

It was like the two classes of nuns in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, who were urged to uphold the sutra; because they desired to hear a prediction before they could practice and study, he granted them the prophecy.
This is not the time for the formal bestowal of a prediction (vyākaraṇa), as it has already been bestowed previously.
Therefore, that sūtra states: "I have already declared that all śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood; the great assembly here is likewise so."
It is asked: "If one who upholds this sutra attains Buddhahood, who are such persons?
Since there is this doubt and they have not yet resolved to study, [the Buddha] bestows the prophecy upon Wondrous Banner and others in order to sever it."
This was intended to let the assembly know that he would become a Buddha and was certainly capable of practicing;
otherwise, he should have been granted his prediction either after the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstacles" or after the "Chapter on the Lotus Praise."
If he had already attained awakening at that time, why did he not bestow a prediction [of his future Buddhahood]?

It is like the three assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where after each assembly of the teaching, a prediction was bestowed upon each person; it was not because they were not yet among the final group.
Question:
If that is so, why was it not previously answered? Answer:

Because the Bodhisattva Subhaketu had already entered the eighth stage and had previously received a prediction [of his future enlightenment], he was exhorted to uphold the sutra; therefore, it is explained again.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that while the prediction should have been given earlier, it is given here because it encompasses multiple meanings: first, to grant the prediction to Subhaketu and others, and second, to further substantiate what preceded it.

Furthermore, since the previous ten thousand [bodhisattvas] had not yet arrived at the assembly, this also demonstrates that upon hearing it once, all can attain Buddhahood; how much more so for those who have long practiced and studied?
Therefore, bestowing predictions at this time provides manifold benefit through a single word, and thus there is no fault.
Question:

Why is it that the great assembly gathered there was not granted a prediction of enlightenment, whereas those ten thousand people were granted predictions immediately upon hearing [the teaching] for a brief moment? Answer:
Because their faculties have matured, whereas these have not yet matured;
furthermore, because the assembly has already heard and upheld the sutras and attained Buddhahood,
whereas these have not yet heard them, and because it was fitting for it to be so.

Sūtra: At that time, after the Tathāgata had extensively expounded the Dharma within the great assembly, he desired to bestow the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the Bodhisattva Subhaketu and his two sons, Rajaketu and Rajaprabha.
The commentary states:
This chapter is divided into two parts: first, the assembly gathers; second, the bestowal of predictions.
Within the assembly gathering, there are two sections:
First, this is the prologue to the compilation of the Sūtra:

At that time, ten thousand devaputras, with Varaprabha as their leader, all came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and listened to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
The following clarifies the assembly.
The Sūtra says: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, saying:

“In a future age, after immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas have passed, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the world-system called Suvarṇaprabhāsa. You shall appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Suvarṇaparvatarāja.”
After descending, he bestowed two types of prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*):
first, the prophecy for the three types of practitioners, and later, the prophecy for ten thousand [beings].
Regarding the three types of practitioners, there are three sections; within the first, there are further five.
First, the designation of the title;
second, the recording of the time;
third, the recording of the country.
The fourth is the prediction of the fruit, which is unsurpassed bodhi;
the fifth is the prediction of the name, such as "Golden Treasure Mountain" and so forth.
These names have both general and specific aspects, as can be understood from the text.
The meaning of the prophecy (vyākaraṇa) shall be briefly analyzed by way of four sections:
first, the causes for the prophecy; second, the person who bestows the prophecy; third, the recipient of the prophecy; and fourth, the distinctions among prophecies.
Regarding the reasons for this, there are three points:
first, because the Bodhisattvas have cultivated manifold merits and realized the Dharma-nature, they are granted the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Thus, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* asks: "Is it because those Śrāvakas and others will truly attain Buddhahood that they are given the prediction?"
Is it that you have not attained Buddhahood and thus receive this prediction?
If you have indeed attained Buddhahood, for what reason would a bodhisattva cultivate and accumulate immeasurable merit over immeasurable kalpas?
The treatise answers: "Those śrāvakas who receive a prediction of enlightenment attain a mind of certainty, but it is not because they have accomplished the *dharmatā*.

This meaning clarifies that bodhisattvas receive predictions because they have accomplished the *dharmatā* through practicing immeasurable merit over many eons; this refers specifically to those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46, states: "Furthermore, there are three kinds of certainty for bodhisattvas:
first, certainty of lineage; second, certainty of generating the mind [of enlightenment]; and third, certainty of non-empty practice."

...and so on, up to: "Based on their final entry into the state of certainty (*niyāma*), the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, bestow upon the Bodhisattvas the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of their entry into certainty.

Second, to eliminate the doubt regarding the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) of lesser Bodhisattvas, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises state: "In order to attract one class [of beings] and to sustain another class—the Śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage and the remaining Bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage—fearing that these Bodhisattvas might regress from the Great Vehicle to the Lesser Vehicle, they are granted a prediction, saying they shall become Buddhas."
Third, for those who rejoice in the Buddha, seeing this prediction inspires them with the joy that they too shall personally attain it.
It further demonstrates that by hearing this sutra, one will certainly become a Buddha, as upholding and practicing this sutra cultivates the causes for Buddhahood.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has now received the sublime prediction.
We, too, have all attained the most wondrous and foremost Dharma," and so forth.

This sutra also states: "At that time, ten thousand devaputras, having heard that the three great bodhisattvas had received their predictions, and further hearing this most excellent King of Sutras, felt joy in their hearts; they became pure and stainless, like space."
This mind is joyful and free from doubt; it thus delights in becoming a Buddha, and with faith in the Dharma, it practices.
Regarding the second point, the one capable of making the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), there are further three meanings:
first, the provisional person upon whom the prediction is based; second, the essence of the prediction; and third, the function of the prediction.
Regarding the basis for making predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), according to the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are six stages through which one achieves this:

first, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); second, the stage of superior intention (*adhyāśaya-bhūmi*); third, the stage of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti-bhūmi*); fourth, the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*); fifth, the stage of certain practice (*niyata-caryā-bhūmi*); and sixth, the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
These six stages are all capable of bestowing predictions (vyākaraṇa).

However, regarding the ultimate stage, there is a distinction between Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. A Buddha possesses three bodies (trikāya); it is only the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya)—which are both provisional—that are capable [of this], as they are distinguished from the ten stages and the stages prior to them.

However, within the ultimate stage, Bodhisattvas of the tenth bhūmi and those of the five preceding stages can only provide a general prediction; they cannot know such details as the name of the land when that person becomes a Buddha, because those in lower positions cannot know the affairs of those above them.
If one relies on the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) to prophesy that one will attain Buddhahood based on causes, even a bodhisattva is capable of doing so.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*) prophesied that the fourfold assembly would all attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, the bestowal of prediction does not exceed these six cases.
Alternatively, those who are not deluded regarding the fixed nature of the Dharma and who believe that the Two Vehicles possess the Mahāyāna may also receive a general prediction.
As stated in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*:
In the past, there was an Arhat who, while leading a śrāmaṇera, gave rise to a great resolve and consequently developed a sense of reverence;
thus, he attained the capacity for comprehensive recollection.

Second, as for the essence of this capacity for recollection, it refers to the conventional wisdom obtained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*), because it knows the dispositions and faculties of beings.
Even the subsequently attained wisdom that contemplates reality cannot record it.
This refers to the noble ones (*ārya*); as for those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), they possess only inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
As for the three capacities for recording, these are what are called verbal teachings, because they express and signify meanings.
Regarding the three types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there are two:
first, the basis of the prediction; second, the essence of the prediction.
As for the basis of the prediction, there are four:

First, the stage of the single lineage; second, the stage of generating the resolve for enlightenment; third, those of indeterminate two-vehicle disposition; and fourth, all great bodhisattvas—this is according to the explicit teaching.
If one considers the implicit prophecy and the intention of equality, these also apply to those of fixed [two-vehicle] disposition and those who lack the potential for enlightenment.
That which constitutes the essence of what is recorded is the untainted wholesome, comprising both actualities and seeds, as well as the fruits obtained.
Regarding the fruits, they include those of retribution and transformation, excluding the *dharmatā-kāya*.

Within the *saṃbhoga-kāya*, the benefit for others is predominantly discussed because it possesses lands, retinues, and so forth; because it manifests compassion; and because it possesses distinctions.
Regarding the fourth distinction, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states that the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind:
"There are four kinds of bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*):

there is the bestowal of prophecy before one has yet resolved for enlightenment; there is the bestowal of prophecy at the very moment one resolves for enlightenment; there is the secret bestowal of prophecy; and there is the manifest bestowal of prophecy upon attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). These are called the four kinds."
"Only the Tathāgata can know this matter.

The *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, like the forty-sixth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, states briefly that there are six characteristics by which one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of unsurpassed enlightenment from all Tathāgatas.

What are the six? First, the stage of abiding in the lineage before the arousal of the thought of enlightenment; second, the stage after the arousal of the thought of enlightenment; third, the stage of manifestation; fourth, the stage of non-manifestation—these four preceding stages are identical to those in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
That secret prophecy is "not manifest" because it occurs in a secret place;

alternatively, those who have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) are said to have it "manifest," while those who have not yet attained it are said to have it "not manifest."
Alternatively, "being present" refers to being seated [in the assembly], while "not being present" refers to not being seated.
The fifth has a fixed time limit, meaning that within such a period of time, one shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The sixth is that there is no fixed time limit; that is, one bestows a prediction (vyākaraṇa) without declaring a definitive time limit.
The twelfth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* explains these six types in the same way.
It states: "There are two kinds of predictions: those distinguished by person and those distinguished by time.
Those distinguished by person refer to the former four; those distinguished by time refer to the latter two.
That treatise further states: "The transformative prediction and the great prediction—these, moreover, are of two kinds."

"Regarding the 'prediction' (vyākaraṇa): it means that at a future time, such a Bodhisattva shall receive a prediction from a Tathāgata in such a manner. Regarding the 'great prediction' (mahā-vyākaraṇa):

it occurs upon attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) in the eighth stage, by virtue of severing the conceit of thinking 'I shall become a Buddha' and severing all conceptualized marks," and so forth.
The "Minor Record" (*kṣudraka*) is subsumed within the first three sections of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, while the "Major Record" (*mahā-vastu*) is subsumed within the fourth.
Furthermore, that [text] speaks of six categories, which differs from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
What are the six? First, the buddha-field; second, the name; third, the time period; fourth, the name of the kalpa; fifth, the retinue; and sixth, the duration of the Dharma.
Regarding the predictions for Wondrous Banner and the others, there are three elements within the text:

Regarding the names of the buddha-fields such as Suvarṇaprabhāsa and the names of the golden jewel mountains and so forth, you shall, in a future age after immeasurable and incalculable periods of time, [attain them].
The names of the kalpas, the retinues, and the duration of the Dharma are omitted.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, after this Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all his teachings shall also completely perish."

At that time, his eldest son, named Silver Banner (Rūpyadhvaja), shall succeed him in this world-system to fill the place of the Buddha. At that time, the world-system will change its name to Pure Banner (Vimaladhvaja). He shall become a Buddha, known as White Silver Banner Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The second major section, the prediction for the Great Being, also consists of five parts:
first, the prediction regarding the time;
second, the citation of the name; [and so forth].
Third is the record of the place;
from "In this very realm" onwards is the fourth, the record of the country;
fifth is the record of the name, which also has both general and specific aspects.
Sūtra: “At that time, after this Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all his teachings shall likewise perish.

His second son, Silver Light (Rūpyaprabha), will succeed him on the Buddha’s throne and shall attain Buddhahood in this very realm, known by the name Tathāgata Suvarṇaprabhāsa, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The third major section, the prediction for the Great Being, also consists of five parts:
first, the prediction regarding the time;
second, the citation of the name; [and so forth].
Third, the prediction concerning the fruit, which is to succeed the Buddha;
fourth, the prediction concerning the land, returning to this very realm;
fifth, the prediction concerning the name.

Sūtra: At that time, ten thousand devaputras, having heard that the three great bodhisattvas had received their predictions and further having heard this most excellent King of Sūtras, gave rise to joy in their hearts; they became pure and stainless, like space.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the roots of goodness of these ten thousand devaputras had matured, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of great bodhi, saying:
"O you devaputras!..."
"In a future age, after immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
The second major section below is divided into four parts:
first, the bestowing of the prediction; second, the arising of doubt; third, its severance; and fourth, joyful faith.
The beginning has three parts:

first, the devaputra’s joy upon hearing and seeing; next, from "At that time, the Tathāgata" onwards, the Tathāgata’s knowledge that their faculties have matured; and finally, from "immediately" onwards, the actual bestowing of the prediction, which consists of eight sections, the first of which is the introductory heading.
Second, the citation of the name;
third, the recording of the time.
Now, there are many kinds of *kalpas*; as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, there are five types, namely: day, night, month, season (*ṛtu*), and year.
Some explain that the three calamities—famine, pestilence, and warfare—constitute the three *kalpas*.
Others explain that one cycle of increase and decrease constitutes one *kalpa*, such as the twenty *vāsakalpas* (abiding *kalpas*).
Some say that eighty cycles of increase and decrease constitute one kalpa, which refers to the kalpa of fire calamities.
Some say that seven fires constitute one kalpa, which refers to the kalpa of water calamities.
Others say that eight cycles of seven fires and one cycle of seven waters constitute one kalpa, which refers to the kalpa of wind calamities.
Some say that an immeasurable number of wind-disasters constitutes one kalpa, namely the three great asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.
Others say that two, eight, or ten kalpas constitute one kalpa, such as this present Bhadrakalpa.

Alternatively, it is said that eighty kalpas constitute one kalpa—namely, a *tārakā-kalpa* (star-constellation kalpa)—because the entire duration from the appearance of the first Buddha until the appearance of the thousand Buddhas is collectively designated as one *tārakā-kalpa*.
Regarding the number of kalpas as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they are mostly calculated in terms of days, nights, months, seasons, and years.

When it is said that each stage, such as the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), requires a certain number of kalpas, these refer specifically to kalpas such as those ending in wind-disasters (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*).

Regarding the phrase "passing beyond immeasurable and incalculable [aeons]," this refers to passing beyond the periods of increase and decrease, or the calamities of wind and so forth; it does not refer to the great *asaṃkhyeya* aeons, for one attains Buddhahood through practice in no more than three such aeons.
Question:

Since there are distinctions between diligence and laxity regarding the faculties and natures of those who practice, how can it be definitively stated that [the path] requires three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Answer:

When taking up the mental attention (*manasikāra*) through skillful means, the duration of the moment-to-moment continuity of the mind lasts for three great eons (*mahākalpa*); this does not refer to the total time spent in both cultivated and uncultivated practice.

Because of the application—or non-application—of mental attention (*manasikāra*) over such kalpas, although diligence and the nature of the faculties (*indriya*) differ, all are said to require three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Question:

If that is so, since from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward the mind of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-citta*) continues uninterrupted at all times, how can there be the matter of "leaping over" kalpas?
For example, at the beginning of the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, Śākyamuni Buddha encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha; by spreading his hair to cover the mud, he transcended eight *kalpas*.

At the completion of the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, while cultivating the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), he first encountered the Buddha Vipāśyin—also called Puṣya—whom he praised with joined palms, thereby transcending nine *kalpas*.
Answer: There are two interpretations. One says:
There may be a certain class of practitioners who dwell frequently in a state of contemplative wandering, or who remain long immersed in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);

in contrast to these, there is the "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*). If this is so, how can it be said that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one progresses with ever-increasing refinement moment by moment?
Answer: This is stated with reference to the long duration following the emergence from the dwelling in the eighth stage and above.
If that is so, how can it be said that from the first stage upward, the minds of entering, dwelling, and emerging are each equal?
Answer: Based on non-attention (*amanasikāra*), their functional power is equal, which differs from the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*).
Even when attention is applied, their functional power is unequal.

If one holds that all [stages] are equal, how can one speak of the distinctions between the increase of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the increase of compassion (*karuṇā*), or between being afraid of and not being afraid of the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
One explanation states:

The categories of the increase of compassion, the increase of wisdom, fear, and lack of fear are each equal within every stage (*bhūmi*). However, when it is said that [a bodhisattva] "surpasses" [others], this is said in reference to surpassing others in terms of wisdom relative to compassion.
If that is so, then since one whose wisdom predominates would naturally succeed in surpassing one whose compassion predominates, why is it necessary to mention such acts as the offering of hair?
Answer: These instances of surpassing and increasing are exceptional; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Alternatively, this is a metaphorical teaching of transcendence through skillful means, not a literal reality.
Why is this? Within the lands received by others from the eighth stage upward, where could there be mud for one to smear on their hair and beard?
How could there be a stone cave for a Buddha to dwell in meditative absorption?
If that were so, which [tradition] would the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*—which increases wisdom and compassion—be describing? Answer:
According to Jñānavardhana, the Sūtra states:

"In the world-system called Most Excellent Indra-Lofty Banner, they shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they shall be of the same lineage and bear the same name, namely, Pure Face Utpala Fragrant Mountain, fully endowed with the ten titles."
"In this manner, ten thousand Buddhas appeared in succession in the world.
The following four lines record the names of the lands.
*Indra* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Imperial High Banner" (*Dìgāodāng*). Land.
Next, from "attaining the state of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" downward, five [points] record the fruits.
"Belonging to the same lineage" refers to six [points] recording the lineage and seven [points] recording the marks.
8. The following section is recorded as "Thus" (evam).
Sūtra: At that time, the deity of the Bodhi tree addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

These ten thousand devaputras have come from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the presence of the Buddha in order to hear the Dharma; why has the Tathāgata immediately bestowed upon them the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood?
“World-Honored One!

I have never before heard that these sons of the gods have fully practiced the six pāramitās and performed such difficult asceticisms as giving away their hands, feet, heads, eyes, marrow, and brains; their kinsmen, wives, and children; their elephants, horses, and carriages; their slaves, servants, and attendants; their palaces, gardens, and groves; and their gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, jade, and shells; as well as their food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—just as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas have done by offering all manner of requisites to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of past Buddhas.”
In this way, each of these bodhisattvas must pass through immeasurable and boundless kalpas before they finally receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhy-avyākaraṇa*).

World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions, by practicing what superior conduct, and by planting what roots of goodness, have these sons of heaven come from that celestial realm and, upon hearing the Dharma for a brief moment, immediately received their prediction?

Alternatively, that which first arises is called the root (*mūla*), and that which is subsequently cultivated is called the practice (*caryā*);

Regarding the intent of its introduction: this is for the purpose of removing doubts;
whereas the preceding chapter was for the purpose of establishing the exhortation to accept [the teaching].

Although I have previously provided a brief response, I feared that my previous general exposition might be difficult to understand upon hearing; therefore, I shall now explain it more extensively, which is why the "Curing Illness" and "Flowing Water" chapters were composed.
However, as for the distinction: since the ten thousand past causes are about to be explained, their causal origin is first related, which constitutes the "Chapter on Eliminating Illness.
Furthermore, fearing that the suffering of illness might hinder the preaching and hearing of the sutra, it is also clarified how to eliminate it, so that one may rely upon and study [the teaching].
Since the dependent origination has already been elucidated, it is necessary next to provide a formal analysis; thus, the "Flowing Water" chapter begins.
Paramārtha’s commentary states:

"This 'Curing Illness' chapter correctly clarifies the causes for bestowing the prediction [of enlightenment], thereby forming the 'Bestowing Prediction' chapter; it incidentally reveals Śākyamuni’s practice, thereby forming the 'Life Span' chapter."

The subsequent "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body" (*Śarīra-parivarta*) correctly elucidates the causal practices of Śākyamuni, thereby forming the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta*);
the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) incidentally reveals the cultivation of the disciples.

However, while curing illness serves as a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) and flowing water serves as a proximate condition (*āsanna-pratyaya*), although the meaning may indeed be so, the textual structure is somewhat loose.

Since the causes for the lifespan have already been extensively explained previously, including the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) and so forth, why is the cause now being explicitly clarified once again?
Since these are cultivated in a single lifetime, how can they be distinguished as distant or near?

It would not be problematic to interpret them as having the sense of inferior, middling, and superior; nor would it contradict reason to distinguish them as distant or near based on their respective strengths and weaknesses. However, to judge them as the primary causes for the lifespan itself is a rather remote interpretation of the text.

Regarding the explanation of the title: "illness" (*vyādhi*) refers to the various major elements being in conflict and causing harm; "removal" (*apoha*) refers to the ability of medicine to counteract and dispel them. Since this chapter extensively clarifies these matters, it is titled the "Chapter on the Removal of Illness" (*Vyādhipraśamana-parivarta*).
Regarding the resolution of this objection:
A question is raised concerning the previous "Chapter on the Lifespan," where Wondrous Banner reflects:
"The Tathāgata cultivated the causes for a long life through compassion and non-harming; why then is his lifespan so short, lasting only eighty years?"
Although it was previously stated that his lifespan is boundless, the practice of compassion and non-harming has not yet been explained.
Now, these three chapters precisely clarify this very practice; how could they not be the primary teaching?
Answer: Sudarśana merely doubted that the causes and conditions for his practice would result in long life; he did not doubt that his long life was due to causes from the past.

Furthermore, this chapter states, "I shall now explain to you the causes and conditions of the original vows of ten thousand devaputras," but it does not say that it explains the causes and conditions for [his] long life.

Furthermore, the "Flowing Water" chapter states: "By virtue of hearing the twelve links of dependent origination from Ratnaśikhin and listening to this sutra, through the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, he has now received the prediction of enlightenment."
It does not state that one obtains a long life by means of this;
therefore, it belongs to the *pravartana* (circulation) section and is not part of the *mūla* (main teaching).
The Sūtra records: The Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree deity:

Sūtra: “At that time, within the king’s realm, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who all encountered pestilence; oppressed by manifold sufferings, they lacked even a heart of joy.”
"Good Woman Devī!

At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water (Jalavāhana), seeing these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings suffering from various ailments, gave rise to a heart of great compassion and thought to himself:

'Immeasurable sentient beings are oppressed by extreme sufferings. Although my father, the elder, is skilled in medical formulas and proficient in the eight arts of healing, capable of curing all diseases caused by the increase or decrease of the four great elements, he is now advanced in years, decrepit, aged, and frail; he can only move forward with the aid of a staff and can no longer travel to cities, towns, or villages to rescue those suffering from illness.'"

"Now there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have all contracted grave illnesses for which no one can provide a cure; I shall now go to my father, the Great Physician, to inquire about the secret methods of medical prescriptions for treating diseases."

Once you have attained this understanding, you should go to cities, towns, and villages to rescue sentient beings from their various diseases, enabling them to experience peace and happiness throughout the long night of saṃsāra.
Below, the fourth section clarifies the conditions for practicing medicine; it consists of six parts: first, the simultaneous arising of various illnesses;

Sūtra: At that time, having formed this thought, the son of the householder went immediately to his father’s place. He prostrated at his feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side. He then addressed his father with a verse, saying:
“Compassionate Father, please have pity on me; I wish to save sentient beings.”
I now request the methods of the physicians; I pray that you will explain them for me:
How does the body decline with advancing age, and how do the great elements increase or diminish?
Furthermore, at what time do various diseases arise?
How may one consume food and drink so as to obtain peace and happiness, and ensure that the internal bodily heat does not diminish?
Sentient beings have four types of illness—wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination; how are these to be treated?
When does the wind disorder arise?
When does the heat disorder manifest?
When is the phlegm-mucus stirred up?
"When will they all assemble and be born?
Below this, the fifth section concerns approaching his father to seek instruction, which has two parts:
first, the etiquette of the inquiry; second, from "Then with a gāthā" onwards, the actual request made in verse.
The five verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse is a plea for compassion and a request for the teaching;
the subsequent four verses constitute the formal entreaty, which consists of five points:

The first half-verse asks about the cause of the illness; the next half-verse asks about the time the illness arose; the following verse asks about the method of nursing; the next verse asks about the method of medical treatment; and the final verse asks about the season when the illness originated.
The previous question concerned the time of initial onset; this question concerns the timing of when the illness has already been provoked.
There are two such times:

Sūtra: “At that time, having heard his son’s request, the elder replied to him with a verse, saying:
‘I shall now explain to you, in due order, all the methods for treating illness according to the ancient seers; listen well as I save sentient beings.’”
Three months constitute the spring season; three months are named summer; three months are named the autumnal equinox; and three months are called the winter season.
Based on this division of the year into groups of three, each consisting of two [two-month] periods, there are thus six seasons in a year.

The first two months are the season of flowers; the third and fourth are called the Hot Season; the fifth and sixth are called the Rainy Season; the seventh and eighth are said to be the Autumn Season; the ninth and tenth are the Cold Season; and the final two are called the Season of Ice and Snow.
Having understood these distinctions, administer medicine so as not to cause harm.
One should adjust one's diet according to the current season, ensuring that what enters the stomach is digested and dispersed; thus, manifold ailments will not arise.
When the seasonal nodes change and the four elements shift, if one lacks medicinal support at such times, suffering from illness will inevitably arise.
A physician who understands the four seasons and further knows the six nodes, who is clear and proficient in the seven constituents of the body, can employ food and medicine without error.
This refers to the realm of taste, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and brain; when disease enters these, one must know whether it can be cured.
There are four distinct types of disease—namely wind, heat, phlegm, and their combined accumulation—and one should recognize the time of their onset.

In the middle of spring, phlegm and mucus are stirred; in summer, wind diseases arise within; in autumn, yellow-fever increases; and at the winter solstice, all three arise together. In spring, one should eat astringent, hot, and pungent foods;
in summer, unctuous, hot, salty, and sour; in autumn, cold, sweet, and unctuous; and in winter, sour, astringent, unctuous, and sweet.
Among these four periods, regarding the administration of medicine and food: if one follows such flavors accordingly, no illnesses will arise.

Illness after eating arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*); when digestion is occurring, it arises from heat (*pitta*); and when digestion has ceased, it arises from wind (*vāta*). One must recognize the illness according to these times.

Once the source of the disease has been identified, one prescribes medicine according to that ailment; even if the symptoms differ, one must first treat the root cause. For wind disorders, oily substances are prescribed;

for heat disorders, purgation is excellent; for phlegm disorders, emesis should be applied. When these are combined, all three medicines are required; when wind, heat, and phlegm coexist, this is termed "combined" (saṃnipāta).
Although one knows when the illness arises, one should contemplate its fundamental nature.
Having thus contemplated and understood it, one administers medicine according to the timing; providing food and medicine without error—this is called a skilled physician.
The sixth section below provides an explanation by the father.
This consists of the initial summary of the compilation, followed by thirty-two verses beginning with "I now rely on the ancient seers," which constitute the father’s formal versified commentary.
This is divided into three parts:
first, one verse that grants permission to explain; second, thirty verses that provide the actual explanation; and third, one verse that provides a concluding summary.

The first four verses establish the seasonal periods.

Second, blood; third, flesh; fourth, fat; fifth, bone; sixth, marrow; seventh, brain.

Inferring from these five elements accordingly: phlegm is water, wind belongs to wood, and heat is fire.

When [the disease] manifests violently, it can also be treated at this time.

First observe their physical form, speech, and temperament; then inquire about their dreams to discern the distinctions between wind, heat, and phlegm disorders.
One who is emaciated, has scant hair on the head, and whose mind lacks stability [is afflicted by wind].
One who talks much, dreams of flying, and possesses a windy nature;
one whose hair turns white in youth, who perspires profusely, and who is prone to anger;

The mind is settled and the body is upright; one’s deliberations are careful and the head feels oily.
Dreaming of water or white objects—these should be known as the nature of *āmaya* (phlegm).

Having already understood one's own fundamental nature, one prescribes medicine according to the illness; only when it is verified that there are no signs of death can one be called capable of saving a person.

The left eye changes to white, the tongue turns black, and the bridge of the nose slants; the earlobes differ from their former state, and the lower lip droops downward.
The *harītakī* fruit alone possesses six tastes; it can eliminate all diseases and, being free of dietary prohibitions, is the king among medicines.

The Chapter on the Householder’s Son Jalavāhana (6). The twenty-fifth chapter, "The Chapter on the Householder’s Son Jalavāhana," is analyzed according to three headings.

Regarding the purpose of this discourse: although ten thousand beings received their predictions at the end of the previous "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions," the celestial maidens gave rise to doubts.
Because it was not yet clearly explained there, the two subsequent chapters, "Curing Illness" and "Flowing Water," provide a more extensive analysis so that the assembly may gain deep understanding.

Thus, it says below: "Because in the past I rescued fish with water, gave them food until they were full, explained to them the profound twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) along with the corresponding dhāraṇī-mantra, and further invoked the name of that Buddha Ratnaśikhin, by virtue of these roots of goodness, I was born in the heavens."
"Those who now come to me and joyfully listen to the Dharma, I shall all bestow upon them the prediction of Bodhi.

Named after its practice, this represents the simultaneous manifestation of both conduct and virtue.
