The meaning of Liu-shui (Flowing Water) is broad; because he saved fish, he also benefited other species, and thus it is not titled solely "The Chapter on Saving Fish."
Sūtra. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess: "Good Goddess!

In the past, the son of a householder named Flowing Water (Jalavāhana) healed all the ailments and sufferings of sentient beings within the realm of King Sovereign Light of Heaven (Devasvairaprabha), restoring them to health and enabling them to experience peace and happiness."
At that time, because their illnesses had been cured, the sentient beings cultivated many meritorious deeds and practiced extensive acts of giving to bring themselves joy.
They went together to where the son of the elder was, and all conceiving feelings of reverence, spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O son of a great elder!
You are truly skilled at nurturing matters of merit and increasing our peace, security, and lifespan.

You are indeed a king of physicians of great power; a compassionate Bodhisattva, expertly versed in medicine and pharmacology, who skillfully cures the immeasurable sufferings and illnesses of sentient beings."
"In this manner, they offered praise throughout the city.

This chapter is divided into four parts: first, praising the physician’s capability; second, from "Good Goddess" onwards, clarifying the practice of saving the fish; third, from "At that time the Buddha told... onwards, correlating the present with the past; and fourth, from "At that time the great assembly... onwards, their realization and reliance upon the teachings.
The first section further contains four parts:

first, the elimination of various illnesses through the initial binding; second, the increase of meritorious karma among the multitude, beginning with "At that time, all sentient beings..."; third, the multitude’s journey to pay homage and offer praise, beginning with "...they went together to visit..."; and fourth, the summary of their renown, beginning with "...thus they extolled and praised... and so forth.
Sūtra: "Good Woman Devī!
At that time, the wife of the elder’s son was named Jaladhārāgarbha, and she had two sons: the first was named Jalamati, and the second was named Jalagarbha."
The following section clarifies the practice of rescuing fish.

The text is also divided into four parts: first, it clarifies the bodhisattva’s retinue; second, from "At that time, Flowing Water... onwards, it clarifies his rescue of the fish; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, it clarifies how the various devas heard his praise; fourth, from "The Buddha addressed the Good Goddess... onwards, it clarifies how the fish repaid his kindness.
This is the first [section].

The Sūtra says: "At that time, Śrotapāla took his two sons and traveled gradually through cities, towns, and villages. Passing through a vast wilderness and a place of deep peril, he saw various beasts of prey—jackals, wolves, foxes, monkeys, vultures, and eagles—all of whom were carnivorous; yet they all fled and flew away in one direction."
At that time, the son of the elder had this thought:
"For what cause and condition are these birds and beasts all flying up together?
I should follow after them for a moment to observe."
He then followed after them and saw a great pond named Wild Growth, its waters nearly exhausted.
Within this pond there were many fish; upon seeing them, the flowing water gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half of its body and spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You who possess the true meaning of the name 'Flowing Water' (Srotas-vāha), you should take pity on these fish and give them water.
There are two reasons for being named 'Flowing Water':
first, one can cause water to flow; second, one can bestow water."
"You should now act in accordance with its name.
At that time, Flowing Water asked the tree deity,
"How many heads do these fish have?"
The tree deity replied,
"The number is ten thousand. O Good Goddess!
When the son of the elder heard these numbers, his heart of compassion redoubled.
At that time, this great pond had been scorched by the sun until very little water remained.

These ten thousand fish were on the verge of death; they rolled their bodies and writhed about, and seeing the elder with a look of hope, they followed him and gazed at him, never once averting their eyes.
When the son of the elder saw this, he ran toward the four directions seeking water, but in the end he could find none.
Looking off to one side, he saw a great tree, whereupon he immediately climbed it, broke off branches and leaves, and made a shade for himself.
He further investigated from where the water in this pool came.
Searching without ceasing, he saw a great river named Jālinī.
At that time, there were fishermen by the side of this river who, for the sake of catching fish, had diverted the water at a steep and dangerous point upstream so that it would not flow downstream.
Since the place where it had been cut was extremely difficult to repair, he thought to himself:

"This cliff is deep and precipitous; even if a hundred thousand people were to work for three months, they would not be able to finish the cutting, let alone a single person like me being capable of completing the task."

Then the son of the elder quickly returned to his native city and went to the place where the great king was. He prostrated himself with his head at the king's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:
"For the sake of the great king, I have treated the various ailments of the people within the kingdom, causing them all to be secure and at ease."

Traveling by stages, he arrived at a desolate marsh where he saw a pond named Wild Growth; its waters were nearly exhausted, and ten thousand fish lay exposed to the sun, on the verge of death before long.

I only pray that Your Majesty, out of compassion and pity, will grant me twenty great elephants for a short time to go and carry water to save the lives of those fish, just as you have preserved the lives of myself and these other sick people.
At that time, the great king immediately commanded his ministers to swiftly provide this King of Physicians with a great elephant.
Having received the king’s command, the ministers said to the son of the elder:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
"O Benevolent One, you may now go yourself to the elephant stables and select twenty elephants as you please, to benefit sentient beings and bring them peace and happiness.

At that time, Flowing Water and his two sons took the twenty elephants and borrowed many leather bags from a wine shop; they went to the place where the water was being diverted and filled the bags with water. The elephants carried the bags back to the pond and poured the water into it, whereupon the water immediately filled it completely, restoring it to its former state.
The following clarifies his rescue of the fish, which consists of eight parts:
first, the father and son travel abroad;
second, from "He saw various birds and beasts" onwards, it clarifies the observation of extraordinary signs.
3. From "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards is the Bodhisattva’s reflection.
4. From "He then followed after them" onwards is his observation immediately following his reflection.
5. From "He saw a large pond" onwards is his eventual sight of the parched fish.
6. From "Having seen this, the Flowing Water [King]" onwards, he immediately gives rise to a heart of compassion.
7. From "At that time, there was a tree deity" onwards, the tree deity exhorts him to rescue [the beings]; herein there are three parts:
first, manifesting its form for the sake of the urgent distress;...
Second, from "He spoke these words" onwards is the section on praise, intended to inspire the arousal of the bodhicitta;
third, from "Good son, you possess the true meaning" onwards is the section on exhortation to rescue others, so that the name may accord with its meaning.
Within this, there are again three parts:

first, the initial exhortation; second, the explanation of the exhortation beginning with "There are two causes and conditions"; and third, the concluding exhortation beginning with "You should now..."
8. "At that time, the Water-Flowing [Merchant]" and below, according to the request, provides the means for salvation.

This section further contains six parts: first, the question regarding the number; second, from "The Tree Spirit replied" onwards, the answer that there are ten thousand; third, from "Good Goddess" onwards, the intensification of compassion; fourth, from "At that time, this great pond" onwards, the clarification of the suffering endured by the fish; fifth, from "Seeing this elder" onwards, the various fish’s longing for rescue; sixth, from "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards, the actual salvation through compassion.
Within this, there are further two parts:
first, saving others from suffering through compassion; second, "furthermore reflecting" and below, bestowing happiness through loving-kindness.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Proclaiming the True Dharma is happiness, for it serves as the cause for experiencing happiness in future lives."
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts to the relief from suffering:
first, the giving of water; second, the giving of food, beginning with the passage "At that time, the Elder, the Good Woman Devī...
There are eleven instances of giving water:

1. First, he searched everywhere for water and found none; 2. Second, from "Again looking toward one side" onwards, he acted temporarily to provide coolness; 3. Third, from "Again further searching" onwards, he sought out the source of the pool; 4. Fourth, from "At that time, by the riverbank" onwards, he saw that the source had been breached; 5. Fifth, from "Then he thought this" onwards, he reflected on the difficulty of repairing it; 6. Sixth, from "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards, he requested an elephant from the king; 7. Seventh, from "At that time, the great king" onwards, the king issued an urgent command to grant it; 8. Eighth, from "At that time, the chief minister" onwards, the official in charge selected [the elephant]; 9. Ninth, from "At that time, Jalavāhana" onwards, he obtained the elephant and his wish was fulfilled; 10. Tenth, from "Furthermore, from the tavern" onwards, he borrowed a wine-sack; 11. Eleventh, from "Going to the place where the water was breached" onwards, he transported water to fill the pool, and it was restored to fullness.
Sūtra: “Good Goddess!
At that time, the son of the elder walked around the four sides of the pond, looking about; at that moment, those many fish also followed him, moving along the bank.”
At that time, the son of the elder again thought to himself:
"For what reason do these many fish follow me?
They must surely be tormented and oppressed by the fire of hunger, and wish to seek food from me."
"I shall now give it to you.
At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water said to his son:

"Take one of the most powerful elephants and go quickly to our home. Inform your father, the elder, and collect all the edible things available in the house—including the portions for your parents' own consumption, as well as those for your wife, children, and servants—and bring them all here."

At that time, having received their father’s instructions, the two sons mounted the largest elephant and went quickly to their home. Upon reaching their grandfather, they related the aforementioned matter; they then gathered all the edible items from the house, placed them upon the elephant, and returned swiftly to their father’s location at the edge of the pond.

At that time, when the Flowing Water saw his son arrive, his body and mind leaped with joy; he then took food and scattered it throughout the pond, and once the fish had received the food, they were all fully satiated.
2. The second of the practices for rescuing suffering through the cultivation of compassion: the offering of food, which consists of twelve parts.

1. First, the elder surveys the scene; 2. Second, from "At that time, those fish... onwards, the fish also look back in response; 3. Third, from "At that time, the elder’s son... onwards, the elder reflects upon them; 4. Fourth, from "Surely they must be tormented by the fire of hunger... onwards, he knows the afflictions of the fish; 5. Fifth, "I shall now give [them]" refers to his compassionate thought of giving; 6. Sixth, "At that time, the elder’s son... commands his sons to fetch food; 7. Seventh, from "At that time, the two sons... onwards, the sons go to their grandfather and report; 8. Eighth, from "He gathered the food from the house... onwards, they obtain the food and return; 9. Ninth, from "At that time, Jalavāhana... onwards, the elder’s heart is filled with joy; 10. Tenth, from "He then took the cakes and food... onwards, he immediately distributed it everywhere to the fish; 11. Eleventh, from "The fish, having received the food... onwards, the fish are satisfied and satiated.
The Sūtra says: "He then thought:
'I now give this food so that these fish may obtain life; I vow that in future lives I shall provide the food of the Dharma to sustain and deliver infinite beings.'"
Thus ends the twelfth section, "The Elder’s Vow," from the Sūtra.
The text continues: "He further reflected:
'In the past, while in a secluded forest, I saw a bhikṣu reading a Mahāyāna sūtra, which expounded the profound essential teachings on the twelvefold dependent origination.'"
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
"If there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death, hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens.
I shall now expound for these ten thousand fish the profound twelvefold dependent origination, and I shall also recite the name of the Buddha Ratnaśikhin.
However, there are two kinds of people in Jambudvīpa:
first, those who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna;
second, those who lack faith and disparage it. One should also act for the sake of increasing the faith of the latter.
In the section on "Compassion and Right Rescue," the second part concerns bestowing happiness through a compassionate mind.
This has two sections:
first, internal reflection; second, from "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards, external practice for benefit and happiness.
The beginning and middle [of this section] further consist of three parts: first, recollecting what was heard in the past;
second, from "I now" onwards, contemplating the intention to preach for the sake of the fish; [and third, the actual preaching].

The subsequent section, beginning with "Now, as for Jambudvīpa," also benefits human beings; this is because, in the following passage, the fish receives a beneficial reward for its kindness toward the elder, and the king, ministers, and others hear the cause and thereby develop deep faith.
The three phrases follow their respective order in the Sūtra: "At that time, the son of the elder thought to himself:
'I shall enter the pond and preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the sake of the fish.'"
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the water and cried out:
"Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān of the past, Ratnaśikhin!"
In the past, when this Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this vow:
"May all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who hear my name at the time of their death be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three after they pass away."
"Thus it is said. Regarding the benefit and happiness for those outside [the assembly], there are two parts:
first, the intention to enter the pond;
"making this thought" and below is the actual performance of the benefit, which further contains two parts:
The first part is for the purpose of invoking the Buddha’s name;

from "At that time, Flowing Water" onwards is for the exposition of the profound Dharma, which serves both to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed and to bring understanding to those who already believe.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the section]: first, the name of the Buddha is invoked; the passage from "In the past, this Buddha... onwards explains the reason for invoking this particular Buddha.

In the sutra, the section from "At that time, Flowing Water further expounded such profound and wondrous Dharma to the fish in the pond" onwards constitutes the teaching of the Dharma, which has two parts:
First is the explicit teaching, followed by the esoteric teaching.
Alternatively, first the Dharma is taught so that they may understand, and subsequently the mantras are taught for protection.
Within the former [the explicit teaching], there are again two parts:
First is the general heading, followed by the detailed explanation.
This is the heading.
Sūtra: “Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.”
There are two explanations below.
The first clarifies the dependent origination of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), which follows the sequence of the forward progression (*pravṛtti*) through birth and death;

the second, beginning with "Because this ceases, that ceases," clarifies the dependent origination of purification (*vyavadāna*), which follows the sequence of the reverse cessation (*nivṛtti*) through the elimination [of afflictions].

However, each of these two types of dependent origination has two modes of contemplative practice: the forward and the reverse. Here, each is explained according to the forward order, which implicitly reveals the two reverse orders.
Within the first [of the two], there are again two parts:
first, the individual headings; second, the detailed explanations following the words "That is to say."
This is the first [section].
According to the fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, it is taught that there are three types of dependent origination:
first, non-active dependent origination; second, impermanent dependent origination; and third, functional dependent origination.

The first two types of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) apply to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whereas the third type of dependent origination pertains specifically to sentient beings.
However, in most textual passages, the explanation is primarily based on the twelve links of dependent origination, as these constitute the fundamental framework.
Regarding the statement "because this exists, that exists" and so forth, these correspond respectively to the first two [principles].
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because this exists, that exists" clarifies the meaning of dependent origination without agency (*nirīha*).
It is solely because conditions exist that resultant phenomena come to be; it is not that conditions possess a real, functional activity capable of producing resultant phenomena.

This is stated in order to refute the arbitrary assertions of various non-Buddhists who maintain that the Great Brahma or the Self (ātman) possesses a real, functional activity that serves as the cause of things; thus, it is said that conditions do not possess a real, functional activity capable of producing resultant phenomena.
Furthermore, in order to refute the false speculations of non-Buddhists regarding causelessness, it is said: "Because this exists, that exists;
because this arises, that arises. This clarifies the meaning of dependent origination through impermanent conditions.
Since it is not the case that non-arising phenomena serve as causes, few arising phenomena can be established.
This refutes the non-Buddhist view that eternal phenomena serve as causes capable of producing all things, and it also precludes the existence of the future.

The Mahīśāsaka school and others maintain that there are twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because they enable the arising of dependent origination without confusion; thus, it is said that even if there were no dharmas produced by causes, a small number of produced dharmas could still be established.

As for what is called "profound," there are five kinds: it is profound because of its cause, because of its characteristics, because of its arising, because of its abiding, and because of its transformation; such is the meaning of profundity.

The details are as explained in that commentary. The Sūtra says: "That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair."

With the cessation of this, that ceases; that is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; and with the cessation of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"In this way, this entire mass of pure suffering is completely extinguished.
This concludes the specific explanation of dependent origination; it is the third [section], concerning the functional efficacy of dependent arising.

Because the causes and conditions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are distinct, each possesses its own functional efficacy. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Although all phenomena are uncreated and impermanent, it is not the case that a single phenomenon acting as a condition gives rise to all effects, for the capacities of phenomena are each distinct."

The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "At the time of separation through death, the contact of the mental faculty (*manas*) is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*); the contact of the five physical faculties is called suffering (*duḥkha*); the utterance of weeping cries is called lamentation (*parideva*); and the feverish heat of the ignorant mind is called despair (*upāyāsa*)."
This is based on the sequence of the arising of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
The statement "with the cessation of this, that ceases" and what follows clarifies the sequence of the progressive contemplation of purification (*vyavadāna*) leading to its cessation.
The text consists of three parts:
First is the heading, second is the explanation, and third, from "Thus, purely and utterly" onwards, is the specific conclusion.
Regarding the meaning of this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it shall be briefly analyzed by way of four sections:
first, the determination of its essence; second, the explanation of its name; third, the contemplative practice; and fourth, questions and answers.
First, regarding the essential nature of the member of ignorance (*avidyā*):

within the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), that which specifically refers to the capacity to produce and induce either general or specific retributions—or exclusively general retribution—within the category of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) constitutes the essential nature of the member of ignorance;
as for the inclusive members, this extends to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual discrimination, since ignorance is their underlying essence.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 8, states: "In this context, ignorance refers exclusively to that which can initiate karma that truly brings about good or evil results in future lives.
It further states: "That which directly initiates karma is severed only by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*); its auxiliaries are not so determined."
"This [karma] is associated with both common and uncommon entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) as well as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

As for the nature of the constituent of formative action (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), it comprises wholesome and unwholesome bodily, vocal, and mental karma; its nature consists solely in producing collective retribution and in producing both collective and individual results."
Only that which produces a specific retribution (*pratiniyatavipāka*) is not a member of the *saṃskāra* (formative) stage.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Only that which is produced by those [ignorance and craving] is called *saṃskāra*.
For this reason, all karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and all auxiliary karma for future lives are not members of the *saṃskāra* stage."

This also encompasses both the manifest and the seeds; conventionally, it may be said to include the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—and their informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*), but in reality, it is solely volition (*cetanā*).
As for the essence of the "consciousness" member (*vijñāna-aṅga*), it refers exclusively to the seeds of the eighth retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "In this context, 'seeds of consciousness' refers to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). It specifically refers to the seeds of the eighth consciousness that are the maturation (*vipāka*) induced by the member of 'formative forces' (*saṃskāra*), because it is that which first links rebirth and serves as the sovereign of the total retribution; it does not include active manifestations (*pravṛttivijñāna*) or other evolving consciousnesses."

In some places, it is stated that [the *vijñāna* branch] includes both active manifestation (*samudācāra*) and the six consciousnesses; however, this is a general explanation of the *vijñāna* branch and does not correctly define its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, it is said to include active manifestation based on the state of its future arising; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because at the time of the cause there is definitely no sense of active manifestation... and so it is for the *vedanā* branch as well."
Regarding the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Excluding the last three causes, all other causes are subsumed within the seeds of name-and-form.
As for the last three causes, they correspond in sequence to the latter three types [of seeds]."

This explains that these five members are not intermingled, constituting a presentation of the actual dependent origination as it is gathered within a single moment by the process of activity (*saṃskāra*).
In reality, even the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) within the causal phase do not possess a sequential order.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This is explained according to the sequence of their actual manifestation.
If based on actual manifestation, it is not only the case that they are produced by karma, nor are they substantial entities."

Speaking in terms of developmental stages (*avasthā*), the seeds of the six ripening sense-faculties are called the limb of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the seeds of ripening contact and feeling are the limbs of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*); and all other ripening phenomena apart from these four are called the limb of form (*rūpa*).

However, when the sūtras state that "name" refers to the four non-material aggregates and "form" refers to the kalala and so forth, this is also based on future and present form, as well as on form in a general sense; it does not refer to the specific link of "form" within the dependent origination formula.
As it is said that consciousness and name-and-form (nāmarūpa) serve as mutual supports for one another, like bundles of reeds, they likewise depend upon both future and present name-and-form.
Within the explanation of "name" (nāman), the seventh [consciousness] is generally designated as "name"; otherwise, the analogy of the bundles of reeds would not be established.

Furthermore, according to the actual reality, the constituents of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) consist of only two aggregates (*skandha*); feeling (*vedanā*) constitutes the limb of feeling, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitutes the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), because the treatises state that name-and-form and the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are neither provisional nor composite.
Furthermore, it is said that this is because the last three causes are excluded.
If that is so, how can it be stated that "name" refers to the four aggregates that are not form?
This also does not contradict [the previous explanation], as it has already been reconciled above.

The treatise further explains: "Alternatively, 'name-and-form-seeds' (nāmarūpa-bīja) subsumes all five causes; among these, the other four types are established according to their predominance. The same applies to the relationship between the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and consciousness (vijñāna), whether taken collectively or individually."
Therefore, the Sūtra states that "name" refers to the four types of affection (*maitrī*); this is according to the general designation.
If divided into five branches, it is explained according to their specific distinctions.
As for the essential nature of the branch of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is also exclusively innate (*sahaja*); its auxiliary moistening function is not fixed.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That which directly moistens rebirth is exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The afflictions (*kleśa*) of all realms are all capable of moistening rebirth," which is said by way of including those that assist [the process].

Furthermore, regarding the grasping for delusive phenomena, although it generally takes both internal and external dharmas as its objects, treatises mostly state that what arises by taking external objects as its condition is termed the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
As for the essential nature of the limb of grasping (*upādāna*), it generally employs all co-emergent afflictions (*kleśa*), while its auxiliary function extends to conceptualized afflictions.

In some places, it is taught that "clinging" (*upādāna*) is defined solely by the intensification of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although other afflictions are included within the member of clinging, craving is predominant in its moistening [of rebirth]; therefore, it is said that craving increases."
Furthermore, based on their initial and final stages, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished; in reality, they subsume the remaining afflictions.

Both the members of craving and grasping encompass both seeds and manifest states. The member of existence (*bhava*) consists of the seeds of the five results—namely, the preceding formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which, once moistened by craving and grasping, are designated as "existence."

In some places, only karma is designated as a "limb of existence" (*bhavāṅga*); the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains this by stating: "Because it is this [karma] that directly brings about the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

In other places, only the five factors beginning with consciousness are designated as limbs of existence; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because they directly produce the five factors, beginning with consciousness, during the future stages of birth, aging, and death."
"This refers only to seeds and does not extend to active manifestations.

Regarding the nature of the branch of birth (*jāti*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "From the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) and before it undergoes decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the branch of birth."

Regarding the members of old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The various stages of decay and transformation are collectively termed 'old age,' while the dissolution of the body and the end of life are termed 'death.'"
"The substance of these two members both pervades the five aggregates; they consist solely of active manifestations and are subsumed under the category of maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The twelve links of existence all possess both the 'time of the seed' and the 'time of the fruit.'"

Regarding the statement that both seeds and manifest states are simultaneously present, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains: "The factors that project and those that are projected arise at one and the same time; they are taught in succession merely for the sake of exposition, as there is no difference in their essential nature."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states: "Based on the stage already moistened, it induces [the result] simultaneously; for the times when [the seed] is moistened and not yet moistened are necessarily not concurrent.

This is stated from the perspective of mutual dependence (*lakṣaṇānugama*), and does not mean that, in their actual essential nature (*dravya-svabhāva*), both seeds and manifest phenomena are universally pervasive.
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction arise from old age and death; they are not included among the [twelve] members.
Second, regarding the explanation of names: this explains only the general name and does not analyze the individual names.
While there are many explanations in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, I shall now provide a brief fourfold explanation based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
One explanation states:
Because one is bound by afflictions (*kleśa*) and repeatedly arises within the various realms of existence (*gati*), it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is an interpretation based on the characters *pratītya* (arising from conditions) and *samutpāda* (origination).
The second [teacher] says:
It is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because, having rapidly perished based on various conditions, it arises again in a continuous synthesis;
this is an explanation based on the meaning of momentary arising and ceasing.

This distinguishes [the Sarvāstivādins] from the Mahāsāṃghikas and others who hold that [conditioned phenomena] are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as well as from the Saṃmitīyas, who maintain that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) exist throughout the duration of a single life.
The third [explanation] states:
"Because the various conditions have passed away yet are not abandoned, and because [the effect] arises based upon its own continuum, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*)."
As it is said: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.
This is not another meaning, as explained previously.
The fourth [point] says:
Having awakened to the nature of conditions in past lives, they arise in equal succession; therefore, it is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As the Blessed One said:
"I have awakened to this, and thus I proclaim its equal arising."
It is precisely because it is transmitted from one to another by this name that it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the practitioner of the three contemplations, there are two distinct types of contemplation:
first, that which relies on the contemplation of defilement; second, that which relies on the contemplation of purity.

Each of the two contemplations has two categories—conformable and inverse; thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium of Higher Knowledge), chapter four, states: "Because of the conformable and inverse [orders] of defilement, and because of the conformable and inverse [orders] of purification."

Regarding those that accord with defilement, they are explained according to the sequence of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*): namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations, up to birth conditions aging and death; this is the successive arising of birth and death.
Regarding the "adversaries of affliction" (*saṃkleśa-pratipakṣa*), according to the teaching on the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*), there are two distinct types:
first, the contemplation of the distant preparatory stage (*dūre-prayoga*) prior to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), which constitutes seventy-seven cognitions (*jñāna*).
Second, regarding the observation of the proximate preparations (*upakaraṇa-prayoga*), one generates forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*).
This is either because there is a distinction between the two paths of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*),
or because both constitute the application, differing only in their sequence.
Furthermore, regarding the observation of the seventy-seven knowledges (*jñāna*): one contemplates that present old age and death exist by virtue of what?
One concludes that they exist by virtue of present birth.
Furthermore, one observes that it is not the case that old age and death do not arise from present birth; because the present self-body is produced by oneself, two knowledges are thus established.
The same applies to old age and death conditioned by the past and future; with two [contemplations] for each, they constitute six modes of observation.

Since beginningless time, all instances of old age and death have been conditioned by birth; although they have not yet arisen in the future, there remains the possibility of their being defiled or of their cessation.
Therefore, observing the defiled states now also accomplishes two types of wisdom.
Within the three periods of time, first, because old age and death exist due to the member of birth, one observes that the effect has a cause; this is the wisdom that infers the cause.
Second, one further contemplates that old age and death do not occur without arising; this is the wisdom that scrutinizes causes.

First, the notion of causeless arising is refuted, and subsequently, notions such as spontaneous arising are refuted, thereby distancing oneself from the false conceptualizations of the various non-Buddhist schools.

Seventh, furthermore, the various types of contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) not subsumed under the [twelve] links (*aṅga*) are called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) because they have the sense of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Thoroughly knowing the teachings on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) throughout the three periods of time is what is meant by "not subsumed under the links."
The first six [knowledges] take principles as their object and know them as they truly are; these are the wisdoms of reflection and cultivation, termed "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*).

The seventh takes the teachings as its object; because it is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), it is termed "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthitijñāna*) and is also called "conventional knowledge" (*prajñaptijñāna*).
These combine to form seven types of knowledge.

Just as there are seven types of knowledge when contemplating old age and death, there are likewise seven types of knowledge for each link down to the constituent of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

With the sole exception of ignorance (*avidyā*), which lacks a knowledge of its own cause, the total becomes seventy-seven due to this omission of the causal factor; this applies equally to both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the forty-four knowledges: this refers to contemplating old age and death as the truth of suffering; contemplating the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death; and so on, up to contemplating the suffering of the constituent of formations (*saṃskāra*), the origin of formations, the cessation of formations, and the practice leading to the cessation of formations. Since there are four aspects for each of these eleven [constituents], they constitute forty-four [knowledges].
Because ignorance has no cause, it is not one of the forty-eight [factors].
This is a contemplation of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); therefore, it is called "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*).
Alternatively, whether one contemplates the essence as being with outflows, or contemplates phenomena that are with outflows, this then accords with noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
The scriptural text contains only the forward progression and not the reverse.
Regarding the contemplation of the pure forward progression, it means that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until because birth ceases, aging and death cease.
Contemplating in forward order refers to explaining this based on the sequence of the stages of abandonment.
Contemplating in reverse order means: "Due to the absence of what is there the absence of old age and death?
Due to the cessation of what does old age and death cease?"
"Up to: by the absence of what are the volitional formations absent?
By the cessation of what do the volitional formations cease?
This is stated in reverse order based on the contemplation of the ultimate stage upon attaining the fruit, for the purpose of bringing [the practitioner] to maturity.

Regarding the fourth section, the analysis through questions and answers: Question—For what reason are there many distinctions among the members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as taught in various places, such as being presented as either manifest or seeds, or collectively or individually?
Answer: All the various distinctions have been largely concluded in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
This present exposition of the essential nature is based on the authentic Mahāyāna teaching of true dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Other explanations differ; some combine the provisional and the real regarding the states that will arise in the future, because not all stages of arising in the present are produced by karma.

Alternatively, there are cases where this is explained generally according to the three vehicles; for example, the simultaneous faculties are called "name" (*nāman*), and the mind that has just ceased following form is called "name," and so forth.
Question:

Within the context of the sequential contemplation, as it is stated in certain passages, why is it said that when one contemplates the links of dependent origination, one may retreat back as far as the link of consciousness?

Answer: This is stated with reference to the initial stage of cultivation within the inverted contemplations based on defilement, specifically the preparatory practice of the contemplation of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*). Why is this so?

Just as one contemplates the suffering of old age and death, the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death—likewise, one should sequentially contemplate all the truths as they apply, since they are subsumed within the truth of suffering by way of the factor of old age and death.
Within dependent origination, one first observes it in reverse order, contemplating the factor of old age and death through three aspects:
first, its subtle causal conditions; second, its coarse causal conditions; and third, its causal conditions that do not produce birth indeterminately.
The subtle refers to craving, grasping, and becoming; the coarse refers to the factors of birth and the physical body. From these two, birth arises, and with it, old age and death.
Herein, the intention is to explain the dependent origination of mixed conditions by observing two lifetimes in conjunction.
One should contemplate that old age and death have subtle birth as their cause, which consists of craving, grasping, and becoming;
whereas the old age and death of the present life have gross birth as their cause, which is the link of birth itself.
Apart from these two births, nothing else can certainly produce the fruit of old age and death; this is called "not indeterminate.
This [birth] is also a scrutinized cause, which is called "not indeterminate.
By analogy, one should know that the two births are the causes of old age and death; this is the inference of the cause.
This is the contemplation on the origin of aging and death.

Although one contemplates the truth of the origin of aging and death back as far as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one is not yet fully satisfied regarding the suffering of the future limit (*aparānta*) along with its origin. Consequently, one further examines the present sufferings that have their cause in the future origin—namely, by contemplating in reverse order feeling (*vedanā*), contact (*sparśa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Contemplating future suffering is the contemplation of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) for the future; contemplating its causes is the contemplation of the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*) for the future.
From what does the truth of the origin of future suffering arise?
One knows it arises from the prior accumulation, with consciousness as its limit.
Since one already knows that the existence of suffering in the present life arises from prior accumulation, one should not further contemplate how it comes to be.

Furthermore, consciousness and name-and-form are like a bundle of reeds, mutually conditioning one another without an agent; therefore, when one investigates, the process turns back at the level of consciousness and does not extend to the factors of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Having thus observed the ten branches of the arising of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*), one next contemplates the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*): how shall these factors, beginning from old age and death back to ignorance, be brought to an end?
By not creating new formations (*saṃskāra*) conditioned by that ignorance, that suffering will finally cease.

Seeking in succession to realize the path to this cessation, one recollects the teaching on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) received from former teachers and friends, causing right view regarding the world to arise in the present.
By observing in this manner repeatedly, the vision is increased; this is the contemplation of the reverse order of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
This contemplation of the cessation of aging and death, as well as the path leading to their cessation, leads directly to ignorance.
Herein, for the time being, we refer only to the two present and future branches of aging and death along with their causes, and thus briefly omit the past aging and death and their causes.
Furthermore, regarding that which has already ceased, one does not seek its further cessation; this is because the four truths are observed in conjunction.
If one applies the seventy-seven knowledges (*jñāna*), they are distinguished according to the three periods of time.
Another interpretation:
Alternatively, when one contemplates present old age and death by observing their proximate and remote causes, all such causes are past, extending back to the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
If one contemplates future old age and death, they proceed from existence (*bhava*) down to craving.
If craving and what precede it are considered future suffering, this is based on the sequence of their arising.
Otherwise, seeds do not function as successive conditions (*pāramparyapratyaya*).
According to the former interpretation, present and future old age and death should be contemplated together, whereas their causes are contemplated separately.
This interpretation views "causes" collectively and views "old age and death" individually.
It is not only the branch of old age and death that is viewed in reverse; viewing the future accumulation of suffering is also a reverse contemplation.
Question:
Question: Why is it stated in some places that the sequence from the contemplation of ignorance up to birth stops there?
Answer: This is explained in accordance with the faculties, inclinations, and dispositions [of sentient beings] when investigating cause and effect.
Old age and death have no further fruit; they simply culminate in the link of birth.
Question:
Why is it that some [contemplate] in reverse order up to the link of name-and-form?
Answer: This is explained according to the seed of karma as the "consciousness link," because consciousness is subsumed within "name-and-form.
The Sūtra states: "Having spoken this Dharma, he further spoke the Dhāraṇī associated with the twelve links of dependent origination, saying:"

Kill the peacock!
Kill the peacock! Sphaliṣaṇi!

Jāti (the first *jāti* pronounced with the *ting-li* [tǐng-lǐ] tone; the same applies to the following) *nir-jāti* (without birth).
Niṣaṭi niṣama ni niṣamani niḥ.
"Jamanini svāhā. This concludes the second section on the secret exposition of the origin story (*nidāna*).
First, the preceding section is summarized and introduced; next, the mantra is formally recited.
[End of] Sūtra.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was expounding for the great assembly the past karmic conditions of the elder’s son, the multitude of devas and humans marveled at what they had never before experienced.
Then, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each in their respective places, spoke with one voice in these words:

“Excellent, Śākyamuni Honored One! You have proclaimed this sublime Dharma and illuminating mantra, which generates merit and eliminates all evils, corresponding to the twelve links [of dependent origination].”

We, too, shall recite mantras to protect such a Dharma; should there be those who give rise to opposition or fail to comply with it, their heads shall split into seven pieces, just like the tips of a *lāṅgalī* flower.
"In the presence of the Buddha, we shall together recite this mantra:

Tadyathā | Hirimaye | Kete-gandhāri | Caṇḍāli-dhare | Sādhare | Śikhivare | Pūṣpavare | Damanati | Kīramati-dadhimukhe | Kurupamurupa | Kutamuru-kandhe | Duru duru-vire | Ene-sitte | Datta-uṣṭrā-vati | Apsarā-vati | Padumā-vati | Kusumā-vati | Svāhā. [This concludes] the third section on the various devas hearing the praise within the "Saving the Fishes" chapter.
There are three parts:
first, the heading;
second, from "At that time, the great assembly... onwards, the entire assembly rejoices together.
Following this, the section beginning with "At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings" constitutes a separate praise, which has two parts:
first, praising the Buddha’s teaching; second, reciting the dhāraṇī for protection.
Within the first part—praising the Buddha’s teaching—there are further two sub-sections:
First is the heading, followed by the praise.
The subsequent section, beginning with "We also shall recite mantras," constitutes the second vow of protection, which has three parts:
the first two lines provide the heading; the next four lines offer exhortation and instruction; and the final section, beginning with "In the presence of the Buddha," sets forth the mantras.
Sūtra: The Buddha told the goddess Bhadrayaśā:
"At that time, the elder’s son Flowing Water and his two sons, having provided water and food for the fish in that pond and having preached the Dharma to them, all returned home together."
Later, at another time, the merchant’s son Flowing Water was gathered with others for a banquet; having enjoyed various musical performances and become intoxicated, he lay down to sleep.
At that moment, ten thousand fish simultaneously passed away and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. They then had this thought:
"By what causes and conditions of wholesome karma have we been born in this heavenly realm?"
They then said to one another:

"Previously, within Jambudvīpa, we fell among the animals and shared the bodies of fish. The elder’s son, Flowing Water, bestowed water and food upon us, and further expounded for us the profound Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination and the dhāraṇīs, as well as the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin. By these causes and conditions, we have been able to be born in this heaven."
"Therefore, we should now all go to that son of a householder to repay his kindness and make offerings.
At that time, the ten thousand devaputras immediately vanished from the heavens and arrived at the place of the Great King of Physicians in Jambudvīpa.

At that time, the son of the householder was sleeping peacefully atop a high tower. Then, ten thousand devaputras together placed ten thousand pearl necklaces at his head, another ten thousand at his feet, another ten thousand at his right side, and another ten thousand at his left side. They rained down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers until they reached the height of his knees; their radiance shone everywhere, and various celestial musical instruments produced wondrous sounds, causing all those in Jambudvīpa who were asleep to awaken.

The merchant’s son, Flowing Water, also awoke from his sleep; at that time, the ten thousand devaputras, having made their offerings, immediately soared away through the air, raining down exquisite celestial lotuses everywhere throughout the kingdom of King Sovereign Light of Heaven.

These devaputras returned once more to their original location at the pond in the empty marsh, where they rained down various celestial flowers; then, vanishing from that place, they returned to their heavenly palaces, where they enjoyed the pleasures of the five desires as they pleased.
When King Devendraprabha reached the break of dawn, he asked his ministers:
"For what reason did such a rare and auspicious omen suddenly appear last night, emitting such a great radiance?"
The minister replied:

"Great King, you should know that there were hosts of devas who rained forty thousand pearl necklaces and celestial māndārava flowers upon the house of the elder’s son, Jalavāhana, until they reached the height of his knees."
The king said to his ministers,
"Go to the house of the elder and summon his son.
Having received the command, the great minister went immediately to that house and proclaimed the king's decree to summon the elder’s son.
Then the son of the elder went to the king’s presence, and the king asked:
"For what reason did you manifest such a rare and auspicious omen last night?
The son of the elder replied:
"As I reflect upon it, these must surely be the fish from within that pond who, as the sutra describes, were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after their lives ended."
"He has come to repay his debt of gratitude; therefore, he manifests such a rare and extraordinary sign.
The king asked, "How do you know this?"
The Flowing Water replied, "Your Majesty may dispatch a messenger along with my two sons to that pond to verify its truth or falsehood: whether those ten thousand fish are dead or alive."

Upon hearing these words, the king immediately dispatched messengers and his son to the edge of that pond; there they saw that within the pond many *mandārava* flowers had accumulated into a great heap, and all the fish were dead.
Having seen this, he hurried back and related it in detail to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
This concludes the fourth section, clarifying how the fish repaid its debt of gratitude within the narrative of "Rescuing Fish from Below," which consists of fourteen parts.
1. The three youths return home.
2. From "This son of the elder" onwards, the son of the elder lies drunk and asleep.
3. From "At that time, ten thousand fish" onwards, the fish pass away and are reborn in heaven.
4. From "He gave rise to this thought" onwards, he recollects and knows his past karma.
5. From "Therefore, I now" onwards, he deliberates upon the debt of gratitude that ought to be repaid.
6. From "At that time, ten thousand" onwards, he repays the kindness; herein there are further three [sections]:

First, descending from heaven; second, from "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards, repaying his debt of gratitude; third, from "Then he vanished from this place" onwards, concluding his affairs and returning to heaven.

Within the section on repaying his debt of gratitude, there are three parts: first, repaying the kindness of the elder; second, from "To King Svayambhūprabha of the devas" onwards, repaying the kindness of the king—since it was the king who lent him the elephant and protected the Buddha-dharma so that he might hear it; and third, from "These sons of the devas" onwards, repaying the kindness of his place of birth.
7. From "The King, Sovereign Light of Heaven" downward, the king inquires about the auspicious omen.
8. From "The Great Minister replied" downward, the various ministers provide a full account.
9. From "The King said to his ministers" downward, the king orders a messenger to summon [the subject].
10. From "At that time, the son of the elder" onwards: the elder’s son attends to the summons.
11. From "The King said" onwards: the King personally questions him. 12.
From "The son of the elder said" onwards: the elder’s son provides a full response.
13. From “The king asked, ‘Why... onwards, he examines the reality of the matter.
14. From “When the king heard this... onwards, he gives rise to faith and joy.
Sūtra: At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree deity:
“Good Goddess! You should know that the son of the elder Flowing Water of former times was none other than myself, and the elder Holding Water was none other than Wondrous Banner.”
Of those two sons, the elder, Jalamdhara, was this very Silver Banner; the younger, Jalagarbha, was this very Silver Light.
That King Divākaraprabha was none other than you, the tree deity of the Bodhi tree; and the ten thousand fish were none other than these ten thousand devaputras.

Because in the past I rescued fish with water, fed them until they were full, and for their sake expounded the profound twelvefold dependent origination along with this associated dhāraṇī mantra, and further invoked the name of that Buddha Ratnaśikhin—by virtue of these roots of goodness, they have been born in the heavens and now come to me to joyfully listen to the Dharma. I shall bestow upon them all the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and proclaim their respective names.
“O Good Goddess!

Just as I, in the past, while cycling through the various realms of birth and death within saṃsāra, extensively benefited others, causing immeasurable sentient beings to all gradually attain unsurpassed awakening and bestowing upon them their predictions of enlightenment.”
"You all should diligently seek liberation; do not be negligent.
This third section of the lower grade concludes by correlating the present with the past.
It consists of four parts:
First, the reconciliation of the Bodhisattva and his father;
second, from "That Deva-Īśvara" onwards, the reconciliation of the tree deity;

third, from "The ten thousand fish" onwards, the reconciliation of the devaputra, which further consists of three parts: first, the reconciliation of the person; next, from "Because of me" onwards, the reconciliation of the Dharma; and finally, from "By virtue of this root of goodness" onwards, the reconciliation of how the attainment of the prediction results from these roots of goodness.
IV. "The Good Goddess" below exhorts faith and practice.

At that time, having heard this teaching, the great assembly all attained realization and understanding: that it is only through great compassion to rescue and protect all beings and through the diligent cultivation of ascetic practices that one can realize unsurpassed bodhi. They all gave rise to a profound mind of faith, accepted it with joy, and were filled with gladness.
The fourth section below concerns realization based on training.
Question:

Since this chapter states that it is for the purpose of removing the doubts of the great assembly regarding the causes by which the sons of the gods receive their predictions, how can it be understood that the great assembly’s realization arises from practicing various ascetic austerities through great compassion in order to attain bodhi?

Answer: According to the assembly where the prophecy was conferred, only the devaputras were formally prophesied; it is clear that this was solely for the purpose of removing the doubts of the great assembly regarding why the devaputras received their prophecies.
As for the statement that they attain bodhi by practicing great compassion and so forth, this is merely an incidental meaning.
Furthermore, knowing that ten thousand others had also practiced asceticism and so forth before finally attaining bodhi, he therefore practiced and studied them all as well.
Chapter 26: Relinquishing the Body (Six). Chapter Twenty-Six: Relinquishing the Body is analyzed according to three sections.

Regarding the intent of this passage: within the section on "Learning, Practice, and Dissemination," there are five parts. The fifth part establishes the intent for learning and practice as presented in the preceding chapters; this intent has three aspects, and this is the third, which further exhorts and encourages by means of this teaching on the relinquishment of the body.

Why is this? Fearing that those who hear it said that by practicing for one's own benefit one shall attain Buddhahood might still be unable to apply themselves to it, [the text] cites the *sattva* who, for the sake of benefiting others, should sacrifice even body and life; how much more so, then, should one practice this sutra for one's own sake?
Therefore, it is said that he sacrificed his body.
Thus, the subsequent sutra states: "I have recounted for you the conditions of my past altruistic deeds; such bodhisattva practices, which are the causes for attaining Buddhahood, should be studied."

Furthermore, fearing that upon hearing it said that Buddhahood is achieved through minor practices, their minds might give rise to contempt and negligence, [the Buddha] cites the practice of self-sacrifice to exhort the assembly to rely upon and study it.

Thus, the subsequent sutra states: "The Bodhisattva’s supreme virtues correspond to wisdom; with courageous diligence, they perfect the six perfections. Constantly practicing without ceasing for the sake of Bodhi, they enter into a firm mind of equanimity, free from weariness."
The preceding section concerned the primary intention, while this section provides a comprehensive clarification; both serve to explain the underlying purpose. Regarding the title:

for the sake of seeking Great Enlightenment, one constantly cultivates compassion and wisdom. Encountering a field of suffering, one vows to sacrifice body and life rather than preserve a noble position, looking down with pity upon those in distress and performing deeds that are difficult to practice. This is designated as the chapter title and called the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body" (Śarīraparityāga-parivarta).
To resolve this objection, one asks:
Within the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, during which eon (*kalpa*) is this relinquishing of the body performed?
The answer is:
The original text has not been seen.

According to tradition, [the bodhisattva] relinquishes [his body] during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa; this is because his practice during the first kalpa was still inferior, and he was thus unable to perform such a sacrifice of body and life.
By this standard, it should be understood that the latter two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are also applicable.
Question:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, one definitely undergoes the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; how, then, can there be the discarding of physical remains?
Answer: This is a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
Question:
If that is so, why not manifest other flesh to give to the starving tigress instead of manifesting the sacrifice of one's own body?
Answer: Giving by manifesting one's own body brings greater benefit to sentient beings.
Question:
If that is so, why does the old *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* state, "By sacrificing his body to feed the tigress, he transcended eleven kalpas"? Answer:
This too is a transformation.
Question:
If that is so, why do the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* and other texts state, "Maitreya Buddha awakened his bodhicitta forty kalpas before Śākyamuni"?
The *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* and other texts state: "Due to his diligence, Śākyamuni surpassed Maitreya by forty kalpas and attained buddhahood first.
Answer: Because the roots of those to be converted (vineya) ripen at different times—earlier for one and later for the other—it is said that these two bodhisattvas have such a surpassing of kalpas.
If that were not so, how could it be said that from the eighth ground onwards there is progress moment by moment?
Since both increase simultaneously, how could there be any skipping? Furthermore, another explanation states:

Regarding "increasing manifold," while one may progress manifoldly compared to previous stages and one's own practice for self-benefit, such increase is not necessarily the case regarding the practice for the benefit of others; therefore, it is said that the obstacle of being unwilling to practice for the benefit of others is abandoned upon entering the ninth stage.
Another interpretation:
because it combines the two preceding meanings, it can be said to be "transcendent.
Question:

If the severance of obstacles to benefiting others occurs in the ninth bhūmi, how is it that Śākyamuni completed his cultivation over three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas, yet within the hundred kalpas [of the final period], upon encountering Puṣya Buddha, he stood on one foot in praise and thereby transcended nine kalpas?
Answer: Because it is for the sake of producing what is appropriate, there is no fault.
Question:

Why is it that sacrificing one’s body is not the fruit of accomplishing the Tathāgata’s lifespan, yet the practice of asceticism is cited to exhort others to uphold the sutra for the sake of self-benefit?
Answer: According to the previous account, the Bodhisattva Subhaketur merely doubted the lifespan, as it did not correspond to the cause of long life.
Having no doubt as to what practice must be cultivated to attain long life, there is no need for further elaboration.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One had already explained to the great assembly these past causes and conditions of the ten thousand devaputras.
The commentary states:
Regarding the text of this chapter, it is divided into four major sections:

first, the account of the past sacrifice of the body; second, from “Again he addressed Ānanda” onwards, the correlation between the ancient and the present; third, from “I shall speak for you all” onwards, the exhortation to practice and study; and fourth, from “At that time the World-Honored One” onwards, the benefits obtained by the assembly upon hearing [the teaching].
The first part is divided into three sections:

first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent one to serve as the opening of the discourse; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the sequence of the offering of the body at the Caitya is presented; third, from "Again he addressed Ānanda" onwards, the primary benefit of the past offering of the body is discussed for the sake of the assembly.
This first section further consists of three parts;
this first part is the sūtra-master’s summary of what preceded.
The Sūtra continues: He again addressed the Bodhi-tree deity and the great assembly:

"In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not merely provide water and food to save those fish from death; I even sacrificed my own beloved body. You should all observe these causal conditions together."
Next, following the World-Honored One’s lead, there are four sections:

first, the announcement to the assembly; second, from "Not only... onwards, pointing back to the previous brief explanation; third, from "Even unto... onwards, further elaborating on the superior causes; and fourth, from "In this way... onwards, exhorting and admonishing the assembly at that time.

Sūtra: At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the most supreme and most honored one above and below heaven, whose hundred thousand rays of light illumine the worlds of the ten directions, who possesses all-encompassing wisdom and is perfected in merit—accompanied by the bhikṣus and the great assembly, went to a forest near the village of Pañcāla. That ground was level and free of thorns, and it was strewn with exquisite flowers and soft grasses.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You may prepare a seat for me beneath this tree.
Then, having received these instructions and prepared the seat, Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!
The seats have been prepared; may the Sage know the proper time.
Following this, there are two introductory points for the discourse that follows:
First, praising the Buddha’s virtues, the Honored One manifests light to assemble the multitude.
Second, from the passage "taking the bhikṣus" onwards, he leads the assembly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As for the term *Pañcāla*, it means "total gathering"; it is also called *Pañcāla* because one cages lions and other such animals in a net.
Because the people of this very place capture lions and other such beasts and keep them in cages, this name was established.
A place where people gather is called a *grāma* (village);
*grāma* also refers to a courtyard.
According to the *Account of the Western Regions*, this site is located in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, which belongs to the territory of North India and lies to the northwest of the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

This place where he sacrificed his body is on the northern border of Takṣaśilā; crossing the Indus River and traveling two hundred li southeast, one passes through a great stone gate, where Prince Sattva sacrificed his body to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.
The soil there, along with all its grasses and trees, was tinged slightly with a crimson hue, as if stained with blood.
When people stepped upon that ground, it felt like walking on thorns; regardless of whether they were skeptical or faithful, none failed to feel profound sorrow.
3. From "The Buddha addressed the Venerable One" onwards, the Buddha commands Ānanda to prepare the Dharma seat; first the command, then the acceptance of the decree, and finally the request.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon the seat, with body upright and mind fixed in right mindfulness, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to see the original relics of that Bodhisattva who practiced austerities in the past?"
The bhikṣus said, "We wish to see it.

The World-Honored One then pressed down upon the ground with his hand, adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits. At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways and immediately split open; a caitya made of the seven precious gems suddenly surged forth, its summit adorned with nets of various jewels.
When the great assembly saw this, they were filled with wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, paid homage, circumambulated it to the right, and returned to his original seat.
He then addressed Ānanda: "You may open the door of this caitya."
Then Ānanda opened the door and saw a casket of the seven precious gems, adorned with various rare treasures; he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Here is a casket of the seven precious gems, decorated with many jewels.”
The Buddha said, "You may open the casket.
Then Ānanda, having received these instructions, opened it and saw that the śarīra were as white as snow or the *kumuda* flower. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The casket contains śarīra, their color wondrous and extraordinary.
The Buddha said: "Ānanda!..."
"You may take these bones of the Great Being and bring them here.
At that time, Ānanda immediately took those bones and presented them to the Blessed One.
Having received them, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You all should contemplate the bodily relics of the Bodhisattva who practiced asceticism.
Then he spoke in verse:

“The Bodhisattva’s wisdom was conjoined with supreme virtues; Through courageous diligence, the six perfections were perfected. He constantly cultivated them without ceasing for the sake of enlightenment, With great renunciation and firm resolve, his mind never weary.”

"You monks, you should all pay homage to the original body of the Bodhisattva; these relics are the most supreme field of merit, perfumed by the incense of immeasurable morality, concentration, and wisdom, and are exceedingly difficult to encounter."
At that time, all the bhikṣus and the great assembly, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms in reverence and prostrated themselves before the śarīra, exclaiming that it was unprecedented.
Then Ānanda came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
“The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has transcended all things and is revered by all sentient beings; for what reason and by what cause do you pay homage to these skeletal remains?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“It was because of these bones that I swiftly attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. To repay his past kindness, I now pay him homage.”
The following section presents the sequence of Cien’s self-sacrifice.
This is further divided into eighteen segments;
the first inquires into the sentiments of the assembly.
2. From "The bhikṣus said" onwards is the assembly’s response, expressing their joy in seeing [the miracle].
3. From "The World-Honored One then" onwards is the Buddha manifesting his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Question:
"Why not simply cause the stupa to appear directly, rather than having it ascend only after being pressed down by his hand? Answer:
"If he were to cause the stupa to appear directly without pressing it with his hand, the great assembly would not know of the Buddha's supernatural power."
There are three [stages]:
first, the hand presses the earth; second, the earth shakes; third, the earth opens.
Fourth, beneath the "Stūpa of the Seven Jewels," a precious stūpa surges forth.
The term *caitya* is a Sanskrit word that generally refers to the halls and stupas of the Buddha.
To distinguish them specifically: a Buddha hall is called a *caitya*, which here means "sacred deposit" (or "enshrinement"). The older transliteration *zhiti* is erroneous.
The term *stūpa* is translated here as "highly manifest" (*gāoxiǎn*). Former translations such as "Buddha-tower," "tāpó," or "lún pó" are all erroneous.
This section consists of three parts:
first, the emergence of the *caitya*; second, the various adornments; and third, the vision of the great assembly.
Question:
Why did the stūpa where [the Buddha] relinquished his body not vanish into the air but instead sink into the earth? Answer:

To reveal that the *dharmakāya* relics within the cause are obscured by hindrances and cannot manifest until they are brought forth through the Buddha’s skillful means, they remained hidden in the earth and rose up only when the ground was pressed.
5. From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards is the section on repaying kindness and paying homage.

This is comparable to hungry ghosts whipping their own corpses or devas prostrating before withered bones; the intent is to cause the multitude to cultivate the causes [of virtue], and thus repay past kindness.
6. From "He addressed Ānanda" below, he issues the command to open the stūpa.
7. From "At that time, Ānanda" below, he receives the mandate and respectfully opens it.
This section contains two parts:
First the stūpa was opened, and next the casket was beheld.
Section Eight: From "He addressed the World-Honored One" onwards, he offers his report based on what he has seen.
He reveals that the Tathāgatagarbha is endowed with inherent merits; therefore, the precious casket is adorned.
9. From "The Buddha said" onwards, he further commands the opening of the casket.
10. From "At that time, Ānanda" onwards, the Joyful One (Ānanda) acts according to the instruction; this section has two parts:
first, the opening of the casket, and second, what is beheld therein. This represents that the nature of reality is pure and not defiled by external things, like a white lotus flower.
11. From "He immediately said" onwards, Ānanda speaks again.
12. From "The Buddha said" onwards, the Buddha commands him to bring it.
13. From "At that time, Ānanda" onwards, Nandika (Ānanda) presents the offering.
14. From "The World-Honored One accepted" onwards is the section on the conditions for the Buddha’s acceptance and exposition, which has three parts:
first, the Buddha’s acceptance; second, the exhortation to contemplate; third, the eulogy in verse. 15.
From "You all" onwards is the World-Honored One’s instruction on prostration, which contains two parts:
First, he commands them to prostrate; second, he explains the reason why.

Regarding the fivefold dharma-fragrance, three categories are cited as examples for two types: "precept" refers to *prātimokṣa*; "concentration" and "path" refer to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); "wisdom" is according to its name; "liberation" is the mental factor of resolve (*adhimokṣa*); and "knowledge and vision of liberation" is wisdom that takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
These matters are explained in detail in works such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* and the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.
Section sixteen, from "At that time, all... onwards, concerns the worship and praise according to the teaching.
Section seventeen, from "At that time, Ānanda... onwards, concerns the inquiry into the reason for the Buddha’s worship.
18. From "The Buddha told" below, the reason for the veneration is answered.
The Sūtra continues: He further addressed Ānanda:
"I shall now, for you and the great assembly, sever all doubts by explaining the past causes and conditions of these śarīras."
"Reflect well upon this; you should listen with a single-minded focus.
Ānanda said, "We are eager to hear it; we pray that you will explain it for us."

“Ānanda! In a past age, there was a king named Mahāratha. He was immensely wealthy with vast treasures filling his storehouses; his army was brave and martial, held in awe and submission by all. He constantly transformed the common people through the True Dharma, and his subjects were flourishing and prosperous, free from any enemies.”

The State Lady gave birth to three sons, whose countenances were so upright and handsome that all who beheld them found them pleasing. The eldest son was named Mahāpāla; the middle son was named Mahādeva; and the youngest son was named Mahāsattva.
The following section discusses the occasion when [the Buddha] in the past sacrificed his body for the sake of true benefit;
