the text is divided into three parts:
first, the command to listen and permission to speak.
Second, the two assemblies desire to hear;
third, the correct exposition for their benefit, which itself consists of two parts:
first, the prose (long passage), and second, the verse (repeated stanzas).

The prose section consists of ten parts: first, the description of the former retinue; second, from "At that time, the Great King" onwards, the narration of past joyful excursions; third, from "The eldest prince" onwards, the arising of sorrow upon encountering suffering; fourth, from "At that time, the Sattva" onwards, the contemplation of sacrificing one's life; fifth, from "At that time, the prince" onwards, the relinquishing of the body for rescue; sixth, from "At that time, the great earth" onwards, the auspicious signs moving gods and humans; seventh, from "At that time, the starving tiger" onwards, the tiger’s subsequent ability to eat; eighth, from "At that time, the Great King" onwards, the lamentation and longing of the retinue; ninth, from "At that time, the Great King" onwards, the erection of a *caitya*; tenth, from "Ānanda" onwards, the conclusion showing the benefit to sentient beings.
Regarding the description of his former kinsmen, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the time; second, describing his parents; and third, speaking of his brothers—the textual sections are clear.
As for "Mahāprajāpatī," this is translated here as "Great Leader."
Mahādeva means "Great God" in this language. Mahāsattva means "Great Heroic Resolve.

One who seeks great bodhi and gives rise to great heroic resolve does not shrink from sacrificing body or life throughout time and circumstance; because they seek the Dharma and benefit sentient beings with constant lack of parsimony or retreat, they are called "Great Heroic Resolve."
Therefore, the following verse says: "The prince named Courageous always gave with a heart free from stinginess. The Sūtra states:

"At that time, the Great King, wishing to travel and enjoy the sights of the mountain forests, was followed by his three princes. Seeking flowers and fruits, they left their father and wandered about until they reached a great bamboo grove, where they rested within it."
The following section recounts past joyful excursions.
This passage consists of three parts:
first, the king goes out on an excursion; second, his ministers and attendants all follow him; and third, the prince separately pursues the pleasures of the hunt.
Question:
Since it was said that when the king went out on an excursion, the prince followed him, why is it stated that upon hearing the prince had sacrificed his body, he was in the palace? Answer:
According to previous translations, it was simply stated that the prince departed without mentioning his father;
this [account] omits the circumambulation and lacks the detail of the return to the chariot.
In reality, the son followed behind while the king returned ahead; therefore, the report that he abandoned his body in the palace is not erroneous.
Sūtra: “The first prince spoke thus:
‘Today my heart is filled with great alarm; will there not be some fierce beast in this forest that will harm me?’”
The second prince spoke again, saying:
"I have no initial reluctance toward my own body; rather, I fear the suffering of separation from those I love.
The third prince addressed his two elder brothers, saying:
"This is the dwelling place of the divine seers; I have no fear or sorrow of separation. My body and mind are suffused with joy, and I shall attain all manner of supreme merits."
"At that time, each of the princes spoke of the matters they had been contemplating in their own minds.
This concludes the third section, "Encountering Suffering and the Arising of Compassion," which contains three parts:
The initial account of their prior reflections consists here of two parts:
first, the three younger princes each present their own statements; second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the princes... onwards, the narrator provides a summary conclusion.

Sūtra: “Proceeding further on, he saw a tigress who had recently given birth to seven cubs; only seven days had passed since their birth. Surrounded by her offspring, she was oppressed by hunger and thirst, her body so emaciated that she was on the verge of death.”
Later, he saw the tiger again, emaciated with hunger.
He asked:
"I saw the tiger give birth; how do you know it has been exactly seven days?"
Answer: The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha offers two interpretations.
The first states:
"That which is sustained by solid food lasts for only seven days; beyond this, one dies."
The tiger was so famished that it knew [the time] to be seven days;
another account says that at that time there must have been spirits or deities who told it, though the compilers of the sutra did not record this.

It is also like making a vow while sacrificing one's body such that no one hears or knows of it, yet later a celestial deity reports it, as when the tree spirit spoke of the number of fish in the pond.
The Sūtra states: "The first prince spoke thus: 'Alas!
This tigress has been giving birth for seven days; her seven cubs surround her, leaving her no leisure to seek food. Driven by hunger and thirst, she will surely devour her own offspring.'"
Prince Sattva asked, "What does this tigress usually eat?
The first prince replied:
"Tigers, leopards, jackals, and lions feed only on warm flesh and blood; there is no other food or drink to sustain these tigers from their emaciation.
Having heard these words, the second prince spoke thus:
"This tiger is so thin and weak, oppressed by hunger and thirst that its remaining life is but a short time. How can we possibly seek such rare food and drink for it?"
"Who else could sacrifice their own life for this purpose to rescue them from the suffering of hunger?
The first prince said,
"Of all things difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one's own body."
The Prince Sattva said:
"We now each harbor attachment to our own bodies; furthermore, lacking wisdom, we are unable to bring benefit to others."
Afterward, they were filled with sorrow and deliberated together.
Within this section, there are seven parts;
first, the Prince beholds suffering and feels compassion.
2. From "The Prince Sattva" downward, Sattva asks what he eats.
3. From "The First Prince" downward, the Crown Prince answers that he eats flesh and blood.
4. From "The Second Prince" downward, Mahādeva hears [the account] and gives rise to stinginess and fear.
5. From "The First Prince" downward, the Crown Prince describes the difficulty of sacrificing his body.
Six: Regarding the "Prince Sattva," the discussion on his advancing and retreating consists of three parts:
first, reproaching one's own incapacity; second, attributing power to others; and third, reflecting through mental examination.
First, the critique of their own incapacity has three causes:

first, they possess attachment; second, from the phrase "furthermore, they lack wisdom" downward, it is because they lack great wisdom; third, from the phrase "they are unable to" downward, it is because they lack great compassion.

Because of attachment, one cannot generate a mind of weary detachment toward conditioned phenomena; because of a lack of great wisdom, one cannot generate the mind that seeks enlightenment; and because of a lack of great compassion, one cannot generate the mind that benefits sentient beings. Consequently, one is unable to sacrifice one's body for the sake of benefiting others.
The Sūtra says: "However, there are superior persons who, harboring a heart of great compassion, constantly benefit others by forgetting their own selves to save all beings.
This passage below demonstrates the power of benefiting others.
This also has three aspects:
first, possessing great wisdom, which refers to those who are superior persons;
second, possessing great compassion, which refers to those who harbor a mind of great compassion and so forth.
Third, forgetting one’s own body to save others is itself non-attachment, through which one can cultivate weary detachment from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
As the Sūtra says: "Again, he reflects:

'This body of mine has been wasted and decayed in vain throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, providing no benefit day by day; why then today cannot I renounce it to relieve the suffering of hunger, as if discarding mucus or spittle?'"
Thus, he lowered his mind to reflect and examine himself.
Within this, there are three points:
first, he reflected on how he had previously wasted his life and body to no end.
Next, from "How is it that today... onwards, one reflects on why one is currently unable to relinquish what benefits sentient beings.

Subsequently, from "Just as one discards mucus and spittle... onwards, one should generate a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*); for just like mucus and spittle, one should relinquish impermanent form (*anitya-rūpa*) in order to attain permanent form (*nitya-rūpa*).

Sūtra: “At that time, after the princes had deliberated thus, each gave rise to a heart of compassion and, moved by sorrowful pity, they gazed together at the emaciated tigress without blinking for even a moment; after lingering there for a long while, they all departed together.”
The seven younger sons, overcome with grief, bowed their heads and departed.
At that time, Prince Sattva thought to himself:
"Now is the very moment for me to sacrifice my body and life."
For what reason?
For a long time I have maintained this body, which is foul-smelling, filthy, and flows with pus—unlovely.
Yet I have provided it with bedding and requisites, as well as clothing, food, drink, elephants, horses, carriages, and precious wealth.

The nature of things subject to transformation and decay is impermanent; they are ever difficult to satisfy and difficult to preserve. Though constantly provided for, they harbor resentment and malice, ultimately abandoning me without acknowledging my kindness.
Furthermore, this body is not firm; it is of no benefit to me.
It is as terrifying as a thief and as impure as excrement.
Today, I shall cause this body to cultivate vast deeds, acting as a great vessel upon the ocean of birth and death, casting off saṃsāra so that liberation may be attained.
The fourth section below, "Contemplating that one should relinquish life," has six parts:
first, the arising of the thought to relinquish life;

second, from "For what reason" onwards, employing mental attention (*manasikāra*) as a strategy—namely, entering into the desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*), because this is produced by fundamental mental attention.

That is to say, one applies attention according to reality to the four foundations of mindfulness: with the first two lines, one contemplates impurity; with the next three lines, one contemplates impermanence; and with the final two lines, one contemplates suffering.
Constantly seeking what is difficult to satisfy is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
that which is difficult to preserve is the suffering of separation from the beloved;
harboring resentment and malice is the suffering of old age, sickness, and death.

The next line contemplates non-self (*anātman*): although the mind may aspire for happiness, it does not arise from a self; ultimately, it returns to abandoning the self. Within the cycle of the five destinies, it abandons that which is ungrateful; therefore, there is no self.
Third, from "Furthermore" onwards, there is the abandonment of aversion and the seeking of aspiration, which has two parts:
first the cause, and later the result.
Within the cause, there are three [subdivisions]:
First, one becomes weary of and detached from the conditioned; this consists in contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness:
that this body is not solid and is impermanent;
that it is of no benefit to a self and is without self.
It is as terrifying as a thief—there is no joy in it;
it is as impure as excrement—it is not pure.
Next, from "On this day" onwards, he seeks bodhi.
Regarding the section following "In the ocean of birth and death," it concerns the benefiting of sentient beings.
Because one performs deeds with this very body to benefit living beings, it is termed "cultivation in the causal stage";
however, once one has passed into a subsequent birth, it is simply termed "the fruit."
The Sūtra says: “Again, he reflects thus:
‘If one relinquishes this body, one relinquishes immeasurable abscesses, malignant diseases, and hundreds of thousands of fears.

This body contains nothing but excrement and urine; it is as unsubstantial as a bubble, a gathering place for various worms, and held together by veins, arteries, sinews, and bones—it is truly loathsome.’”

Therefore, I should now renounce [this world] in order to seek unsurpassed, ultimate *nirvāṇa*, forever departing from affliction, impermanence, and suffering; bringing an end to birth and death and severing all worldly entanglements; and through the power of concentration and wisdom, fully cultivating the hundredfold adornments of merit to achieve the omniscience and the subtle *dharmakāya* praised by all Buddhas.
"Once he has attained this realization, he shall bestow immeasurable Dharma-joy upon all sentient beings.
At that time, the prince aroused great valor and made a vast vow, strengthening his resolve with thoughts of great compassion.
The following clarifies rejoicing in the fruit, which also has three parts;
first, the wearying detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
According to the *Vimuttimagga*, there are ten perceptions of impurity (*aśubhasaṃjñā*):

First, bloated; second, livid; third, festering; fourth, discarded; fifth, devoured by birds and beasts; sixth, the flesh of the body torn apart; seventh, hacked and scattered; eighth, smeared with blood; ninth, worm-infested and foul-smelling; tenth, the contemplation of bones.
These ten are exclusively impure; in this present passage, however, the four foundations of mindfulness are explained collectively. Regarding the abscesses and so forth, there is no pleasure;
regarding the excrement and urine, there is only impurity;
and as for their lack of solidity, like bubbles, they are impermanent.
Regarding the phrase "the locus where various insects gather" and so forth, there is no self (*ātman*).
However, since that treatise states, "Within the very nature of the body, there are eighty thousand insects at intervals," it is said to be "the locus where various insects gather."
Next, from "Therefore, I now" onwards, he seeks Bodhi.
Both the awakening of Bodhi and the severance of Bodhi are termed Bodhi.
This is because Mahāprajñā, liberation, and the Dharma-body are all Great Nirvāṇa, as they both universally encompass wisdom and principle.
In this passage, the first part clarifies *nirvāṇa*.
The section beginning with "By the power of concentration and wisdom" clarifies *bodhi*.
The final section, beginning with "Having realized and attained it," clarifies the benefiting of sentient beings.

The two passages concerning the knowledge of cessation and the qualities of grace, as well as cause and effect, are each assigned accordingly, for the cultivation and pursuit of bodhi do not exceed these.
Fourth, from "At that time, the King" onwards, his compassionate vows become even more urgent.
Sūtra: "He considered that his two elder brothers, harboring feelings of fear and apprehension, might together create obstacles so that his prayer would not be fulfilled.
The following five [points] concern the fear that difficulties might arise.
The Sūtra says: "He then said, 'Two elder brothers, please go on ahead; I shall follow behind.
" This concludes the sixth [section] on skillfully cultivating expedient means.
Sūtra: “At that time, Prince Mahāsattva returned to the forest and went to where the tigress was. He stripped off his clothes and placed them upon a bamboo pole, making this vow:

‘For the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, I resolve to seek the state of unsurpassed Bodhi; with a Great Compassionate Mind that is unshakable, I shall relinquish this body, which is cherished by ordinary people.’”

Bodhi is free from affliction and feverish distress; it is that which all the wise delight in. For all sentient beings within the ocean of suffering of the three realms, I shall now deliver them and bring them peace and happiness.
After the prince had spoken these words, he cast his body down and lay before the starving tigress.
By the power of this Bodhisattva’s compassion, the tiger was rendered powerless.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva immediately climbed a high mountain and threw himself to the ground, thinking further:
"The tigress is now so emaciated that she will not be able to eat me."
He immediately rose to seek a knife but was unable to find one; he then pierced his own neck with dry bamboo to draw blood and gradually approached the tiger’s side.
This concludes the fifth major section: Sacrificing the Body for Rescue.
The text contains four sections:
first, traveling along the long road to meet the tiger;
second, from "stripping off his clothes" onwards, the commencement of the preliminary preparations.
3. From "Making this vow" onwards, he generates the bodhicitta; the first two lines are general, while the subsequent six lines are specific. Within the specific section:

the first two lines concern the mind of weary detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the next two lines concern the mind seeking enlightenment (*bodhi*); and the final two lines concern the mind benefiting sentient beings (*sattva*).
IV. From "At that time, the prince" onwards, he truly relinquishes his body and life.

This section further contains six parts: first, offering his body to feed the tigers; second, from "This was due to the Bodhisattva," the two tigers are unable to eat him; third, from "The Bodhisattva having seen this," he leaps from a high mountain; fourth, from "Again he thought thus," he further considers the inferiority of the tigers; fifth, from "He immediately rose to seek a knife," he again employs skillful means; sixth, from "Gradually approaching the side of the tigers," blood flows so that they may eat it.
Sūtra: "At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, surging and subsiding like water stirred by a violent wind;
the sun lost its brilliance as if eclipsed by Rāhu, and all directions were shrouded in darkness, devoid of any radiance."
Heavenly rain of named flowers and exquisite fragrant powders fell in profusion and scattered everywhere throughout the grove.
At that time, the hosts of devas in the void, having witnessed this event, gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, all praising him together, saying:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
Then he spoke in verse:

"The Great Being, out of compassion, brings rescue and protection; he regards all sentient beings as his only child. With courageous joy and a heart free of stinginess, he sacrifices his body to relieve suffering—a merit beyond imagining."

One shall reach the fixed, true, eternal, and sublime state, forever free from the various fetters of birth and death; before long, one shall attain the fruit of Bodhi, realizing the unborn within tranquil peace and bliss.
"Thus ends the sixth section, on the portents that move gods and humans.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, the manifestation of portents, which has three sub-sections:"
First, the earth shook in six ways; second, the sun and moon lost their radiance; third, the heavens rained down fragrant flowers that filled the grove as an offering.
"At that time, in the void," and below, the assembly beheld [these signs], which also consists of three parts:
first, the witnessing; second, the sympathetic joy; and third, the praise.
There are three types of praise:
the first two lines praise the equality of compassion; the next two lines praise his generosity; and the final four lines praise the fruits he shall attain.

Within the section on attaining the fruits, the first two lines jointly praise *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*; they are termed "eternal" because they are designated as such based on the three kinds of eternity that always coexist.
The latter two lines separately praise *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. "Quiescence" (*śānti*) refers to *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, both the subject and the object of quiescence are termed "quiescence.
"Non-arising" (*anutpāda*) is *nirvāṇa*.

Sūtra: "At that time, having seen the blood flowing from beneath the Bodhisattva’s neck, the starving tigress immediately licked the blood and devoured the flesh until it was all gone, leaving only the remaining bones."
The seventh tiger below was finally able to eat [the flesh].
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the first prince, having seen the earth tremble, said to his younger brother:

'The great earth, mountains, and rivers all shake; the various directions are shrouded in darkness and the sun has no light; celestial flowers fall in profusion throughout the air—this must surely be the sign of my younger brother’s sacrifice of his body.'"
Having heard his elder brother’s words, the second prince spoke these verses:

“I have heard the compassionate words of the Sattva; I see that tiger’s body is emaciated, bound by the suffering of hunger and fearing it will devour its cubs. Now I suspect my younger brother has sacrificed his own body.”

At that time, the two princes were overcome with great sorrow and grief; they wept and lamented as they followed one another back to where the tigress was. There they saw their younger brother’s clothes hanging from a bamboo branch, while his bones and hair lay scattered here and there, and the blood had formed a mire that defiled the ground.

Having seen this, he fainted and could not support himself; throwing his body onto the bones, he regained consciousness only after a long time. He immediately rose, raised his hands, and wailed with great lamentation, exclaiming at once:
"My younger brother was handsome and dignified, the object of my parents' special affection; why have you both gone forth together, abandoned your bodies, and not returned?"
"If our parents should question us, how shall we answer?
We would rather both sacrifice our lives than preserve our own bodies.
At that time, the two princes wept with grief and distress, and gradually departed.
The eighth section, "The Lamentation of the Retinue," has three parts:
first, the brothers' weeping; second, the pursuit and sighting of the attendants led by the young prince; and third, the parents' sorrowful wailing.

The beginning and middle sections consist of six parts: first, beholding the auspicious signs and conversing with the merchants; second, from "At that time, the two princes" onwards, lamenting and searching for [the body]; third, from "Seeing his younger brother’s clothes" onwards, seeing the corpse strewn about; fourth, from "Having seen this, he fainted" onwards, fainting and wailing in grief; fifth, from "He immediately rose and raised his hands" onwards, the brothers expressing their sorrow; sixth, from "At that time, the two princes" onwards, departing after weeping piteously.
Sūtra: At that time, the attendants accompanying the young prince said to one another, "Where is the prince?
We should search for him together."
The attendants below searched for him.
As the sutra says: "At that time, the Queen Mother of the state was sleeping on a high tower when she saw inauspicious signs in a dream: her two breasts were sliced off and her teeth fell out."
She obtained three young doves; one was snatched away by a hawk, and the other two were struck with terror.
At the moment the earth shook, the lady suddenly awoke; her heart was filled with great sorrow and distress, and she spoke these words:

"Why does the great earth shake now? The rivers, forests, and trees all tremble and quiver. The sun lacks its brilliant radiance as if it were shrouded, and my eyes twitch and my breasts throb unlike at any other time."

As if an arrow had pierced my heart, I am oppressed by grief and suffering; my entire body trembles and finds no peace. This dream I have seen is an inauspicious omen; there will surely be extraordinary calamities and transformations.
Suddenly, milk flowed from both of the lady’s breasts, and she thought to herself, "There must certainly be some portentous event.

At that time, a maidservant heard people outside saying they had been searching for the prince but had not yet found him; her heart was filled with great alarm and fear, so she immediately entered the palace and said to the lady, "Does my lady know?..."
"Outside, we have heard that various people have been searching for the prince everywhere, but have not found him.
When the queen heard these words, she was overcome with great distress and grief, her eyes filling with tears; she went to the Great King and said to him, "Great King!"
"I have heard outsiders say these words:
'I have lost my youngest and most beloved son.
Upon hearing these words, the king was struck with such alarm and confusion that he could not maintain his composure; choking back his sobs, he spoke:"
"Alas! Today I have lost my beloved son.
Having thus wiped away his tears, he comforted the lady and said to her:
"O Worthy One! Do not grieve.
I shall now go out with you to search for our beloved son."
The king, together with his great ministers and the multitude of people, immediately went out of the city, dispersing in all directions to search for him.
Before long, one minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"We have heard that the prince is still alive; pray, do not grieve."
"The smallest of them has not yet been seen even now.
Upon hearing these words, the king sighed with grief and said, "Alas, alas! How bitter it is!"
I have lost my beloved son.
When I first had a son, my joy was slight; now that I have lost him, my grief and suffering are great.
If only my son could have his life restored, even if I myself were to die, it would not be a source of sorrow.
Upon hearing this, the lady was shrouded in grief and distress as if she had been struck by an arrow, and she sighed, saying:

"My three sons and their attendants have all gone together to the forest to enjoy themselves; that my youngest and most beloved son alone has not returned, surely there must be some calamity or misfortune involving his separation from them."
Next, the second minister came before the king, who asked the minister, "Where is my beloved son?
The second minister was overcome with grief and wept; his throat and tongue were parched, and he was unable to speak, ultimately offering no answer at all.
The lady asked:

"Report quickly where my young son is now; my body is tormented by feverish distress and burns all over, and I am so dazed and bewildered that I have lost my original mind. Do not let my chest burst asunder now!"
At that time, the second minister reported in detail to the king the matter of the prince’s self-sacrifice.
Upon hearing this account, the king and his consort were overcome with grief and sobbing; they hurried their carriage forward toward the place where he had given up his body.

He went to the Bamboo Grove and arrived at the place where that Bodhisattva had sacrificed his body; seeing the skeletal remains strewn about in every direction, he fell to the ground all at once, fainting and on the verge of death, like a great tree toppled by a violent wind, his mind lost its thread and utterly devoid of consciousness.
Then the ministers and others sprinkled water everywhere over the king and the queen; after a long while, they revived.
Raising their hands, they wept and lamented, sighing and exclaiming:
"Alas! Our beloved son of such dignified appearance—why does the suffering of death first come to press upon us? Had I perished before you, how could I have witnessed such a great calamity?"

At that time, the lady’s fainting fit gradually subsided; her hair was disheveled and she beat her breast with both hands, rolling upon the ground like a fish cast up on dry land. As if she had lost her child at birth, she wept bitterly and said:
"Who has butchered and carved my son? His remaining bones are scattered upon the earth."
Having lost my beloved son, I am overcome by grief and sorrow. Alas!
Who has killed my child, causing such a matter of distress? My heart is not made of diamond; how could it not shatter?
"In my dream, I saw both my breasts severed and all my teeth fallen out; now I am beset by great agony.
Furthermore, I dreamed of three young pigeons, one of whom was seized and carried off by a hawk; now I have lost my beloved child—these evil omens are clearly not false."
"Thus ends the third section on the lamentation of the parents within the mourning of the subordinate retinue.
Within this, there are eleven parts;
first, the eight sections concerning the Queen’s astonishment and wonder:"

1. An inauspicious dream at the beginning of sleep; 2. Awakening from a startle due to an earthquake, as indicated by the passage beginning with "At the time of the earth shaking"; 3. Describing the evil omens, as indicated by the passage beginning with "He spoke these words"; 4. The flowing of milk from the two breasts of the lady, as indicated by the passage beginning with "The lady’s two breasts"; 5. The maidservant hearing her words, as indicated by the passage beginning with "At that time there was a maidservant"; 6. Running in to report [the news] out of great terror, as indicated by the passage beginning with "Her heart was greatly terrified"; 7. The mother hearing [the report] and becoming distressed, as indicated by the passage beginning with "At that time the lady"; 8. Arriving before the Great King and weeping with grief toward him, as indicated by the passage beginning with "She went to the place where the Great King was."
The preceding inquiry is fully explained according to the verse, while the text here is abbreviated.
Second, from "Having heard these words" onwards, the father becomes sorrowful and terrified.
Third, from "He then wiped away his tears" onwards, the King consoles the lady.
It is the constant custom in the Western lands (India) that upon meeting, people address one another with words of praise, calling each other "Virtuous One" (*bhadramukha*).
Regarding the fourth section, "The King and the Great Minister," and below: the king and minister go out to search.

According to the subsequent verses, it should first be the minister who searches, followed by the king and queen going out together; however, the current text abbreviates this entirely, simply stating that they "go out to search."

Within this, there are further seven sections: first, the fourfold searching; second, from "Not long thereafter" below, the arrival of the ministers' report; third, from "When the king heard these words" below, the father’s lamentation upon hearing it; fourth, from "When the queen had heard it" below, the mother’s repeated mourning; fifth, from "Then the second minister" below, the ministers arriving at the palace and the king inquiring after his life or death; sixth, from "The second minister" below, the minister sobbing and unable to answer; seventh, from "The queen asked" below, the queen’s frantic confusion and urging for a report.
Regarding the fifth section, "Then the second minister," and below, the details concerning the obtaining of a son:
according to the verse, there should be two ministers each reporting [the news], but in this prose version, one minister is omitted.
Sixth, from "The King and His Consort" downward, they recognize [the truth] and are overcome with grief.
Seventh, from "Hoping for the Place of Self-Sacrifice" downward, they proceed to the site where he sacrificed his body.
Eighth, from "Beholding His Skeleton" downward, they behold the ruins and wreckage.
Ninth, from "At that time, the ministers and others" downward, the subordinate officials sprinkle water [upon him].
Tenth, from "The king and his consort" downward, they lament once he has revived.
Eleventh, from "At that time, the consort" downward, the mother weeps and expresses her grief; these constitute the initial narrative of the household.
Next, the stepmother expresses her grief; therein, two verses describe her sorrow and two verses describe the evil omens.

The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Great King, the Queen, and the two princes all wailed in mourning; casting off their jeweled ornaments, they joined the multitude in collecting the relics of the Bodhisattva’s remains and enshrined them within a stūpa for the sake of making offerings."
The ninth major section concludes with the establishment of the *caitya*.
The Sūtra states: "Ānanda! You should know that these are the bodily relics (*śarīra*) of that Bodhisattva."
He further addressed Ānanda:

"In the past, although I possessed afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, I was able to provide relief according to circumstances for those within the five destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, enabling them to attain liberation."

How much more so now, when his afflictions are entirely exhausted and no further residual habits remain, and he is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans, endowed with all-encompassing wisdom—could he not, for the sake of each and every sentient being, undergo many eons in the hells and other realms to undergo various sufferings in their stead, thereby causing them to emerge from birth-and-death and the cycle of afflictions?
The tenth major section concludes by indicating the benefit for sentient beings.
It has three parts:
first, the conclusion that returns to the *śarīra*; second, from "Again he addressed Ānanda" onwards, a brief indication of the past causes.

Although it is said that this encompasses both gain and loss—with afflictions and the like constituting loss, and the ability to practice cultivation constituting gain—this intent encourages those possessed of afflictions to engage in practice; this is the first stage of refinement (*parikarma*).

He also exhorted the noble ones: "In the past, even while I was an ordinary person, I still benefited sentient beings; having realized the state of holiness, why do you not apply yourselves with diligence?

Later, in the passage beginning with "How much more so now," he describes his current capacity to benefit others—that is, how he manifests various forms in response to the needs of beings to bring them benefit.

This intention is even capable of taking the place of those undergoing suffering to bring them liberation; therefore, what has been taught here is certainly the cause for the means of benefit and happiness. You all should propagate and practice it.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

“I recall past lives, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, when at times I was a king, and at other times a prince. I constantly practiced great giving and even sacrificed my beloved body, vowing to transcend birth and death and reach the state of sublime Bodhi.”
In ancient times there was a great kingdom, whose ruler was named Mahāratha and whose prince was named Śūra; the prince’s mind was ever intent on giving without stinginess.
The prince had two elder brothers, named Mahānada and Mahādeva; the three of them went forth together on a journey and gradually reached a place outside the forest.
Seeing the tiger pressed by hunger, he gave rise to this thought:
"This tiger is scorched by the fire of hunger and has nothing else left to eat.
Observing this, the Great Being feared the tiger would devour his children; disregarding his own body, he sacrificed it to save the children and prevent them from being harmed.
The great earth and all its mountains shook simultaneously; rivers and seas surged and leaped, with startling waves flowing upstream.
Heaven and earth lost their radiance, shrouded in darkness where nothing could be seen; birds and beasts of the forests and wilds fled in haste, losing their refuge.
The elder brother, wondering why he had not returned, was overcome with grief and sorrow; he immediately set out with his attendants to search throughout the forests and thickets.
The brothers consulted together and went once more to a remote mountain region; looking in all directions, they found nothing, until they saw the tiger in the empty woods.

The mother and her seven sons all had blood-stained mouths; their remaining bones and stray hair were strewn across the ground, and further, one saw blood flowing, scattered throughout the bamboo grove.

When the two elder brothers saw this, great terror arose in their hearts; they fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground, so bewildered that they lost all consciousness. Dust covered their bodies, and their six sense-faculties were all deprived of mindfulness.
The prince’s attendants wept with hearts filled with grief; they sprinkled water to revive him and raised their hands in wailing cries.
When the Bodhisattva relinquished his body, his compassionate mother was within the palace, together with five hundred court ladies, enjoying exquisite pleasures.
The two breasts of the lady suddenly began to flow with milk; her entire body felt as if pricked by needles, and she could find no peace from the pain.

Suddenly, the thought of losing her child arose, and the arrow of grief pierced her heart. She immediately informed the Great King of this distressing matter, weeping so bitterly that she could not endure it. In a piteous voice, she spoke to the King:
"Great King, you should now know that I am suffering great anguish."

My two breasts suddenly began to flow with milk; though I tried to restrain them, my mind could not do so. It was as if needles were piercing my body all over, and my chest felt as though it would burst from distress.
I had previously seen evil omens in a dream; surely I shall lose my beloved son.
I pray that Your Majesty will save my life and let me know whether my son lives or has perished.
In a dream I saw three young pigeons; the smallest was my beloved child. Suddenly it was snatched away by a hawk, and my grief and sorrow are beyond description.
"I am now submerged in an ocean of grief; death approaches before long. Fearing that my son’s life may not be preserved, I pray you seek him out with all speed.
Furthermore, I have heard the words of outsiders that the younger son cannot be found; my mind is now ill at ease. I pray the King will take pity on me."
Having addressed the King in this way, the Queen prostrated herself, falling to the ground; overcome with grief, her heart fainted, and she lay there in a state of bewildered unconsciousness.
Seeing the Queen fallen on the ground in a swoon, the palace attendants raised their voices and wept aloud, filled with anxiety and despair, losing all sense of composure.
When the king heard these words, he was overcome with grief and could not restrain himself; he therefore commanded his ministers to seek out his beloved son.
They all went outside the city together, searching everywhere, and weeping, they asked the people:
"Where is the prince now?"
Is he now living or dead?
Who knows where he has gone?
How may we come to see him, so that you might dispel our hearts' grief and distress?
All the people spread the word together, saying that the prince was dead.
Those who heard it were all stricken with grief and lamented their sorrow beyond measure.
At that time, King Mahāratha rose from his seat wailing in mourning, went at once to where the queen was, and sprinkled water upon her body.
When the lady was sprinkled with water, she finally regained consciousness after a long time;
weeping, she asked the king, "Is my son still alive?
The king replied to the lady.
I have already dispatched people in all four directions to search for the prince,
yet no news has been received as yet.
The King further addressed the Queen, saying:
"Do not give rise to affliction; rather, comfort yourself and let us go together to search for him.
The King and the Queen then prepared their carriage and proceeded forward, wailing with a voice so piteous it moved all hearts, their sorrow burning like fire within them.
Hundreds of thousands of officials and commoners also followed the king out of the city, each seeking the prince; their cries of lamentation were unceasing.

Because the king sought his beloved son, he gazed in the four directions and saw a man approaching, with disheveled hair and his body smeared with blood, his entire frame covered in dust and soil, wailing as he came forward to meet him.
Seeing these evil omens, the king’s grief and distress redoubled; he raised both hands and wailed piteously, unable to restrain himself.
At that moment, a high minister hurriedly approached the king and addressed him, saying:
"I pray you, do not give way to such sorrow!"
"The king's beloved son, though sought now, has not yet been found; he shall arrive before long and dispel the Great King’s sorrow.
The king proceeded further and saw the next minister arrive. That minister approached the king and, with tears streaming down his face, addressed him, saying:
"The two sons are currently alive, yet they are tormented by the fire of grief."
The third prince had already been swallowed by impermanence.

Seeing a starving tigress who had recently given birth and was about to devour her cubs, that Prince Sattva gave rise to a heart of compassion; he vowed to seek the unsurpassed path in order to deliver all sentient beings.
Fixing his thoughts upon the wondrous Bodhi, vast and deep as the ocean, he immediately ascended to the summit of a high mountain and threw himself before a starving tigress.
The tiger was too weak to devour him, so he wounded his own neck with a bamboo splinter and allowed her to consume his body until only his skeletal remains were left.
When the king and his consort heard this, they both fainted; their hearts sank into an ocean of sorrow, consumed by the fires of affliction.
The ministers sprinkled sandalwood water upon the king and his consort, who both rose up with great cries of lamentation, raising their hands to beat their chests.
The third minister came and addressed the king with these words:
"I saw the two princes lying unconscious in the forest; I sprinkled them with cold water, and only then did they briefly regain consciousness."

He looked around in the four directions as if a fierce fire were spreading everywhere; rising for a moment, he then sank back down, wailing with grief beyond his own control. Raising his hands, he spoke words of lamentation, praising his younger brother’s rarity.
When the king heard these words, the fire of his grief flared up all the more.
The lady wailed aloud and spoke in a loud voice:
"My little son, the object of my every fond affection, has already been swallowed by the rākṣasa of impermanence."
I have two other sons who currently survive, yet they too are tormented and oppressed by the fires of grief.
I must now quickly go to the foot of the mountain to comfort them and ensure they preserve their remaining lives.
He immediately urged his carriage forward, looking toward the path ahead, with a single-minded resolve to reach that precipice from which he would sacrifice his body.

On the road, he encountered his two children walking along, weeping and wailing; they beat their breasts in anguish, their composure utterly lost. Seeing them, the parents were seized with grief and sorrow, and together they proceeded to the mountain forest where he intended to cast away his life.

Having arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva had relinquished his body, they gathered together and wailed in grief, giving rise to great suffering; removing their necklaces and exhausting their hearts of sorrow, they collected the remaining bones of the Bodhisattva’s body.

Together with the multitude, they made offerings and collectively constructed a stūpa of the seven precious substances; having placed those relics within a casket, they prepared their carriages and, filled with grief, proceeded toward the city.
Below, fifty-six verses are presented in verse form, divided into two parts:
the first two verses provide a general outline of the practice, while the subsequent fifty-four verses specifically eulogize the relinquishing of the body.

The preceding prose section consisted of ten segments; now, in this verse section, the fourth segment—on the resolve to sacrifice one's life—and the seventh segment—on the tiger finally being able to eat—are omitted. Furthermore, the tenth segment—the conclusion showing the benefit to sentient beings—is excluded.

Thus, it is divided into seven parts: first, one and a half verses praise the first [segment], describing the former retinue; next, half a verse praises the second, recounting past joyful excursions; next, one verse praises the third, on the arising of sorrow upon encountering suffering; next, one verse praises the fifth, on sacrificing the body for rescue; next, two verses praise the sixth, on the auspicious response that moved gods and humans; next, forty-six and a half verses praise the eighth, on the lamentation and mourning of the retinue; and finally, one and a half verses praise the ninth, on the establishment of a *caitya*.
The first five sections may be understood according to the text.
Within the prose commentary on the verses concerning the lamentation of the retinue, there are three parts:
first, the six verses beginning with "The two elder brothers marvel at his non-return" eulogize the brothers' weeping; these can be further subdivided as follows.
The verses on the attendants’ search are omitted.

Regarding the forty and a half verses beginning with "When the Bodhisattva abandoned his body," these eulogize the parents' lamentation. Although there were eleven prose sections previously, this version lacks the initial dispatching of the minister; however, that section is present here in the verses. Nevertheless, because it lacks the tenth and eleventh sections—the mother’s sorrowful petition, the king’s consolation of the queen, and the king and minister’s departure to search—it is divided into only ten parts.

The first eleven stanzas describe the Queen’s astonishment; the next half-stanza describes the second king’s ensuing grief and alarm; the following fourteen stanzas, beginning with "He then commanded his ministers," describe the fourth king and his ministers going out to search; the next five and a half stanzas, beginning with "The king proceeded further on," describe the fifth section concerning the circumstances of obtaining the child; the next seven stanzas, beginning with "At that time the king and the queen," describe the sixth section where, having learned the news, they weep with choked voices; the next two stanzas, beginning with "I shall now quickly go to the mountain foot," describe the seventh section of proceeding to the place where the body was sacrificed; and the final half-stanza describes the eighth section of beholding the collapsed ruin.
Within the Queen’s state of astonishment and wonder, there are five parts:
first, one verse on the joy within the palace;
next, one and a half verses on the flow of milk from her breasts out of deep emotion.

The next six and a half verses describe the weeping with compassion and the petitioning of the King; the inauspicious dreams mentioned in the preceding prose, the maidservant hearing the words and rushing in to report them, and the mother’s distress upon hearing them, are all included within this petition to the King and are not treated in separate verses, as the text is abbreviated to avoid redundancy and excessive prolixity.
The following single verse describes his fainting after having made the petition;
the next single verse concerns the anxiety of the palace ladies, beginning with "When the King heard these words," which concludes the second section on the King’s subsequent grief.

"Because he commanded his various ministers... These fourteen stanzas concern the king and his ministers going out to search; while there were seven in the preceding prose, the current section in verse is divided into three parts:
the first half-stanza commands the ministers to pursue the search, which is not present in the prose.

Next, nine verses follow; the first four analyze through individual investigation. Among these, the first three verses concern the search by the ministers and attendants, while the subsequent four verses—beginning with "At that time, the great chariot"—correspond to the third section above, the King’s consolation of the lady, as this follows the natural sequence of the text.

Furthermore, in the prose section, he wept with compassion and addressed the king, but it does not mention his fainting and being revived by water; this is because the text is abbreviated in the present verse.

Below the line beginning with "The king then, together with his consort," there are two verses concerning the king’s departure to search: the first verse concerns the king, and the second verse concerns the minister.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Because the King sought his beloved son," the following four and a half verses describe the second minister’s arrival among those sent out by the king and his ministers to search for him; this section is divided into three parts:

first, one and a half verses on the king seeing the messenger arrive; second, one verse on the king raising his hand to beckon and question him; and third, two verses on the minister’s formal address.
"The King proceeded further on" refers to the following five and a half verses, which elaborate upon the fifth section concerning the circumstances of obtaining the son;

this is divided into four parts: first, the half verse on the king seeing the minister arrive; second, the one verse on reporting that the two sons are alive; third, the half verse on reporting the death of Sattva; and fourth, the three and a half verses describing the causes of his death.

"Then the King and his Consort... and so forth, the sixth verse concerning their realization [of the truth] and their subsequent sobbing. This section is divided into four parts: first, one verse on the parents fainting; second, one verse on the ministers sprinkling water [on them]; third, three verses on the ministers' further report; and fourth, two verses on the parents' lamentation.
Next, two verses concern the seventh [section]: going to the place where he sacrificed his body.
Next, half a verse concerns the eighth: beholding the collapse.
Next, one and a half verses constitute the ninth major section: the erection of a caitya.
The Sūtra further addressed Ānanda:
"The *sattva* of that former time was none other than I, the Muni; do not harbor any other thought.
The King was my father, Śuddhodana; the Queen was my mother, Māyā; the Crown Prince was Maitreya; and the next was Mañjuśrī."
"The tigress was Mahāprajāpatī; her five cubs were the five bhikṣus: one was Mahāmaudgalyāyana and one was Śāriputra.
This concludes the second major section of the "Lower Grade," which correlates the present with the past.
Sūtra: “I shall explain to you the conditions for benefiting others in the past; you should study such bodhisattva practices as they are the causes for attaining buddhahood.
When a bodhisattva relinquishes his body, he makes this great vow:
‘May the remaining bones of my body benefit sentient beings in future lives.’”

"This is the place where he sacrificed his body; a stūpa made of the seven treasures, having remained submerged beneath the thick earth for immeasurable time, has now surged forth from the ground by the power of his original vows, appearing in accordance with conditions to bring salvation and benefit to humans and devas."
The third major section within the "Inferior Grade" (Hapin) encourages the practice of study.
Within this, the first verse points to past exhortations for cultivation, while the subsequent three verses conclude by indicating the purpose of the *caitya*.

Sūtra: At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking of these past causes and conditions, an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya of the great assembly of devas and humans were filled with great compassion and joy; they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence and all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He further addressed the tree deity:
"I pay this homage for the sake of repaying my debt of gratitude.
The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and the stūpa sank back into the earth.
The fourth major section, "The Benefits Gained by the Assembly upon Hearing [the Teaching]," is divided into three parts:

first, a restatement of what was previously taught; second, from "Immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*s" onwards, an explanation of the extent of the benefits gained; and third, from "Again he addressed the tree-spirit" onwards, a response to questions and a concluding summary.

Following the preceding prose section, this passage merely records Ānanda’s question to the Buddha regarding the reasons for worshipping a stūpa; here, however, the Buddha answers the question posed by the tree deity. Therefore, within the preceding inquiry, there must have been a joint question from the tree deity concerning the reasons for worship, though it is omitted for brevity.
Following the section "The Buddha Withdraws His Supernatural Power," the text clarifies that the stūpa returns to its original place because the task has been completed. 27.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Praise of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions (Part Six). The Chapter on the Praise of the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Directions is analyzed according to three sections.

Regarding the purpose of this discourse, there are three aspects for its circulation: namely, the practice of learning, the praise and veneration, and the entrustment—these three distinct sections intended to cause future generations to practice according to the Dharma.
Since the benefits obtained are manifold, this expression of celebration and praise is offered; thus, this chapter arises after the preceding one.
Regarding the explanation of the title: "praise" (zàn) means to extol, and "eulogy" (tàn) means to chant; that is, to extol and chant in verse.
It should be said that praising refers to extolling the virtues of things, while eulogizing (kṣānti) refers to the principle of exalting [virtues] through instruction.
The former refers to persons, and the latter to dharmas.
Alternatively, both may apply to persons and dharmas alike; thus, a bodhisattva is one who is capable of praising.
The "ten directions" refers to the realms from which they have come.
To inspire earnestness in sentient beings, he mentions that they have traveled from afar across the ten directions.
If even superior persons would still praise themselves, why should those who are inferior not sing their own praises?
Furthermore, this demonstrates that it is for those who are superior and not for those who are inferior, so as to inspire them to aspire toward excellence and advance in their practice.
Therefore, the *Hapiṇḍa* (or *Hapin*) states: "To cause those who do not yet know to follow and train accordingly."
Regarding the resolution of this difficulty: Question—Why was the old translation compiled as a single chapter, while this new translation is divided into four chapters?

Answer—According to the Sanskrit original, at the beginning of each chapter, the name of a bodhisattva is written or marked with a dot. Following the Sanskrit original, the praises of these four individuals were recorded separately; therefore, it is now divided into four.
The former editors, seeing that both sections praise the Buddha, have combined them into a single chapter.
Furthermore, it is explained that the original text lacks a formal record for this; moreover, they are similar in nature to the *Praise* (*Stotra*).
The new translation includes four persons, whereas the old translation lacks the "Praise of Great Eloquence" (Mahāprajñā-stotra); thus, they differ in their arrangement and condensation.
Question:
According to the old version of the sutra, immeasurable bodhisattvas travel from this world to the land of the Tathāgata Golden Jewel Canopy Mountain to pay homage and praise that Buddha.
The new sutra states: "Each from their own native land, they proceeded to Vulture Peak; having paid homage to the World-Honored One, they praised him with one voice.
How can this be inconsistent? Answer: The old version was erroneous; the present one is correct.
Why is this? In this place they hear the sutra and should jointly praise this Buddha.

Furthermore, according to what has been stated above, there are bodhisattvas from the ten directions; for what reason do they all go together to the kingdom of Golden Jewel Mountain to praise that Buddha?

If it is claimed that the preaching of the sutra was by means of his mark of faith— that because of this mark of faith he would later attain Buddhahood under the name "Golden Treasure Mountain," and thus [the Buddha] went to praise him—
this too is not the case.
Why is this? The Buddha Ratnagiri appearing here is not the body of Śraddhālakṣaṇa; furthermore, that Buddha was not the one who bestowed the prediction.
Moreover, since it is not later stated that these bodhisattvas came from that land, how can it be said that they rely upon the power of that Buddha?

Therefore, although the request was made by Subhāṣitadhvaja, it is Śākyamuni Buddha who is able to preach; likewise, those who hear the Dharma and come here do so through the power of Śākyamuni. Thus, that teacher Subhāṣitadhvaja praises Śākyamuni.
The new text is taken as the correct version.
The text is divided into three sections:
first, the gathering of the bodhisattvas; second, the formal presentation of worship and praise; and third, the Tathāgata’s commendation and seal of approval.

Sutra. At that time, while the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was preaching this sutra, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions, each departing from their own native lands to arrive at Vulture Peak Mountain.
This concludes the first section.
First, the introduction by the sūtra compiler; second, from "In the worlds of the ten directions" onwards, the gathering of the bodhisattvas. The sūtra states:
They arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, and having prostrated with their five limbs touching the ground, they paid homage to the World-Honored One.
Below follows the expression of worship and praise.
First is physical prostration, followed by verbal praise.
This is the former.
That which can initiate bodily and vocal actions is itself mental karma (*manas-karman*).
Through these three types of action—prostration and praise—one expresses the depth of one's reverence.
The sutra says: With single-minded palms joined, they praised him with different mouths but in unison, saying:
The following section offers praise.
First is the heading, followed by the praise itself;
this is the former.

Focusing the mind exclusively on the object is called "single-mindedness"; because of deep feelings of reverence, they join their palms; because their bodies differ, their voices differ; because they praise in unison, they have a single voice. The Sūtra says:

"The Buddha’s body is subtle and wondrous, of true golden color; its light shines everywhere like a mountain of gold; it is pure and supple like a lotus flower, adorned with immeasurable exquisite hues."
Adorned throughout by the thirty-two marks and fully endowed with all eighty minor characteristics, his radiant brilliance is peerless; free from defilement, he is like the pure, full moon.
The concluding praise consists of eleven verses, divided into two parts:
the first ten verses praise the three bodies (*trikāya*), and the final verse concludes with a brief aspiration.

Within the praise of the three bodies, the first eight verses praise the qualities of grace of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), the next one verse praises the qualities of wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), and the final one verse praises the qualities of abandonment of the *dharmakāya* (truth body).

Within this praise of his kindness and virtue: the first two verses praise his manifested body; the next verse praises his teaching of the Dharma; the next verse praises his merit and wisdom; and the final four verses praise his benefiting of sentient beings.

In the praise of the manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the first verse concerns the general body as its basis, and the subsequent verse concerns the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), as fully explained previously.

The Sūtra states: “His voice is clear and exceedingly subtle, like the roar of a lion or the sound of thunder; possessing eight kinds of sublime qualities that respond to the capacities of sentient beings, it surpasses even the *kalaviṅka* and other such birds.”
Next, he praised the preaching of the Dharma.
Regarding the eight kinds of subtle and wondrous voices, there are differences among three sutras.
According to the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*, it says:

First, the most exquisite sound; second, easy to understand; third, deep and far-reaching; fourth, gentle and soft; fifth, not false; sixth, not erroneous; seventh, noble and wise; eighth, harmonious and balanced.
The second, the *Antarābhava Sūtra*, states:

first, it is neither male; second, it is neither female; third, it is neither tall; fourth, it is neither short; fifth, it is neither noble; sixth, it is neither base; seventh, it is neither suffering; eighth, it is neither blissful.
Third, according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃgraha-sūtra* (Shizhu duanjie jing), it says:
first, not male; second, not female; third, not rigid; fourth, not soft; fifth, not turbid; sixth, not muddy; seventh, not masculine; eighth, not feminine.
The first two sūtras belong to the Hīnayāna, while the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃyojana* belongs to the Mahāyāna, because their perspectives and what they perceive differ.
As for the kalaviṅka and other birds, these are birds of wondrous song.

Sūtra: “Adorned with a countenance by the wondrous marks of a hundred merits, his radiance is complete, pure, and stainless; his wisdom is as clear and bright as the great ocean, and his merit is as vast as space.”
The latter half praises merit and wisdom; the first half refers to merit and the second half to wisdom.

Each of the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) is adorned by one hundred merits. While the previous praise of bodily radiance referred to the body as a whole, this praise of light refers specifically to the individual marks and signs.
Regarding the term "hundred merits" (*śata-puṇya*), according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 177: "What is meant by 'a hundred merits'?
Answer: In this context, one hundred volitions (*cetanā*) are called a hundred merits."
What are the one hundred thoughts?

They are as follows: when a bodhisattva performs and cultivates the karma that brings about the marks of the feet being well-placed, first fifty thoughts refine the vessel of the body, making it pure and supple; next, one thought arises that correctly draws forth that karma; finally, fifty thoughts arise to bring it to completion.
The karma for even the *uṣṇīṣa* mark upon the crown of the head is likewise so; for this reason, it is said that each and every mark of the Buddha is adorned by a hundred merits (*śatapuṇya*).
What are these fifty volitions (*cetanā*)?

Answer: Based on each of the ten paths of wholesome action, there are five types of volition: first, the volition of abstaining from killing; second, the volition of encouraging others [to abstain]; [and so forth].
Third, praising with intention;
fourth, sympathetic joy;
fifth, dedication.
This refers to dedicating what has been cultivated toward enlightenment;
this applies even up to right view, and these are called the fifty volitions (*cetanā*). Some say:

Each of the ten courses of action gives rise to five grades of wholesome volition—namely, the inferior, the middling, the superior, the superior-excellent, and the superior-extreme—just as in the case of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.

Some say: each of the ten courses of action gives rise to five types of volition: first, purity of the preliminary application; second, purity of the fundamental act; third, purity of the subsequent conclusion; fourth, not being harmed by discursive thought; and fifth, being embraced by mindfulness.
Some say: "Contemplating each individual mark of the Buddha, one gives rise to fifty moments (*kṣaṇa*) of previously uncultivated reflection, which proceed in continuous succession.
There is no formal critique [of this], yet according to reason, the first explanation is superior.

If there were distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior—as there are in the case of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna—then there should likewise be differences in the excellence or inferiority of the primary marks and secondary signs.

If one asserts that there are five stages, such as the preparatory, the fundamental, and the subsequent, then the preparatory effort and the subsequent stage would have to be identical in their resulting effect, with no distinction between them.
If it is granted that they share the same perception, how could there be any distinction among them across the three times, such as superiority or inferiority?
The same should apply to their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
If you claim that fifty [marks] arise from thoughts never before practiced, why do you not allow for some increase or decrease?
Regarding the Mahāyāna, although no explicit textual passage has been found, there are two traditional interpretations transmitted:
it is said that just as the ten wholesome karmas support one another, they constitute one hundred karmas.
It is further stated:

"Just as each individual karma has ten types—namely, (1) performing it oneself, (2) instructing others, (3) rejoicing, (4) sympathetic joy, (5) a small portion, (6) a large portion, (7) the whole portion, (8) for a short time, (9) for a long time, and (10) for the duration of one's life—there are thus one hundred karmas."

Sūtra: “A halo of light fills the realms of the ten directions; according with conditions, it universally delivers all sentient beings. The accumulation of afflictions and defiled attachments is entirely eliminated, and the torch of Dharma burns eternally without ceasing.”
The following praises the benefit of sentient beings.
The first verse is a general praise, [showing that] he manifests his body and preaches the Dharma for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The first phrase concerns the body; the second phrase concerns benefiting; the third phrase praises purity; and the fourth phrase concerns the Dharma.
The middle two lines apply to both the body and phenomena. The Sūtra says:

"Out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings, you are able to bestow happiness in the present and the future; you constantly proclaim the ultimate truth, enabling them to realize the true tranquility of Nirvāṇa."

The Buddha has preached the supreme Dharma of ambrosia, which can bestow the subtle meaning of ambrosia, lead one into the city of Nirvāṇa, and cause one to experience the unconditioned bliss of ambrosia.
The following is a specific praise.
The first two verses praise the taught Dharma as being capable of attaining *nirvāṇa*, while the final verse praises the taught Dharma as being capable of attaining *bodhi*.
Within the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, one verse brings about its attainment, and the other verse confirms it.
That which is taught and that which is attained are both capable of eliminating suffering and bestowing peace and happiness; therefore, they are like nectar.

As the Sūtra says: "Always within the great ocean of birth and death, you liberate all sentient beings from suffering, enabling them to abide upon the path of security and tranquility, and constantly granting them inconceivable, wish-fulfilling bliss."
The following verse causes one to attain Bodhi.
That is, the Eightfold Noble Path is called the "Path of Tranquility. The Sūtra says:

"The ocean of the Tathāgata’s virtues is exceedingly deep and vast; it cannot be known through any analogy. Toward all beings he constantly gives rise to great compassion, and through skillful means he exerts himself with tireless diligence."
The following verse praises the wisdom and merit of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Because of great compassion, it constantly benefits sentient beings, never entering *nirvāṇa* and never ceasing its activity.
Thus, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states: "Because it is supreme and inexhaustible, it does not cease from benefiting others."

Sūtra: "The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is boundless; though all gods and humans together attempt to measure it, even in the course of ten million billion kalpas, they could not know even a small fraction of it."
The following praises the virtue of severance within the Dharmakāya.

Sūtra: "I now briefly praise the Buddha’s merits; they are but a single drop within an ocean of virtues. I dedicate this mass of merit to all sentient beings, that they may all swiftly realize the fruit of Bodhi."
The following concludes the abbreviated aspiration prayer.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

"You have all skillfully praised the Buddha's merits in this way, benefiting sentient beings and extensively promoting the Buddha's work; you are thus able to extinguish all transgressions and generate immeasurable merit."
The Tathāgata’s praise and seal follow below.
The initial section is the praise; the subsequent section beginning with "You all" is the seal.
It is a praise because there is no defiled mind, and it is a seal because it accords with principle and benefits sentient beings.

Chapter 28: The Chapter on the Praise of Bodhisattva Wonderful Banner (6). Regarding the intent behind the title "The Chapter on the Praise of Bodhisattva Wonderful Banner," it is the same as previously explained.
Regarding the explanation of the name: in Sanskrit it is called *kūṭāgāra*, which here means "wondrous" (*miao*).
"Chicken-head" (*jītóu*) here means "banner" (*dhvaja*).
This refers to the preeminent excellence of supreme wisdom, which is likened to a tall, erected banner; because it alone transcends the burdens of worldly defilements, it is termed "wondrous."
The banner (dhvaja) is itself called "exquisite" (miao), thus it is named "Exquisite Banner" (Miaodang); this is an *karmadhāraya* compound.
It is designated by way of metaphor as "Exquisite Banner.
Formerly, it was called "Faith-Aspect" (Xinxiang).
Regarding "lakṣaṇa" (xiàng): in Sanskrit it is called *yaṣṭi*; since it is now rendered as *kūrujila* (鴝嚧只囉), it is translated as "banner" (*dhvaja*).
Faith (*śraddhā*) is pure by nature, and its meaning is similar to "wondrous"; a banner is lofty and prominent, yet it has been erroneously called "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the resolution of this objection: If one asks why it is not only the Wondrous Banner who attains the prediction upon hearing the Dharma, and for what reason he alone is singled out for praise, the answer is:
because he is the foremost.
Sūtra: At that time, the Bodhisattva Subhaketu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
The text of this lower section is divided into three parts:

first, the ritual of praising the person; second, the actual expression of praise beginning with "And he spoke these verses of praise"; and third, the World-Honored One’s commendation and seal of approval beginning with "The Buddha said to Subhaketu."
This is the first [verse].
The sutra then speaks in praise, saying:

"The Muni’s marks of a hundred merits are perfectly complete; His body is adorned with immeasurable virtues. Vast and pure, he is a joy for people to behold, Like the radiance of a thousand suns shining forth."

With boundless flames and radiant, blazing light, it is as majestic in appearance as a cluster of exquisite jewels; like the newly risen sun reflecting in the void, its crimson and white hues are distinct, interspersed with golden tones.

Just as the light of a golden mountain shines everywhere, pervading hundreds of thousands of lands, it can extinguish the immeasurable sufferings of sentient beings and bestow upon them boundless, supreme, and wondrous bliss.

All his marks are fully perfected and utterly pure; sentient beings delight in beholding him without ever wearying. His hair is soft and deep blue-black in color, like a swarm of black bees gathered upon a wondrous flower.
The following eulogy consists of eight and a half verses, divided into three parts:
first, four verses praise the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha);
next, from "Great Joy" onwards, three verses praise the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Buddha); finally, from "The Tathāgata’s Golden Mouth" onwards, one and a half verses apply to both Buddhas.
The *dharmakāya* is not praised in brief because it is profound and hidden; rather, its support is praised, for it is that upon which the reflection depends.
Within the first [section on] the *nirmāṇakāya*, there are four parts;
the first verse praises the body.
Next, one verse praises the light;
next, one verse offers a combined praise of the body and its radiance—the first half praising its all-pervasiveness and the second half praising its capacity for benefiting others;
next, one verse praises the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*).

Sūtra: "Great joy and great equanimity are pure adornments; great loving-kindness and great compassion are fully possessed; adorned with all manner of wondrous marks and signs, they are accomplished through the factors of enlightenment."

The Tathāgata is able to bestow manifold blessings and benefits, causing all beings to constantly attain great peace and happiness; adorned with various sublime virtues, his radiance shines universally upon ten million lands.
The Tathāgata’s radiance is utterly perfect, like the blazing sun pervading the sky; the Buddha, endowed with merits like Mount Sumeru, manifests his presence throughout the ten directions.
The following praises the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), which encompasses both the enjoyment for oneself and for others, divided into four parts:
first, half a verse praises the four immeasurables;
next, half a verse praises the marks and signs, stating that they "are accomplished by the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*), thereby praising the causes of the marks and signs.
Next, half a verse praises the benefits;
next, one and a half verses praise the body and its radiance.
Within the description of the body and its radiance, the first half provides a general summary, while the subsequent verse provides a specific detail.
In the beginning, the first phrase praises the body, encompassing all five aggregates;
the second phrase praises the light, which likewise encompasses both wisdom and form.
From "The Tathāgata’s radiant marks" onwards is the specific praise: the first half-verse praises the light, and the subsequent half-verse praises the body.

Sūtra: “The Tathāgata’s golden mouth is wondrously sublime; his teeth are white, even, and closely set like jade or snow. The Tathāgata’s countenance is without peer; the tuft of hair between his brows always curls to the right. Radiant, smooth, and brilliant white like crystal, it is like the full moon dwelling in the realm of space.”
The following passage praises both the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) of the two Buddhas.
The Sūtra states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner:
"You have been able to thus praise the inconceivable merits of the Buddha, benefiting all beings and causing those who do not yet know them to follow and practice accordingly."
The following is the Tathāgata’s Seal of Praise.
Chapter 29: The Bodhi Tree Deity’s Eulogy (6). Regarding the Chapter on the Bodhi Tree Deity’s Eulogy, the second of its kind, the purpose for its inclusion is the same as before.
Regarding the explanation of its name, according to the *Records of the Western Regions*:
"The tree is originally named the Pippala tree, situated upon the Vajrāsana.
This Vajrāsana was formed in antiquity during the formation of the Bhadrakalpa, arising simultaneously with the great earth."
Situated within this trichiliocosm, extending downward to the Golden Wheel and upward to the surface of the earth, it is composed of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference.
Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sat upon this seat and entered the Vajra-samādhi, it is called the Vajrāsana.
As for the Pippala tree, the Buddha sat beneath it and attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment; therefore, it is called the Bodhi tree.
Its trunk and stem are yellowish-white, while its branches and leaves are lush green; they do not wither in winter or summer, remaining radiant and unchanged.
Whenever it reaches the day of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, all the leaves fall away, and by the following year, they return to their former state.
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpṛthivī manifested as this tree deity for the sake of the celestial maiden; she is the presiding deity of the Bodhi tree.
This is according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis.
Regarding the resolution of the difficulty: Question:"
Why does he not perceive other deities? Answer:
Because he first beheld the Buddha, and because he is never separated from the Buddha.
Question:
Are the Bodhi-tree deity and the Earth deity one and the same, or are they distinct? Answer:
Some say it is one [chapter], while others say they are distinct.
The sutra states: "At that time, the Bodhi-tree deity...
The lower section of the text is divided into three parts:

First, the opening section praises the person; next, the passage beginning with "Also by means of verses" describes the words of praise; finally, the section beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One" records the Tathāgata’s commendation and seal of approval.
This is the first.
The sutra also praises the World-Honored One with a gāthā, saying:

"Homage to the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom; Homage to the wisdom that constantly seeks the true Dharma; Homage to the wisdom capable of departing from what is not the Dharma; Homage to the wisdom that is forever without discrimination."
The eulogies at the conclusion consist of eleven verses in total, which are broadly divided into two parts:
the first five verses are praises, and the latter six verses are aspirational prayers.
Within the praises, the first verse lauds the essence of wisdom, while the subsequent four verses laud the function of wisdom.

Within this body [of the verse], the first line offers a general praise of the essence of wisdom; being free from obstructions and possessing perfected wisdom is termed "pure wisdom" (*viśuddha-prajñā*).
The subsequent two lines praise the capacity of this wisdom: because it enables sentient beings to cultivate wholesome qualities, it is said to "constantly seek the true Dharma."
It is not so; since the fruit is fulfilled, what further could be sought?
Because it enables sentient beings to abandon evil, it is called "wisdom that departs from unrighteousness.
Although it can act in this way, because the three spheres are pure, it is always free from conceptual discrimination.
