Alternatively, the first line praises the fruit, while the latter three lines praise the cause.

Within the discussion of the cause: the first line refers to preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), the second to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the third to subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Because it is free from false discrimination, it is said to be "without discrimination.

Alternatively, as the sequence suggests, it is able to constantly advance toward the good and distance itself from all evils; it always accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is eternally without discrimination.
Alternatively, the first phrase encompasses both the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, while the remaining three phrases praise only the Reward-body.

Since the praise of function refers to the Transformation-body, the old scripture states: "Homage to the Pure, Unsurpassed, Perfectly Awakened, Profound, and Sublime Dharma. Thus, "Pure Wisdom" (Vimalamati) encompasses the Dharma-body.

Sūtra: "How rare, O World-Honored One, are your boundless practices! How rare, as difficult to behold as the udumbara flower! How rare, like the ocean that stabilizes the mountains, profound and mysterious! How rare, O Sugata, is your immeasurable light!"

How rare is the Great Compassionate Vow of the Tamer! How rare is the Śākya Sage, whose brilliance exceeds that of the sun! You are able to expound such jewels within this sutra, out of pity and for the benefit of all living beings.
The following praises the function of wisdom: the first two verses praise its benefit for others, while the latter two verses praise its benefit for oneself.
Within the section on benefiting others, the first line praises the rarity of possessing such practice.
The next line praises the rarity of his manifestation;
the following line praises the rarity of his physical appearance, for his body stands amidst the great assembly like Mount Sumeru presiding over the vast ocean;
the subsequent line praises the rarity of his immeasurable light.
The next phrase expresses the rarity of the great vow;

the next phrase expresses the rarity of the spiritual lineage, for the World-Honored One was born from a lineage nurtured by the sun, and thus it is said that his brilliance surpasses that of the sun;
the next phrase expresses the rarity of preaching this sutra.
The next line concerns the rarity of benefiting sentient beings;
it possesses eight rarities. The Sūtra says:
“The Muni’s faculties are tranquil and concentrated; He can enter the city of tranquil nirvāṇa; He can abide in the gate of tranquil samādhi; He can know the profound realm of tranquility.”

The Honored One among two-legged beings dwells in emptiness and stillness; the bodies of his śrāvaka disciples are likewise empty. The essential nature of all phenomena is non-existent, and all sentient beings are entirely empty and still.
The final two verses praise the benefit for oneself.

Because they describe the manifestation of transformation dwelling in tranquility, being able to enter nirvāṇa, and so forth—and because the terms "Muni" and "śrāvaka disciples" are used—these may also be understood as the enjoyment of the benefit for one's own self-interest.
It is said that the faculties are fixed because they abide in the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
However, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha states that this praises the *dharmakāya*, though the phrasing is somewhat loose.
These two verses are divided into three parts:

The first verse praises the virtue of dwelling in tranquility for one's own benefit; the subsequent half-verse praises the cause by which one is able to dwell in tranquility; and the final half-verse concludes the reason for this.
Because the essence of phenomena is empty and their intrinsic nature is entirely quiescent, one dwells in emptiness and stillness.
Because one abides in emptiness and stillness, one is able to quiet the sense faculties, enter parinirvāṇa, dwell in tranquil samādhi, and realize the realm of tranquility.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "That wheel is capable of quiescence, for its intrinsic nature is quiescent."
Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows:
the first verse praises abiding in tranquility;

the subsequent verses praise the attainment of four types of equality: first, the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*); second, the equality of sentient beings; third, the equality of those to be converted; and fourth, the equality of the Buddha-body.
The meaning may be understood by analogy with the following scripture:
"I constantly recollect all Buddhas; I always delight in beholding all World-Honored Ones. I constantly give rise to a heart of profound respect, and thus always encounter the Sun-like Tathāgatas."

I constantly prostrate to the World-Honored One; may my heart always yearn for you without ceasing, weeping with tears in uninterrupted flow, and may I forever serve you without ever knowing weariness.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will give rise to compassion, and that I may always behold Your serene countenance. May the Buddha and the assembly of Śrāvakas remain pure, and may You always universally deliver all beings among devas and humans.

The Buddha’s body is fundamentally pure like space, resembling a magical illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water; I pray that you will preach the nectar-like Dharma of Nirvana, which can give rise to the entire mass of all meritorious virtues.

The pure realm of the World-Honored One, his inconceivable practice of compassion and righteousness, is beyond the measure of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and cannot be fathomed even by great sages and bodhisattvas.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me, always allowing me to behold your body of great compassion; with my three karmas free from weariness, may I serve the Compassionate Honored One and swiftly transcend birth and death to return to the limit of reality.
Next, there are six types of aspirational prayers (*praṇidhāna*):
the first half-verse concerns the constant vision of the dwelling place of the prayer through mindfulness;
the subsequent half-verse concerns the constant encounter with that which is produced by the prayer through earnestness.
The next single verse expresses the aspiration to serve and attend [the Buddha] constantly without weariness.
The subsequent half-verse expresses the aspiration for constant protection so that one may see [him].
It should have been stated as "see and so forth" (*darśanādi*), but because the meter of the verse was constrained, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been omitted.
The subsequent one and a half verses express the aspiration to constantly benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "humans and devas," this refers to those capable of realization: the Dharmakāya, which is primordially pure like space;
and the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya, which are like illusions and so forth.
The following two verses express the aspiration to witness [the Buddha].
Within them, the first verse praises his supreme excellence:
the sphere of his activity is the *dharmatākāya*, and his compassionate correct practice consists of both compassion and wisdom; both are inconceivable.
The "Great Sage Bodhisattva" refers to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
The first half-verse expresses the aspiration for [the Buddha's] empowerment;
the subsequent half-verse reveals the realization attained through cultivation.
Sūtra: At that time, having heard this praise, the World-Honored One addressed the tree deity with a Brahma-voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O virtuous woman!"

"You are able to proclaim the wondrous marks of my true, non-deceptive, and pure *dharmakāya*, which brings benefit to both yourself and others. By this merit, may you swiftly realize the most supreme *bodhi*; may all sentient beings practice together with you, and if they hear this, may they all enter the nectar-like gateway of the non-arising of phenomena."
The first eulogy, "O Virtuous Goddess," concludes with the seal; there are two parts to this: [the text below].
The first seal is that which is praised; next, from "By this merit" onwards, is the seal of the vow.
Chapter Thirty: The Praise of the Great Goddess of Eloquence (6). Chapter Thirty: The Praise of the Great Goddess of Eloquence. The purpose for its inclusion is the same as before.

She is called "Great Eloquence" because she is fully endowed with the four types of eloquence of a bodhisattva; she is called a "devī" (goddess) because she possesses mastery, and thus manifests as a celestial maiden.
This is an example of a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Alternatively, by excluding other goddesses, the term "Goddess of Great Eloquence" (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-devī) is also explained as a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Question:
Why are others not clarified, while this goddess alone is praised?
Answer: Because among all the deities, the Goddess of Great Eloquence possesses supreme skill in speech, the others are not mentioned.
Sūtra: At that time, the Goddess of Great Eloquence rose from her seat, joined her palms in reverence, and spoke with straightforward words.
The text of the lower grade is divided into three parts.
This first section identifies the person who offers praise, which has three components:
first, the identification of the person; second, their dignified demeanor; and third, the use of direct speech to manifest their distinction.
Not employing verses for praise, he spoke in direct prose.
The sūtra praises the World-Honored One, saying:
"Homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

His body was the color of pure gold; his throat was like a conch shell; his face was like the full moon; his eyes were like blue lotuses; his lips and mouth were a beautiful red, like the color of crystal; his nose was high, long, and straight, like a bar of gold being carried; his teeth were white, even, and closely set, like *kubjaka* flowers; the radiance of his body shone everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns; and his luster was transparent and penetrating, like the gold of Jambudvīpa.
All their speech is free from error; they demonstrate the three gates of liberation, open the path to the three types of enlightenment, and their minds are ever pure, as is their resolute intention.
The Buddha’s dwelling place and his sphere of activity are also eternally pure; he is free from improper conduct, and his movements and pauses are never erroneous.
Through six years of ascetic practice and three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma, he delivers suffering sentient beings, causing them to reach the other shore.
His physical marks are perfectly complete, like the *kūṭaja* tree.
Having cultivated the six perfections, his three karmas are without fault.
Possessing all-knowledge, he fulfills the benefit of both self and others.
All that he proclaims is for the sake of sentient beings; his words are never uttered in vain.
Among the Śākyas, he is the Great Lion—steadfast and courageous, endowed with the eight liberations.
The praise at the end has two parts:
first, the praise of virtues; second, from "May by this merit... onwards, the making of vows.
Within the praise, there are three sections:
First, the prostration; second, the specific praise; and finally, from "I now, according to my power" onwards, the conclusion of the abridgment.
There are ten parts to the specific praise:
first, from "The body is of true golden color," the praise of the marks and signs.
2. From "All that exists" (*sarva*) onwards, there is praise for the absence of faults in speech.
Because the excellence of teaching the Dharma for the benefit of others is included among the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), speech is praised specifically.
3. From "Showing the three gates of liberation" onwards, there is praise for the virtue of external transformation through the Dharma taught; this has two parts:
First, it reveals the three gates of liberation, which are the gates to nirvāṇa.
Second, it opens the path to the three types of bodhi, which are the bodhi of the three Buddhas.
All remaining vehicles of the two vehicles exist in dependence upon these.
4. From "The Mind is Constant" (*cittadhruva*) onwards, there is praise for the four qualities of internal realization that are pure.

Regarding these four purities: first, purity of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*); second, purity of freedom from defilement (*vaimalyaviśuddhi*); third, purity of attaining this path (*tadadhigamamārgaviśuddhi*); and fourth, purity of arising in this realm (*tadviṣayodbhavaviśuddhi*). These are to be assigned in reverse order [to the preceding verses].

The teachings that flow from the purity of mind can give rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); thus, both the means and the results are entirely pure. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "In accordance with the purity of one's mind, there is a pure Buddha-field; in accordance with the purity of the Buddha-field, there is a pure teaching of the Dharma."
...and so on, up to: "With a pure intention regarding merit, one immediately attains the purity of this path.
That in which the Buddha dwells is the dwelling of the stainless *dharmakāya*, which is *tathatā*.

Because its nature and characteristics are divided into two, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "When enveloped by afflictions, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; when free from such envelopment, it is called the Dharmakāya.
As for the sphere of activity, it is the naturally pure, single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because this is the sphere of activity of the Buddha.
As stated in the fifth fascicle of Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*: "These four purities are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is explained:
"These are the four purities of all aspects."
According to Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahopanibandhana*, chapter nine, it says: "Purity of the basis refers to relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Purity of the two objects of focus refers to manifesting all forms through transformation."
Third, through the purity of mind, one exercises mastery over the gates of samādhi according to one's wishes; this is the mastery of entering and emerging from various meditative concentrations.
Fourth, regarding mastery of knowledge, it is the mastery of maintaining the gates of dhāraṇī according to one's wishes.
This purity of mind is the third; the mental disposition (*āśaya*) is the fourth; that which is dwelt upon is the first; and that which is practiced is the second.

Furthermore, it is explained that "mind" refers to the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*), while "mental disposition" refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*); by citing this resolute conviction, other mental factors (*caitasika*) are exemplified.
That which is dwelt upon is suchness (tathatā), and that which is practiced is the conventional realm.
Fifth, from "departing from non-proper deportment" onwards, there is praise for eternal purification;
this is because practice is itself the habituation of the breath.

Wu-xing’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Pervading all modes of conduct and dwelling means that whether begging for food, traveling between villages and cities, or walking in meditation, one remains in the tranquility of the four bodily postures."

Furthermore, his body is without fault; within the four modes of deportment, he constantly acts for the benefit of sentient beings. Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "All the Tathāgata’s movements and gestures of deportment are nothing other than Buddha-work, causing all sentient beings to be benefited."
Regarding the six years of asceticism and so forth, these praise the manifestation of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life].
Among these eight phases, for now, two—asceticism and the turning of the wheel of Dharma—are cited.

The passage beginning with "In order to deliver beings from suffering" praises the manifestation of these phases; its intent is to lead them to the further shore, using this as an illustration for the remaining phases.
Seventh, the perfection of the physical marks praises the excellence of the body's features.
Eighth, the cultivation of the six perfections praises the excellence of practice.
Ninth, the absence of error in the three types of action praises the unique virtues of the three karmas.
Citing three examples to represent the rest:

the ten sections from "Possessing All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) downward praise the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). The first part provides a general heading; the section beginning with "All that is proclaimed" (*yad uktam*) provides a detailed explanation.
In the detailed explanation, the first part concerns benefiting others; the section beginning with "among the Śākyas" concerns self-benefit.
In terms of actual realization, all births are for the sake of benefiting others, but they are described as self-benefit from the perspective of their outward appearance.
Sūtra: "I now praise a small portion of the Tathāgata’s merits according to my capacity, like a mosquito drinking from the waters of the great ocean.
This concludes the abbreviated section.
Sūtra: “By this merit, may it extensively reach all sentient beings, so that they forever leave birth and death behind and accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
This concludes the making of the vow.
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Goddess of Great Eloquence, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

You have long practiced and cultivated, possessing great eloquence; now you further offer extensive praise to me. May you swiftly realize the unsurpassed Dharma-gate, with your physical marks and signs perfectly radiant, bringing universal benefit to all.”
The following is the praise and seal.
Within the praise, the first part is a general praise; from "You have long practiced and cultivated" onwards is the specific praise.
Within the specific praise, the first part praises the cause, because through long practice and cultivation, eloquence has been fully perfected.
Previously there was praise for the fruit; now, furthermore, there is praise.
"May you quickly realize" and below are the seals that issue forth vows.
Chapter 31: Entrustment (6). The Chapter on Entrustment, the thirty-first, is analyzed according to two sections.

Regarding the purpose of this discourse: from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" onwards clarifies the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) section, which consists of three parts. Since the preceding section has already instructed [the assembly] to practice and propagate [the teaching], and the multitude, having heard what was taught, have given rise to joy and praise, it is now appropriate for the third time to entrust [the teaching], so that it may be further protected and transmitted to future generations. Therefore, this chapter arises following the previous one.
Regarding the explanation of the terms: "fu" (付) means to bestow, and "chu" (嘱) means to entrust.
Because the Dharma is entrusted to them and they are charged with its protection and maintenance so that it may circulate through the final age, it is called "entrustment" (fuzhu).
Sūtra: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas, humans, devas, and all others, saying:

"You should know that throughout immeasurable and incalculable great kalpas, I diligently practiced asceticism and attained the profound Dharma—the true cause of Bodhi—which I have already expounded for you."

The text of the lower grade is divided into four parts: first, the Buddha’s exhortation to protect and uphold [the teaching]; second, from "At that time, among the assembly... onwards, the multitude hears the vow and offers protection; third, from "At that time, the World-Honored One... onwards, the Buddha again praises and exhorts them; fourth, from "At that time, immeasurable... onwards, they rejoice upon hearing the instruction and put it into practice.
The first part has two sections;
the first is a general address to the great assembly, concluding what was previously taught.

The Sūtra says: "Who among you is able to rouse a courageous mind and reverently protect this Dharma-gate so that, after my parinirvāṇa, it may be widely proclaimed and disseminated, enabling the True Dharma to abide long in the world?"
He then universally exhorted the great assembly to protect and uphold it.
At that time, within the assembly, there were sixty koṭis of great bodhisattvas and sixty koṭis of the great multitude of devas, who with one voice spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

We all possess a heart of joy and delight; regarding the profound and subtle Dharma—the true cause of Bodhi—attained by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through arduous ascetic practices over immeasurable great kalpas, we shall reverently protect and uphold it, not sparing even our own bodies or lives. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall widely proclaim and disseminate this Dharma-gate, ensuring that the True Dharma remains long in the world.
Regarding the second assembly below, there are two parts concerning the hearing of the vow and its protection:
first, the general; second, the specific, beginning with "At that time, the great bodhisattvas... and so forth.
Within the general section, there are four parts:

First, the total number of the assembly is stated; second, from "with one voice" (*ekasvareṇa*) downward, the mind of joyful aspiration is described; third, from "toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One" (*buddhe bhagavati*) downward, the vow to personally uphold [the teaching] is made; fourth, from "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" downward, the transmission for the final age is addressed concurrently.
Sūtra: At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke these verses (gāthā) before the Buddha.
[The following section] consists of eleven distinct parts;
this is the first, the Bodhisattva’s vow of protection, which has two sub-sections.
First, the prologue by the sūtra compiler.
The Sūtra states: “The World-Honored One speaks words of truth and abides in the true Dharma; because of that truth, he protects and upholds this sūtra.”
Great compassion serves as their armor, and they abide securely in great loving-kindness; by the power of that compassion and kindness, they uphold this sutra.
With the provisions of merit perfected and the provisions of wisdom brought forth, through the fulfillment of these provisions, they uphold this sutra.
Having subdued all Māras and destroyed all heterodox doctrines, and having severed all evil views, they shall protect and uphold this sutra.
The World Protectors, along with Śakra and Brahmā, down to the Asuras, Nāgas, spirits, Yakṣas, and others, shall protect and uphold this sutra.
Those who have long dwelt upon this earth and in the void, because they uphold the Buddha’s teachings, shall protect and maintain this sutra.
Those who are conjoined with the four Brahma-abodes and adorned by the four Noble Truths, because they have subdued the four Māras, shall protect and maintain this sutra.
"Space becomes solid matter, and solid matter becomes space; protected and sustained by all Buddhas, nothing can shake or move it.
Below this, the vows for protection are set forth in eight verses, divided into two parts:
the first four verses express the vow to protect out of seeing the benefits.

Within this, one verse [expresses] the vow because of knowing that the Buddha’s words are true; the next verse, because of knowing the Buddha’s great compassion; the next verse, because of knowing he is endowed with the provisions; the next verse, because of knowing he is able to extinguish hindrances; and the final four verses express sympathetic joy upon seeing others being protected.
Within this, the first verse shows the protection of the eight classes of deities, including Brahmā and Śakra;
the next verse shows the protection of the deities of the earth, space, and so forth;

the following two verses show the Buddha’s own protection: the first of these praises the Buddha’s virtues for being fully equipped to uphold this sutra, while the second demonstrates the certainty of that protection.
This view holds that because the Buddha, Brahmā, Śakra, and all others protect [this teaching], give rise to deep sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), and thus vow to protect it themselves.
Question:
If one sees that Brahmā, Śakra, and others protect this sutra and give rise to sympathetic joy, why is it stated in the subsequent text that Brahmā, Śakra, and others vow to protect it?
Answer: It is stated in the "Chapter on the Protection of the Four Heavenly Kings" and the "Chapter on the Protection of Yakṣas and Others," and thus one gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:

One immediately sees that within the general vow for protection described in the preceding prose section, there are sixty *koṭi* of great assemblies of devas who respectfully provide protection; since these include Brahmā, Śakra, and others, seeing them is without fault.

Sūtra: At that time, when the Four Great Heavenly Kings heard the Buddha speak of this protection and maintenance of the sublime Dharma, each gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) and a resolve to protect the True Dharma.
This section on the protection and maintenance by the Four Kings has two parts:
first, the arising of delight upon hearing the teaching; second, from "with one mind and in unison" onwards, their collective proclamation of protection with a shared resolve.
This is the first [point].
Question:

It was previously stated that these bodhisattvas protect and uphold [the Dharma]; how can it now be said that upon hearing the Buddha preach this sublime Dharma of protection and upholding, each gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and resolves to protect the True Dharma?
Answer: Because they heard the previous Buddha’s exhortation to protect and uphold the sublime Dharma, it is said that "they heard the teaching.
At one time, they spoke these verses with one voice:
“I shall now, with a single mind, protect this sutra, as well as its male and female practitioners and their retinues, so that it may be widely circulated.
If there are those who uphold this sutra, who can create the cause for Bodhi, I shall constantly protect and serve them from the four directions.”
The following is the explanation of the protection (*rakṣā*) according to the shared intention. First is the introduction by the sūtra-master; next is the explanation of the protection.
Within the protection, there are two verses:
The first verse protects the Dharma; the latter verse protects the person.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, joined his palms in reverent salutation and spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas have realized this Dharma; desiring to repay their debt of gratitude, they appear in the world to expound this sūtra for the benefit of the assembly of Bodhisattvas."
"Regarding those Buddhas, I shall repay their kindness by constantly making offerings, protecting and upholding such sutras as well as those who uphold these sutras.
This concludes the third section on protection; first, the person capable of providing protection is designated;
then, from "speaking the gāthās" onwards, the act of protection and upholding is explained in two verses:
The first verse describes the reasons for protecting [the Dharma], while the latter verse sets forth the protection of the Dharma itself.
In the past, the Buddha attained Bodhi upon hearing the Dharma; to repay this debt of gratitude to the sutras, he taught it to the Bodhisattvas.
Having now heard this, I too should repay his kindness by receiving, upholding, and disseminating it.
At that time, the Devaputra of Tuṣita joined his palms in reverence and spoke these verses:
“If there be anyone who can uphold such a sūtra as this spoken by the Buddha, they shall abide in the stage of Bodhi and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.”
“World-Honored One, I am filled with joy; having relinquished my superior celestial retribution, I shall dwell on Jambudvīpa and proclaim this sutra.
This concludes the fourth section, which first identifies the person capable of protection.
From “speaking in verse” (*gāthā*) onwards, it explains the act of upholding, consisting of two stanzas:
The first verse describes the benefits, and the final verse sets forth the protection of the Dharma.
The Sūtra says: At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, joined his palms in reverent salutation and spoke these verses:
"All meditative concentrations and immeasurables, All vehicles and liberations— These all emerge from this sūtra; Therefore, I shall expound this sūtra."
"Wherever this sutra is preached, I shall renounce the bliss of Brahmā; for the sake of hearing such a sutra, I shall also always provide protection.
This concludes the fifth section; the text is identical to the preceding.
Sūtra. At that time, the son of Māra named Śreṣṭhidatta joined his palms in reverence and spoke these verses:
“If there are those who receive and uphold this sūtra, which accords with the true Dharma, they will not follow the conduct of Māra and will purify the evil karma of Māra.”
"We, too, shall diligently protect this sutra; with great resolve for vigor, we shall cause it to circulate widely wherever we go.
The sixth section below is identical to the preceding one.
Sūtra: At that time, the Māra King joined his palms in reverent salutation and spoke these verses:
"If there be those who uphold this sūtra and are able to subdue all afflictions, may I protect such beings as these and cause them to dwell in peace and happiness."
"If anyone shall preach this sutra, no māras shall find an opportunity against them; by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall protect them.
At that time, the Devaputra Mañjuśrī also spoke a verse before the Buddha, saying:
"The wondrous Bodhi of all Buddhas is expounded within this sutra; whoever upholds this sutra is making an offering to the Tathāgata."
"I shall uphold this sutra and preach it for ten million devas; to those who listen with reverence, I shall urge them toward the state of Bodhi.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva joined his palms in reverent salutation and spoke these verses:
"If one sees someone dwelling in Bodhi, I shall act as their uninvited friend; even at the cost of my own body and life, I shall protect this King of Sutras."
"Having heard such a Dharma as this, I shall go to the Tuṣita Heaven; through the protection of the World-Honored One, I shall expound it extensively for the sake of humans and devas.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa joined his palms in reverence and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha, regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle, said that my wisdom is meager; yet now, according to my own strength, I shall protect and uphold such a sutra as this."
"If there be anyone who upholds this sutra, I shall receive them into my care; I will grant them the power of eloquence and always follow them, praising them as 'Excellent!
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke in verse:
"I have personally heard from the Buddha immeasurable collections of scriptures, yet never before have I heard such a king among profound and wondrous Dharmas."
"Now that I have heard this sutra and received it personally before the Buddha, those who delight in Bodhi should proclaim and disseminate it widely.
The seventh section below is also the same as the preceding one.

Within the section on protecting the Dharma, the first verse praises those who uphold the sutra, while the latter verse praises those who preach the sutra; because one protects the person, one thereby also protects the Dharma.
First, each describes the capacity [of the protectors], and only afterwards does it set forth the protection itself.
The eighth, "The Sublime Mañjuśrī," has a textual structure identical to the preceding one.
Within the section on "Protecting the Dharma" (Dharmapāla), the first part describes the benefits of the sūtra, while the latter clarifies the protection of the Dharma.
This teaching on protecting the Dharma was spoken for the sake of the Kumbhāṇḍa gods; those who listen with reverence are the protectors of the Dharma.
The ninth verse concerning the Compassionate Honored One is also identical to the preceding one.
Within the section on protecting the Dharma, the first verse protects persons and the latter verse protects the Dharma.
The tenth verse is also identical to the preceding one.
Among the verses defending the Dharma (*dharmapāla*), the first verse defends the Dharma and the last verse defends the person.
The eleventh [verse] is also the same as the preceding one.
Among the verses defending the Dharma, the first verse is a praise and the last verse is a defense.
Those who delight in Bodhi protect people, and for the sake of widely proclaiming and disseminating it, they protect the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the great assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas had each resolved their minds to circulate and protect this sutra, and he exhorted the bodhisattvas to extensively benefit all sentient beings.
He praised them, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to reverently propagate such a subtle and wondrous King of Sutras, even to the point of ensuring it does not perish after my parinirvāṇa, is the true cause for unsurpassed bodhi; the merit thereby obtained could not be fully described even in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other sons and daughters of good family who make offerings, show reverence, transcribe, circulate, and explain it to others, the merit they obtain shall likewise be thus.
"Therefore, you all should diligently practice.
This concludes the third major section of the lower grade, in which the Buddha again praises and exhorts.
The text is divided into three parts:
First is the praise; next, from "You all" onwards, is the seal of approval; and from "If there be bhikṣus" onwards, is the exhortation.
Within the exhortation, the first part exhorts the fourfold assembly:
if one can protect the Dharma, the merit obtained shall be equal to that mentioned previously.

Practicing these ten modes of Dharma practice is entirely the protection of the Dharma; from among these ten, four are briefly enumerated: first, making offerings; second, copying [the scriptures]; third, circulating them, which means giving them to others; and fourth, explaining them, which means elucidating and expounding them.
Listening, reading, receiving and upholding, reciting, reflecting, and practicing are all embraced by respect; it is because of respect for the Dharma that one listens and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Therefore" concludes by exhorting the great assembly.

The Sūtra says: At that time, the immeasurable, boundless great assembly, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Upon hearing the teaching, one joyfully practices it.
As stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*: "There are three meanings for which one rejoices.
First, the speaker is pure, because they have attained mastery over all dharmas; this implies that through non-attachment, they have attained mastery in preaching."
Second is the purity of the Dharma taught, because one realizes the pure essence of phenomena as they truly are.
Third is the purity of attaining the fruit based on the Dharma taught, because one attains the sublime realm.
This meaning is based on the fact that by relying on what has been taught, one enters into the truth and attains nirvana;
thus, it is said that the teaching accords with the principle, and the fruit corresponds to the cause.

Therefore, one who obtains a single phrase rejoices as if hearing the Way at dawn and dying that very evening; likewise, one who beholds the entire chapter accumulates merit and proceeds to practice and study.
The most wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas, Flowing forth from great compassion, For the benefit of all living beings, Is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.

Now, relying upon the protection of the assembly, I shall praise this sutra according to my ability; May I obtain blessings that benefit both myself and others, And together we achieve supreme enlightenment.

The Commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Fascicle Six, concludes. Carved for printing by Jō on the day of Koku, the month of Frost, in the year Hōei 3 (1706). Printed at Shōrin, located in the Seifū-bō ward of Anjō, Hieizan. Held in the collection of Jii Jōkan.
